a: Welcome to Penpoint, where your manuscript and your worldbuilding live side by side. Write your prose, track your characters, map your relationships, and organize your entire story in one app. Your book stays on your own computer, with optional encrypted backup and multi-computer writing through Penpoint Cloud. This page is your starting point: follow the path below, or jump straight to whatever you're curious about.

New to Penpoint? These six steps take you from an empty screen to a book you're actively writing. Each links to a full guide. Creating Your First Book: Make your first book and pick a template that fits your genre. This is step one. Building Your World: Meet the worldbuilding side: characters, locations, items, chapters, arcs, and the views that tie them together. Characters: Add your cast, then your Locations and Items. Add as much or as little detail as you like. Manuscript Mode: Switch to the writing side (the pen icon at the top) and write your first scene. Searching & Connecting: Link things together with @Mentions, jump anywhere with Search, and add new entries on the fly. Import & Export: Bring in an existing manuscript, or send your finished work out to Word, PDF, EPUB, and more. Two more worth knowing early: Understanding Book Template Types explains what each starting template comes stocked with, and Managing Your Books covers renaming, duplicating, backing up, and organizing your books once you have a few.

Penpoint has two main modes. Manuscript Mode is your writing environment: a distraction-free editor with scenes, chapters, a sidebar that shows all your chapters and scenes so you can jump between them, and Flowstate (a timed writing mode). Worldbuilding Mode is your planning and organizing space, where you build out characters, locations, items, arcs, and everything else that makes up your story. Both modes share the same data. Chapters you create in worldbuilding appear in Manuscript Mode, and prose you write in your manuscript is reflected back in your chapter data. Any changes you make in one mode show up in the other automatically.

The navigation menu on the left is your worldbuilding home. The Worldbuilding Toolbar explains each page; Building Your World is the full section. In short, you can track your Characters, Locations, and Items, structure your Chapters, shape your plot with Arcs, and keep loose research in the Notebook. You'll also find tools for seeing the bigger picture: Relationship Map: See your entire character web as a visual map you can drag, zoom, and click. Timeline: See when every character appears across your chapters, and track key story moments as Events that link to their whole cast. Tags Overview: Tag related things, then view everything with that tag in one place.

Manuscript Mode gives you a full-featured editor built for long-form writing. Organize your prose into scenes and chapters, navigate with the chapter and scene sidebar, and save versions of your work you can return to later. Flowstate: A timed writing mode that locks completed sentences behind you, breaking the urge to endlessly revise. When the session ends, you can edit everything normally. Minipen: A slim sidebar that brings your worldbuilding into Manuscript Mode, so your characters and notes stay a glance away while you write. Chapter Scanner: Scan your prose and automatically detect the characters, locations, and items mentioned in each chapter. Import: Bring an existing manuscript from .docx, .epub, .rtf, .md, or .txt. Penpoint detects chapter boundaries automatically.

As your book grows, Searching & Connecting keeps it navigable. Press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac) to open Search from anywhere, type @ to drop an @Mentions link to any character, place, or note, and use the Quick Add Menu to create new entries without leaving what you're doing.

Planning more than one book? A Writing a Series lets several volumes share one cast and one world, while still tracking which characters and events belong to which book. You can start with a single book and convert it to a series later, and nothing is deleted when you do.

Everything you write is stored on your own computer, in a file you can copy, move, and keep. Penpoint autosaves every change automatically and picks up exactly where you left off when you reopen the app. Penpoint is a one-time purchase, it works completely offline, and no part of your book depends on an account or an internet connection. Backup & Restore: Create full book backups and restore them anytime. Import & Export: Bring work in from other formats, or send your data out to Markdown, Word, PDF, and more. Settings: Customize themes, fonts, and how Penpoint looks and feels.

A file on one computer has one weakness: it lives on one computer. Hard drives fail, laptops get stolen, and coffee finds keyboards. Penpoint Cloud is the optional answer to that, and it is built into the app rather than bolted on. Your book survives the computer: every book and every saved version is backed up as you write. Sign in on a different machine and your work comes back. Write in more than one place: a book stays in step across the computers you sign in on, so the draft on your desk and the draft on your couch are the same draft. Nobody can read it but you: your books are encrypted on your computer with a password only you hold, before anything leaves. Penpoint stores your books and cannot open them. Unlimited version history: go back to any earlier draft, not just the last few. Penpoint Cloud comes in two sizes, and you can write for years without it: nothing in this guide requires a subscription. Penpoint Cloud covers what each plan includes, how the encryption works, and how to set it up. Tip: You can return to this guide anytime by clicking the help icon (a question mark circle in the top-right corner). Every section in the left-side menu has its own articles: click any topic to learn more.

Creating your first book is the first step in organizing your writing project. A book in Penpoint represents a single story, novel, or series volume, containing all your characters, locations, chapters, and other writing elements. (Writing a series? Several volumes can live together in one series file: see Writing a Series.) Penpoint saves your work automatically as you go.

To create your first book, click the Create New Book button in the Book Library. This will open a window where you can set up your new project. This window lets you fill in a few details about your book: Book Name: Give your book a title (up to 50 characters). You can always change this later. Description: Add an optional brief description to help you remember what the book is about (up to 100 characters). Book Color: Choose a color for your book's cover in the library. This helps visually distinguish between multiple projects. Book Template: Select a starting template that determines the initial structure of your book (character traits like appearance, role, or background; location types; item categories; and more).

Templates provide ready-made setups for different types of writing projects. The Standard Template is a good starting point for most projects, offering a balanced set of character traits, location types, and item categories. See Understanding Book Template Types for a detailed comparison of all available templates. You don't need to find the "perfect" template: picking one doesn't lock you in. You can add, remove, or change any trait, location type, or category after creating your book. Templates simply give you a head start with commonly-used fields so you don't have to build everything from scratch. Tip: You can view template details by clicking "View template details" to see exactly what traits, locations, and other elements each template includes.

Once you click Create Book, Penpoint will set up your new project and show a success screen. Click Open Book to jump in. You'll land on the Characters page, where you can start adding your cast. From here, you can explore all the sections of your book using the navigation menu on the left side of the screen: Characters: Build your cast with customizable traits and relationships Items (the objects and props in your story): Track important things like weapons, letters, or artifacts Locations: Map out your world with locations within locations (e.g., a room inside a castle inside a kingdom) Chapters: Organize your story structure and assign characters Arcs: Map out your plot arcs and see them laid out visually Notebook: Jot down research, worldbuilding notes, and loose ideas Tags Viewer Page: Add labels (tags) to any character, location, or item, then view everything with that tag in one place Relationship Map: See your entire character web as a visual map Timeline: See when every character appears across your chapters Compendium: An alphabetical reference of everything in your book (called the Compendium) Tip: When you're ready to start writing prose, switch to Manuscript Mode using the "Manuscript" button (with a pen icon) at the top of the navigation menu.

When you click "Create New Book," you'll see several ready-made templates to choose from. Each template is designed for different types of writing projects, providing specialized custom traits (lists you choose from that you can add to every character, like Role or Alignment), item categories (the types you can assign to items, like Weapons or Clothing), location types, and tags (labels you can attach to characters, locations, or chapters). Templates give you a head start by filling in your book with commonly-used fields and structures. You can fully customize everything after creating your book, so no template choice is permanent. Want to reuse a single note, like a character questionnaire, rather than a whole book's setup? See Note Templates. Tip: All templates can be customized after creation. You can add, remove, or modify traits, item categories, location types, tags, and character sections to fit your specific needs. Note: Trait dropdowns let you pick more than one option when it fits: a character's Demeanor might be both Confident and Charming, not just one. Choose as many, or as few, as you like.
The Standard Template provides a comprehensive, balanced starting point suitable for most novels, series, and creative writing projects.

2 custom traits: Role (Protagonist, Antagonist, Major, Minor, Love Interest, Mentor, Narrator, Foil, Other) and Demeanor (Friendly, Reserved, Confident, Mysterious, and more) 7 item categories: Personal Items, Documents, Clothing & Accessories, Vehicles, Technology, Keepsakes & Mementos, and Miscellaneous 10 location types: City, Town, Village, Building, Room, Landmark, Nature, Region, Country, and Other 9 thematic tags: POV Character, Conflict, Romance, Family, Backstory, Secret, Turning Point, Comic Relief, and Tragic 14 character sections (the individual sections on a character's page, like Name, Age, or Bio): Name, Age, Role, Demeanor, Appearance, Bio, and Notes, plus the standard Character Arc, Events, Chapters, Relationships, Locations, Items, and Tags
General fiction, contemporary novels, literary fiction, or any project that doesn't require genre-specific elements. If you're unsure which template to choose, Standard is a safe, flexible choice.
The Empty Template provides a completely blank slate with only the bare essentials, giving you maximum customization freedom.

0 custom traits: No predefined character traits: build your own from scratch 0 item categories: Add exactly the categories your story needs 0 location types: Define your own from scratch 0 tags: No predefined tags: create exactly what you need 1 character section: Only the name & importance field

Writers who want complete control over their book's structure, experimental projects, or unique genres that don't fit standard categories. This template requires the most manual setup but offers unlimited flexibility.
The Minimal Template provides quick-start essentials (name, appearance, details, relationships, and tags) so you can begin writing immediately without complex setup.

0 custom traits: No trait fields to manage 3 item categories: Personal Items, Documents, and Miscellaneous 6 location types: City, Town, Building, Room, Outdoors / Nature, and Other 3 essential tags: Main Cast, Supporting, and Mentioned 8 character sections: Name & importance, appearance, background, character arc, chapters, relationships, locations, and tags
Writers who prefer simplicity over detailed tracking, short stories, writers who prefer to dive in without a detailed outline, or projects where you'll primarily use the free-form background field.
The Fantasy Template is built for fantasy novelists, with room for magic systems, peoples, and worlds, flexible enough for any setting you can imagine.

2 custom traits: Role and Demeanor 10 fantasy item categories: Weapons & Armor, Magical Objects, Documents & Books, Clothing & Accessories, Symbols & Tokens, Creatures & Companions, Tools & Equipment, Substances, Treasure & Currency, and Miscellaneous 14 fantasy location types: Kingdom, City, Village, Castle, Tower, Temple, Stronghold, Underground, Port / Harbor, Ruins, Forest, Mountain, Realm, and Other 11 thematic tags: POV Character, Magical, Royal, Prophecy, Cursed, Ancient, Exile, Oath-Bound, Alive, Dead, and Missing 17 character sections: Free-text Species / People and Abilities / Powers, plus Backstory and Secrets, and the standard Bio, Character Arc, Chapters, Relationships, Locations, Items, and Tags

Epic fantasy, sword & sorcery, urban fantasy, high fantasy, or any world-building project with magic systems, diverse peoples, and layered lore. The Species / People and Abilities / Powers fields are free-form, so you can describe your world in your own words rather than fitting it into a fixed list.
The Sci-Fi Template is built for science fiction with space for your own species, factions, and technology, plus numeric tools for tech levels and clearance.

2 custom traits: Role and Demeanor 10 sci-fi item categories: Weapons & Armor, Technology & Devices, Tools & Equipment, Medical Supplies, Data & Storage, Clothing & Accessories, Vehicles & Ships, Augmentations, Credits & Currency, and Miscellaneous 10 futuristic location types: Planet, Space Station, Starship, City, Colony, Facility, Sector, Star System, Nebula / Anomaly, and Other 12 thematic tags: POV Character, Military, Scientific, Alien, Exploration, Augmented, AI / Synthetic, Classified, Colonial, Alive, Dead, and Missing 19 character sections: Free-text Species / Origin and Affiliation, numeric Tech Level and Clearance Level, plus Background and Mission Log, and the standard Bio, Character Arc, Relationships, Locations, Items, and Tags

Space opera, cyberpunk, hard sci-fi, dystopian futures, first contact stories, or any science fiction project dealing with advanced technology, alien species, or interstellar settings. The numeric Tech Level and Clearance Level fields are handy for tracking capability and access across a large cast.

The D&D 5e Template is built for Dungeons & Dragons 5th Edition campaigns with complete stat blocks (a set of number fields for things like Strength or Hit Points), Hit Points (HP) tracking, Armor Class (AC), ability scores, and session notes.

5 custom traits: Race, Class, Alignment, Background, and Demeanor 10 item categories: Weapons, Armor & Shields, Magic Items, Potions & Consumables, Scrolls & Books, Tools & Kits, Adventuring Gear, Treasure & Currency, Quest Items, and Miscellaneous 12 adventure location types: Dungeon, Tavern, City, Town, Wilderness, Castle / Fortress, Temple / Shrine, Kingdom, Lair, Ruins, Plane of Existence, and Other 13 gameplay tags: Playable, NPC, Boss, Friendly, Hostile, Commerce, Quest, Companion, Leadership, Monstrous, Recurring, Alive, and Dead 29 character sections: A full D&D stat block (Level, Challenge Rating, Hit Points / Max HP, Armor Class, Speed, and all six ability scores), plus Faction, Personality & Traits, and character & session notes, alongside the standard Character Arc, Relationships, Locations, Items, and Tags

Dungeons & Dragons campaigns, tabletop RPG world-building, game master prep, NPC tracking for campaigns, or fantasy stories with detailed mechanical character progression. Game masters can use this to track party members, NPCs, and monsters with complete stat blocks. Tip: The session notes section is perfect for recording what happened during your last gaming session, tracking character development across gameplay, or noting important plot hooks for future sessions.
The Historical / Non-fiction Template is designed for historical fiction and non-fiction with social class hierarchy, biographical data, and source documentation.

5 custom traits: Social Class, Historical Basis, Status, Religion, and Demeanor 12 period-specific item categories: Documents & Letters, Personal Effects, Clothing & Accessories, Historical Artifacts, Books & Manuscripts, Art & Paintings, Maps & Charts, Currency & Coins, Religious Items, Tools & Equipment, Weapons, and Miscellaneous 16 historical location types: City, Town / Village, Palace, Estate, Church / Temple, University, Theater, Market, Harbor / Port, Prison, Building, Landmark, Battlefield, Farm, Region, and Country 11 research tags: Factual, Fictional, POV Character, Leadership, Artistic, Military, Civilian, Political, Religious, Revolutionary, and Tragic 25 character sections: Birth Name / Historical Name, Born, Died, Occupation, Nationality, Education, Biography, Historical Context, Role in Events, and a Primary Source ID (archive reference), plus the standard Character Arc, Relationships, Locations, Items, and Tags

Historical fiction, biographical novels, historical non-fiction, period dramas, alternative history, or research-heavy projects requiring source documentation. The Primary Source ID field helps track archival references, and the Historical Basis trait distinguishes between documented historical figures and fictionalized characters. Note: The Born and Died fields accept free-form text, allowing you to enter specific dates like "March 15, 1850, London, England" or approximate dates like "circa 1420" for characters with uncertain historical records.
The Horror Template is crafted for horror fiction and psychological thrillers with psychological profiles, dark secrets, and atmospheric settings, focused on dread, not monsters.

3 custom traits: Role (Protagonist, Antagonist, Victim, Survivor, Investigator, and more), Psychological Profile (Stable, Anxious, Paranoid, Obsessive, Traumatized, and more), and Demeanor 10 horror item categories: Keys & Locks, Documents & Letters, Potions & Substances, Occult Objects, Light Sources, Weapons, Protective Items, Medical Supplies, Evidence & Records, and Miscellaneous 10 atmospheric location types: House, Building, Room, Town, Forest, Cemetery, Underground, Ruins, Wilderness, and Other 14 thematic tags: Survivor, Victim, Threat, Cursed, Innocent, Corrupted, Supernatural, Mysterious, Possessed, Missing, Dead, Investigator, Cult, and Red Herring 18 character sections: Alias / Known As, Deepest Fear, and What They're Hiding, plus the standard Appearance, Bio, Character Arc, Relationships, Locations, Items, and Tags

Horror fiction, psychological thrillers, gothic novels, supernatural mysteries, or any story built around fear and suspense. The Psychological Profile trait, plus the Deepest Fear and What They're Hiding fields, help you track each character's mental state and the secrets driving the dread. Tip: The Red Herring tag is great for marking characters who seem suspicious but are ultimately innocent, perfect for mystery-horror plots where misdirection is key.
The Romance Template is designed for romance writers, with emotional wound tracking, attachment styles, and relationship-centered character building.

3 custom traits: Role (Love Interest, Rival, Ex, and more), Attachment Style (Secure, Anxious, Avoidant, Disorganized), and Demeanor 8 item categories: Personal Items, Letters & Messages, Clothing & Accessories, Gifts & Tokens, Photographs & Mementos, Technology, Keepsakes, and Miscellaneous 12 location types: Home / Apartment, Office / Workplace, Restaurant / Cafe, Bar / Club, Park / Outdoors, Hotel, School / University, Shop / Store, Neighborhood, City, Travel Destination, and Other 20 relationship tags: Central Couple, Secondary Couple, Found Family, Slow Burn, Enemies to Lovers, Second Chance, Forbidden, Friends to Lovers, Fake Dating, Grumpy / Sunshine, Meet Cute, and more 18 character sections: Emotional Wound, Core Fear / False Belief, and What They Need, plus the standard Appearance, Bio, Character Arc, Relationships, Locations, Items, and Tags

Contemporary romance, romantic subplots, women's fiction, or any story where the emotional arc between characters is the heart of the book. The Emotional Wound, Core Fear, and What They Need fields help you build the internal journey behind each romance. Tip: The relationship tags (Slow Burn, Enemies to Lovers, Fake Dating, and more) double as trope labels: handy for planning beats or keeping a series consistent.

Selecting the right template depends on your project's genre, complexity, and tracking needs: Not sure? Start with Standard: it's versatile and works for most projects Want complete control? Choose Empty and build exactly what you need Want to start writing fast? Pick Minimal for quick, simple tracking Fantasy world-building? Use Fantasy for magic, peoples, and lore Sci-fi universe? Select Sci-Fi for species, factions, and tech Running a campaign? Choose D&D 5e for full stat blocks Historical accuracy or non-fiction? Pick Historical / Non-fiction for period research and source documentation Writing horror or thrillers? Use Horror for psychological profiles and dark secrets Writing romance? Use Romance for attachment styles, emotional wounds, and trope tags

Remember: templates are starting points, not limitations. After creating your book, you can modify everything: Traits: Add new custom fields, remove unused ones, or modify the options you choose from Items: Create new item categories, rename existing ones, or change icons Locations: Add specialized location types unique to your world Tags: Create unlimited thematic tags with custom colors Layout: Rearrange character sections, resize fields, or add new information types Note: Removing a trait deletes the trait definition, its options, and any values you have entered for your characters. The deletion is permanent. Make sure you no longer need the data before removing a trait. Templates simply save you time by providing genre-appropriate defaults. Your book grows and evolves as your project develops. Tip: You can always check which template you used by viewing your book's trait and item configurations in the Settings page (the gear icon in the sidebar). From there, you can modify anything to better fit your evolving needs.

After creating your books in Penpoint, you have several tools available to manage them. This section covers editing book details, duplicating books, writing a series, backing up your data, and deleting books you no longer need.

Every book in your library has a three-dot menu (⋮) in the upper-right corner of its book card (the rectangle showing your book's name and color in the library). Click it to see the following options: Edit: Update your book's name, description, or color Duplicate: Create a copy of a book, picking what to copy over, perfect for alternate versions or template reuse Convert to Series…: Turn a standalone book into Book 1 of a series, so every volume shares the same characters, locations, and items. See Converting a Book to a Series Export Book: Save your entire book as a single .penpoint file, handy for backups or for sharing it with someone else. See Exporting a Book Restore from Backup...: View backup history and restore a previous version of your book Delete: Penpoint will ask you to confirm by typing your book's name before anything is removed. See Deleting a Book below for details. Tip: If you have a secondary backup location set up in Settings, those external backups are not affected by deletion. Even after deleting a book, your secondary backups remain safe in that folder. Tip: To bring a book IN from a .penpoint file (one you exported, or that someone shared with you), double-click the file or use Import Book… from the top-right menu on the Your Books screen. See Importing a Book for the full walkthrough.

To access these options, go to the Book Library (this is the screen you see when you first open Penpoint, or you can get back to it by clicking the back arrow at the bottom of the left-hand menu). Find the book you want to manage and click the three-dot menu (⋮) in the corner of its card.

Editing Book Details: Change your book's name, description, and color Duplicating Books: Create copies for alternate versions or experiments Converting a Book to a Series: Keep several Books, and one shared cast, together in a single series file Exporting a Book: Save a whole book as a .penpoint file to move or share it Importing a Book: Open a .penpoint file as its own book in your library Deleting Books: Remove books you no longer need (with confirmation) Backup & Restore: Create and manage book backups

As your project evolves, you may want to update your book's name, description, or visual appearance. Penpoint makes it easy to edit these details at any time without affecting your characters, chapters, or other content.

To edit your book's details, go to the book library (this is the screen you see when you first open Penpoint, or you can get back to it by clicking the back arrow at the bottom of the menu on the left side of the screen). Find the book you want to change, click the three-dot menu (⋮) on your book's card, then select Edit. The Edit Book Details window will open, with a live Preview of your book's card beside the settings so you can see each change as you make it. Tip: Changing a book's name, description, color, texture, or cover does not affect any of your content: all characters, chapters, locations, and other data stay exactly as they were.

Book Name: Change your book's title (up to 50 characters). This is the name you'll see everywhere in the app. Description: Update or add an optional description (up to 100 characters). Use this to remind yourself what the book is about at a glance. Book Color: Change the color of your book's cover in the library. Click the colored square to open a palette of colors and choose a new one. This helps visually tell multiple projects apart at a glance. Texture: Add a subtle surface to the cover: Grain, Linen, Canvas, Leather, Parchment, Herringbone, or Crosshatch. Choose None for a plain cover. Cover Image: Upload your own picture (up to 10 MB) to use as the cover. After you choose a file, a Crop Cover Image window lets you frame it. Click the thumbnail later to swap the picture, or click Remove cover to go back to a color. While a cover image is set, Book Color and Texture are hidden, and a Show title & description checkbox appears; uncheck it if your picture already includes the title.

After making your edits, click Save Changes to apply them. The Save Changes button only becomes clickable once you've actually changed something, so there's no risk of saving by accident. Your book will immediately reflect the new name, description, color, texture, and cover in the book library.

If you change your mind and want to leave without saving, click Cancel, click the X in the top-right corner, or press Escape on your keyboard. Any changes you made will be discarded, including a cover you uploaded or removed.

Here are some situations where editing book details is helpful: Series Organization: rather than numbering standalone books ("Vol. 1", "Vol. 2"), keep the volumes together in one series file. See Writing a Series Visual Distinction: Assign unique colors, textures, or covers to related books for quick identification Project Evolution: Update the name or description as your story's focus changes during development Fixing Typos: Correct mistakes in the original book name or description

When creating alternate versions of your story, you often want to reuse characters, locations, and other elements from an existing book. Penpoint's duplication feature lets you create a copy of a book, choosing which parts to copy, so you don't have to manually recreate common elements. The original book is never changed — duplication creates an entirely separate copy.

To duplicate a book, navigate to the book library and locate the book you want to copy. Click the three-dot menu (⋮) on the book's card in the library, then select Duplicate. The Duplicate Book window will appear, allowing you to name the new book and choose which content to include in the copy.

The first field asks for a name for the duplicated book. By default, Penpoint suggests adding " - The Sequel" to the original book's name, but you can change this to anything you like (up to 50 characters). Tip: Writing a series? Don't duplicate: Converting a Book to a Series keeps one shared cast across every volume instead of separate copies.

The duplication window provides checkboxes for different types of content. All checkboxes are checked by default, so everything will be copied unless you uncheck something. You can choose which elements to include in the new book: Characters: All characters with their profile details, traits, tags, relationships, and importance levels Items: All items and all their details Chapters: All chapters, where each chapter sits on the timeline, and their details Manuscript: All scenes, scene drafts (saved copies of a scene from before you made changes), and manuscript versions (frozen snapshots of your full manuscript). This option requires Chapters to be included, since scenes belong to chapters. Locations: All locations, including locations within locations, their types, and all their details Notes: All notebook entries, including their text, tags, colors, and pinned notes (notes you've pinned to the top) Arcs: Story Arcs and Character Arcs can be included together or separately, letting you carry over plot structure without character arcs (or vice versa). Includes your story arcs and their plot points, along with character arc details. Traits: All your custom traits and the choices you set up for them Tags: All tag definitions and colors Types (Location & Item Types): All item types and location types
Some information is intentionally not included in duplicates to prevent confusion: Your Last Position: The new book opens on the Characters page, rather than wherever you left off in the original

After entering a name and selecting which content to include, click Duplicate Book to create the copy. The duplicate is completely independent from the original; changes in one book won't affect the other. The new book will appear in your book library. Click Open Book to jump into the duplicate and continue your story.

Here are some situations where duplicating books is particularly useful: Series Writing: don't duplicate for a series; convert your book with Converting a Book to a Series so characters are shared between volumes, not copied Alternate Versions: Explore "what if" scenarios by duplicating a book and making different character or plot choices Template Reuse: Create a "template book" with your standard traits and item types, then duplicate it for each new project Backup Before Major Changes: Duplicate a book before making large structural changes, giving you a restore point if needed

When you no longer need a book, Penpoint lets you permanently delete it and all its characters, chapters, notes, and everything else in the book. Penpoint includes safeguards to prevent accidental deletion. Note: Before deleting, make sure you have a backup — you can create one using Backup & Restore. There is no way to undo a book deletion, and all of its data is permanently removed.

To delete a book, go to the book library and find the book you want to remove. Right-click the book's card (or Ctrl+click on Mac), or click the three-dot menu icon in the upper-right corner of the card, then select Delete. A warning window will appear, showing what you're about to delete and asking you to confirm before going ahead.

The delete window shows a clear warning with the book's name and explains what will happen. It emphasizes that this action cannot be undone and that all data will be permanently removed. Note: Deleting a book also removes all of its internal backups within Penpoint. However, if you've set up a secondary backup folder (in Settings), those backup copies are safe and can be used to restore the book later.

When you delete a book, everything in it is permanently removed: All Characters: Character profiles, character details, notes, and tags All Chapters & Manuscript: Chapter definitions, scenes, scene drafts (copies of a scene you saved before making changes), and saved versions (snapshots of your full manuscript at a point in time) All Locations: Individual locations, including any locations inside other locations All Items: Individual items and their details All Relationships: Character relationship data All Notes: Notebook entries All Arcs: Story arcs and character arcs All Tags & Custom Labels: Any custom categories or labels you created for characters, items, or locations All Internal Backups: Every backup within Penpoint for this book is also removed, but any backup copies saved to a separate folder on your computer are safe Book Settings: Your book's settings Tip: If you have a secondary backup location (a separate folder where Penpoint saves extra copies, if you've set one up in Settings), those backup copies are not deleted. You can find them in that folder if you need to restore the book later.

To prevent accidental deletion, Penpoint asks you to type the book's exact name in the confirmation text box. This makes sure you know which book you're deleting and gives you a moment to reconsider. The Delete Book button stays grayed out until you type the book's name exactly as shown in the prompt, matching capital and lowercase letters. You can try as many times as you need; the button simply stays grayed out until the name matches. Tip: If you can't remember the exact spelling or capitalization, cancel the window and check the book's name in the library before trying again.

Once you confirm the deletion, Penpoint removes the book and all its data from your system. A confirmation message will appear letting you know the book has been deleted. Click Close to return to the book library. If the deleted book was currently open, Penpoint will close it and return you to the library view.

Before deleting a book, consider these alternatives: Save a Backup Copy: Create a backup and store it safely in case you need the data later Keep for Reference: Leave the book in your library for future reference, even if you're not actively working on it Duplicate First: If you want to restructure heavily, duplicate the book first so you have the original as a fallback. You can do this from the same three-dot menu on the book's card in the library. Note: For more on duplicating, see Duplicating Books.

Deletion is appropriate when: You've saved a backup copy and verified it can be restored The book was a test or experiment you no longer need You're certain you won't need any of the data in the future You want to free up space (though Penpoint books are typically small) Tip: If you're unsure whether to delete a book, save a backup copy first. Backups are small and can save you from regret later.

A .penpoint file is a complete copy of an entire book: every character, location, item, chapter, note, and setting. You import one to open a book a friend shared with you, move a book between your own computers, or bring back a copy you exported earlier. Note: This is different from importing worldbuilding data or a manuscript, which bring content into a book you already have. Importing a book file brings in a whole book of its own.

Double-click the file: Your computer recognizes .penpoint files, so double-clicking one opens it straight into Penpoint. If Penpoint is already open, it brings you back to your library and starts the import there. Import Book…: From the Your Books screen, click the menu in the top-right corner (or right-click an empty area) and choose Import Book…, then pick your file.

Penpoint looks at the file and does the right thing automatically: A book you don't have yet: It's simply added to your library and opened, ready to write. A book you already have: Penpoint recognizes it's the same book and asks what you'd like to do: Replace your current copy with the file's version, or Keep Both as separate books. It also tells you which version is newer, based on when each was last saved, so you can choose with confidence. A file from a newer version of Penpoint: If the book was saved with a newer version of Penpoint than you have installed, you'll get a friendly heads-up to update first, instead of a confusing error.

Importing never overwrites anything without asking, and it can always be undone: Replace saves a backup first: Choosing Replace tucks away a copy of your current book before bringing in the file's version, so you can undo it. Keep Both leaves everything alone: The file comes in as a brand-new, separate book, and your existing copy is untouched. Other books are never affected: An import only ever touches the one book in the file. Tip: To undo a Replace, open your book's backup history and restore the safety backup from the top of the list. See Backup & Restore.

Because Penpoint recognizes the same book across files, you can keep a book in step on two computers without any special setup: Finish a writing session and use Export Book to save a .penpoint file, for example into a Dropbox or OneDrive folder. On your other computer, double-click that file. Penpoint sees it's the same book, tells you it's the newer one, and offers to Replace your older copy. Tip: Keep your books stored locally rather than inside a cloud folder, and move them around with Export Book and import instead. Live book files don't play well with cloud sync, but exported .penpoint files are perfectly safe to keep in one.
Making a Book File to Share

To create a .penpoint file to import elsewhere or send to someone, use the Export Book option from a book's menu on the Your Books screen, or from the Saved indicator while a book is open. See Exporting a Book for the full walkthrough.

Exporting a book saves the whole thing as a single .penpoint file: every character, location, item, chapter, note, picture, and setting, plus your manuscript. You export one to move a book to another computer, send it to someone else who writes in Penpoint, or keep a copy somewhere safe. Note: This is not a manuscript export. A .penpoint file is only readable by Penpoint. To save your prose as Word, PDF, or Markdown, use the manuscript and worldbuilding exports instead.

Note: Export Book and Export Backup are the same thing under two names: the library calls it one, the Saved indicator and Settings call it the other. Both produce an identical .penpoint file. From the Book Library, right-click any book (or Ctrl+click on Mac), or click the three-dot menu (⋮ icon shown) in the corner of its card, and choose Export Book. Penpoint explains what the file is, then asks where to save it. When it's done, it shows you the exact location, with a button to open that folder. You can also export the book you're currently writing in, without going back to the library: click the small Saved text (with a checkmark) near the top of your writing screen and choose Export Backup, or find the same option in Settings > Storage & Backups. Tip: Exported files are safe to keep in a cloud folder like Dropbox or OneDrive. Your live book files are not: keep those on your own computer and move copies around by exporting instead.

Everything: your manuscript, all your worldbuilding, your pictures, and this book's own view and layout preferences, in one file. A whole series, if it is one: exporting a series saves every Book inside it, along with the characters, locations, items, tags, and notes they share. Your book is only ever copied: nothing in it is changed or removed, and it stays right where it is in your library. Penpoint opens the book in the background to package it, then closes it again on its own: your screen doesn't change, and you don't need to close the book yourself first. If you have automatic backups on close, you may see a fresh entry in its backup history afterward. Penpoint suggests a filename based on your book's title, but you can call it anything you like as long as it still ends in .penpoint.

To bring the file back into Penpoint, on this computer or any other, double-click it or use Import Book… from the Your Books screen. See Importing a Book for the full walkthrough, including what happens when you import a book you already have. Tip: An exported .penpoint file is exactly the same format as a backup, so it works as a milestone copy: export before a big rewrite and you can always come back to it. See Backup & Restore.
If You Wanted a Readable Document

Exporting Manuscripts: Turn your written chapters into one document: Word, EPUB (the e-book format used by Apple Books and most e-readers), PDF, Markdown (plain text with simple formatting marks), Rich Text, or Plain Text. Exporting Worldbuilding Data: Save your characters, places, items, notes, chapter outlines, and arcs as documents. Those two save readable files anyone can open. Export Book saves the book itself, which only Penpoint can open. Use the same three-dot menu () on the book's card for the book itself, and the tools inside the book for the documents.
Penpoint includes a clock and a writing timer built into the header bar. The clock keeps you aware of the time while you write, and the timer lets you track how long your writing sessions last.

The clock appears in the top-right corner of the bar at the top of the screen. Click it to open a dropdown (a small menu that appears below the clock) where you can quickly adjust settings or start the writing timer. From the menu you can: Switch between 12-hour and 24-hour format Show or hide seconds on the clock Hide the clock to collapse it to a small clock icon in the top-right corner (click that icon to bring the full clock back) You can also configure these options in Settings > Interface.

The writing timer is a simple stopwatch. Start it when you sit down to write and stop it when you're done: your writing time is automatically saved to your daily stats. To start the timer, click the clock at the top of the screen and choose Start Timer. Once running, the elapsed time appears at the top alongside the clock. Click it again for options to pause, resume, or stop the timer. When you stop, your writing time is saved automatically. You can also choose whether the timer displays alongside the clock or temporarily shows the timer instead of the clock; your clock comes right back when you stop the timer. These options appear in the menu while the timer is active. While the timer is running and Penpoint is the window in front, that time counts as Penpointing time in your stats, even if you stop typing to think (up to 30 minutes). Time spent in another app does not count. Tip: Use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+T (Cmd+T on Mac) to quickly start, pause, or resume the timer without opening the menu.

If you enable Auto-start on typing in the clock menu, the timer will begin automatically when you start typing anywhere you can type: manuscripts, notes, character descriptions, and more. No need to remember to click Start. The timer also pauses itself in two situations: You switch away from Penpoint: If you click on another app, the timer pauses. It resumes when you come back. Idle timeout: If you go 30 minutes without typing or clicking, the timer pauses, so a timer you forgot about cannot run up hours. The half hour before the pause still counts. With auto-start enabled it pauses after five minutes instead, and starts again when you type. Without auto-start, choose Resume when you are back. Timer time is part of the Penpointing time in your stats, not extra time on top of it. If you use Penpoint Cloud, today's stats also include the time you spent on your other devices. Note: The timer works in both Worldbuilding Mode (where you track characters and story details) and Manuscript Mode (where you write your prose), including during Flowstate sessions (distraction-free timed writing sprints).

This is Penpoint's worldbuilding side: everything that makes up your story other than the prose itself. Even a grounded, real-world novel lives here. Track your cast, map your places, outline your chapters, and shape your plot, then step back and see how it all connects. New to the worldbuilding side? Start with The Worldbuilding Toolbar, which walks you through the navigation menu on the left and what each page is for. Everything below hangs off that menu.

Characters: Build customizable character profiles with traits, relationships, and as much or as little detail as you need. Items: Track weapons, artifacts, documents, and other objects that matter to your plot. Locations: Nest places inside places: the kingdom holds the city, which holds the tavern. Chapters: Organize your story structure, assign point-of-view characters, and track who appears where. Arcs: Shape your plot as layered story-arc curves and follow how each character's journey rises and falls. Notebook: Keep research, worldbuilding notes, and loose ideas in rich text, with @Mentions to link to anything.

Timeline: See when every character appears across your chapters, and log key story moments as Events tied to the cast involved. Relationship Map: Explore your whole character web as a visual map you can drag, zoom, and click. Tags Overview: Tags are labels you attach to anything. Tag related things, then view everything with that tag in one place. Tip: None of this is required, and you don't have to fill it all in up front. Start with whoever walks onto the page in your first scene, add a place or two, and let the rest grow as your story does. The connections build as you go: @Mention a character in a location's description to link the two, assign characters to your chapters and they appear on the Timeline, and add a relationship or two to watch the Relationship Map take shape.

The toolbar sits at the top of every page in worldbuilding mode (where you build your characters, locations, chapters, and other story elements). It gives you one-click access to navigation, search, saving, writing stats, help resources, and more. Here is a quick tour of everything it offers, from left to right.

On the far left you will find Back and Forward arrows that work like a web browser: they step through the pages you have visited recently. Back: Alt+Left (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+[ (Mac) Forward: Alt+Right (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+] (Mac) Next to the arrows is the page title, which shows you exactly where you are: Characters, Timeline, Notebook, and so on.

The center of the toolbar is home to the The Glorious Searchbar: it searches through everything in your book, including characters, locations, items, chapters, notes, and manuscript scenes. Press Ctrl+K (or Cmd+K on Mac) to jump straight to it from anywhere.
The + button (or Ctrl+N / Cmd+N) opens the Quick Add Menu, which lets you create a new character, item, location, chapter, note, or tag without leaving the page you are on.

The save indicator shows you the current state of your work at a glance: Saved: everything is up to date Saving...: changes are being written to your book file Click the indicator to open a dropdown with backup options: Backup Now: create a manual backup point right away Export Backup: save a copy of your book file to any folder on your computer Restore from Backup: browse and restore from a previous backup. You can choose to restore as a separate new book (leaving your current book untouched) or overwrite your current book. If you overwrite, Penpoint automatically creates a safety backup of your current version first. The footer shows when your most recent backup was created. For full backup settings and scheduling, see Backup & Restore.

With Penpoint Cloud switched on, this same indicator also tells you about your cloud copy, so there is only ever one place to look. The word gains a third state: Synced: this book is saved here and up to date in your cloud A small cloud icon sits next to the word whenever there is something more to say: a spinning icon means a sync is running right now, and an amber icon means this book needs a hand before it can reach the cloud. Open the dropdown and the top of the menu explains exactly what is happening and what to do about it. The word itself only ever describes your own computer, so a cloud problem never makes it look like your writing is unsaved. The dropdown's Sync now button does both halves in one press: it saves a restore point on this computer, then sends the book to your cloud. Penpoint normally does this on its own shortly after you stop typing, and again when you close the book, so seeing "Cloud backup pending" for a few minutes while you write is completely normal. If you press it with no internet connection, the restore point is still made and the cloud copy follows on its own once you reconnect.

The bar chart icon (three vertical bars of different heights) opens your writing stats panel, which tracks your progress across three sections: Today shows your current writing day, which starts at 4 AM so a late night of writing stays in one day. It lists the words added to your manuscript and worldbuilding, total time spent writing, a breakdown of which sections you worked in, and any new characters, locations, or items you created. You will also see your manuscript's total word count. If you use Penpoint Cloud, Today also includes what you did on your other devices, with a small line under the figures saying how many words and how much time came from them. Your Writing Journey tracks your long-term progress: current and longest writing streaks, lifetime word count, your best writing day, and total time spent in Penpoint. Penpoint Hub shows what the community has been up to this week: how many authors are writing, total words composed, books started, characters created, and more. This section appears once you have joined Penpoint Hub; until then, the panel offers a Join Penpoint Hub button. Tip: Joining Penpoint Hub is completely anonymous and optional. It helps the community see how active the writing world is, and gives you access to this section.

The ? icon opens the help menu, which adapts to whatever page you are on: User Guide: the top link changes based on your current page (e.g. "Characters Guide" when on the Characters page, or "Timeline Guide" when on the Timeline). Click it to jump directly to the relevant help article. Restart Tutorial: re-launches the interactive tutorial for the current page (only shown if a tutorial is available). Keyboard Shortcuts: opens a full reference of every keyboard shortcut in Penpoint. Contact Support: opens a short form where you can report a bug, share an idea, or ask a question. It can start with a screenshot of the page you were on (you can remove it), and "See what's included" shows you everything it will send before you press Send. Join Our Discord: opens the Penpoint Discord server where you can chat with other writers and get support.

The bell icon shows notifications from the Penpoint team: new features, updates, tips, and community news. When you have unread announcements, a small numbered circle appears on the bell showing how many are waiting. Click any announcement to read the full details. For more on the announcement system, see Community & Updates.

On the far right of the toolbar is a clock that displays the current time. Click it to access the writing timer, a simple tool for tracking how long you write in a session. You can start, pause, and stop the timer from the dropdown. Ctrl+T (Cmd+T on Mac) lets you quickly start or pause it. For a deeper look at the clock settings and writing timer, see Tracking Your Time.

The Characters page is the heart of Penpoint, where you create and manage your cast of characters. Whether you're tracking a sprawling ensemble or a tight-knit group, this page gives you complete control over how you organize and view your characters.

On the Characters page, you can: Create new characters with importance levels (such as Primary, Secondary, or Background) View your characters in three display modes: Standard (full detail), Compact (names and key info), or Cards (visual summary cards) Switch between View mode and Edit mode (View mode is for reading; Edit mode is for making changes) Sort and organize your character list Pin important characters to the top of the list: right-click a character and choose "Pin to top" to keep your protagonist or key characters always visible above the rest, separated by a divider from the main list Track character details using customizable sections (like text fields, trait lists, and relationships) Collapse and expand individual sections by clicking their header to keep your sheet tidy Expand or collapse the character list on the left to focus on what matters Right-click for quick access to common actions: add or delete characters, pin or unpin characters, change sort order, switch view modes, toggle edit mode, change importance, swap profile pictures, or jump to the Relationship Map Note: Writing a series? Characters are shared across every Book. Presence: Which Books a Character Is In controls where each one appears, and the This Book vs All Books view narrows this list.

Every character in Penpoint uses a flexible section-based layout. You can add sections for text fields, traits, relationships, items, locations, events, and more. The layout you create applies to all characters in your book, but each character's details are their own. To customize your character layout, visit Character Sheet Setup. You can add, remove, reorder, and configure sections to match exactly how you think about your characters. An Events section tracks the key moments a character is part of. The same event also appears on the items and locations involved. See Events to learn how they work.

This guide covers creating, managing, and deleting characters in Penpoint. All character data auto-saves as you type, so you never have to worry about losing your work — and if you change your mind, you can always edit or re-type anything.

Click the Add Character button in the Characters page toolbar. Enter your character's name (up to 45 characters) and click Add Character. Names don't have to be unique, but keeping them distinct helps you stay organized. You can also right-click anywhere in the character list to quickly add a new character. New characters start with the same importance level as your most recently created character. Creating multiple primary characters in a row? You won't have to keep setting the importance level. In a series, new characters start out present in the Book you're currently working in, and the level they start with applies in every Book until you give one of those Books a different level. Tip: Add all your main characters first, then switch to Secondary or Background importance before adding supporting cast members. The importance level carries over automatically.

Organize your cast with three importance levels: Primary (main characters and major antagonists), Secondary (supporting characters with significant roles), and Background (minor characters with occasional appearances). Change a character's importance level in Edit mode (switch to Edit mode using the pencil button at the top of the character page, or press Ctrl+E, or Cmd+E on Mac) using the dropdown below their name. You can also right-click anywhere on the character detail panel and choose Change Importance to switch between levels without entering Edit mode. Use importance to sort your character list, keeping main characters at the top for quick access. In a series, importance is kept separately for each Book, so a character who leads Book 1 can drop to Background by Book 3. See Importance Across Books.

Give your characters a face by adding a profile picture. In Edit mode, click the profile picture placeholder to upload an image, then crop it to fit. You can also drag and drop an image file directly onto the placeholder. Hover over an existing picture to see options for changing or removing it. Another quick way to change a profile picture is to right-click on the character detail panel and choose Change Profile Image. Profile pictures are completely optional. If you don't add one, the placeholder simply won't appear in View mode - your character sheet stays clean and focused on the details you've added. When a profile picture is set, clicking it in View mode opens a full-size preview so you can see the image in detail. When you export your characters, profile pictures are included automatically. See Exporting Worldbuilding Data for export options.

Give a character the nicknames or aliases that other characters might use. In Edit mode, type in the Nickname field below the character name and press comma (or Enter) after each nickname: each one becomes its own small tag with an X to remove it. Drag a tag by its grip (the dotted handle on its left) to change the order; the first nickname is the one Penpoint shows where space is tight, like a scene's POV label. In View mode the nicknames read as a simple list under the character's name. Every nickname works on its own throughout Penpoint. When you type @ in the manuscript editor (where you write your prose) and search for a nickname, the character appears in the results with an "aka" indicator. The search bar at the top of the screen finds characters by any of their nicknames, the spellchecker recognizes each one so it won't underline them in your prose, and the Chapter Scanner (which detects character names in your manuscript chapters) recognizes each nickname separately when scanning. Tip: List all the names your character goes by, even one-off pet names. Each one becomes independently searchable and recognized everywhere character names are.

Note: Deleting a character permanently removes all of their traits, tags, relationships, items, locations, chapter connections, and any custom information. This action cannot be undone, but a confirmation dialog will show you exactly what will be removed before you confirm. To delete a character, select them, switch to Edit mode, scroll to the bottom of the character's page on the right, and click Delete Character. You can also right-click a character in the list or right-click on the character detail panel to find a Delete Character option there. For more information about editing character details, see View Mode vs Edit Mode.

Penpoint offers three ways to view your character list: Standard, Compact, and Cards. Switch between views using the small gear icon near the top of your Characters page, or right-click anywhere in the character list to change the view mode from there. Switching views only changes how your characters are displayed — it never changes or removes any of your character information.

The default view with comfortable spacing. Character name and importance level (such as Primary, Secondary, or Background) are displayed on separate lines for easy reading. Best for: General browsing, smaller casts, or when you prefer larger cards with clear visual separation.

Name and importance appear on the same line with reduced spacing, allowing more characters to fit on screen at once. Best for: Large casts where you need to see many characters without scrolling, or when quickly scanning through your character list.

Cards View displays data from your character layout blocks (the individual sections on a character's page, like Age, Traits, or Description) directly on character cards. This lets you see important details at a glance without opening each character. When you switch to Cards View, a list of sections to choose from appears, letting you pick which one to display. You can pick which sections to show: things like text blocks, number blocks, traits, tags, items, locations, chapters, and calculate blocks. Why use Cards View? See character details instantly without clicking into each character. For example, display a number block showing character ages, a trait showing their role, or tags showing their story arc. This is especially useful when you need to reference specific information across your entire cast. Tip: Cards View is powerful when combined with sorting (the Sort button next to the gear icon at the top of the Characters page). Display character ages and sort alphabetically to quickly find characters by name while still seeing their age at a glance.

When some of your characters have a profile picture and others don't, the ones without one show a framed placeholder in its place, so your list stays neatly lined up instead of leaving gaps. Your real portraits always show as normal. This is on by default. To hide the placeholders, open the gear menu at the top of the Characters page and uncheck "Show blank profile pictures." The same setting controls the placeholders on your Items list too, so turning it off in one place turns it off in both. To customize which blocks appear in your character layout, visit Settings > Character Sheet Setup. Learn more about available block types in Block Types.

The Characters page has two modes: View Mode for reading character information, and Edit Mode for making changes. Switch between them using the button at the top-right of the character page, with automatic saving. Tip: Press Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on Mac) to switch between View and Edit modes. You can also right-click on the character detail panel to toggle between them.

View Mode displays character information in a clean, readable format optimized for quick reference. A clean layout for reading — you can't accidentally change anything here Clickable links for Tags, relationships, Items, Locations, and Chapters Tip: Use View Mode as your default. It's ideal for referencing characters while writing and prevents accidental changes.

Edit Mode provides text boxes and dropdown menus for modifying character details. All changes save automatically. Text fields save shortly after you stop typing Dropdowns and buttons save immediately No manual save button needed

Your selected mode stays active as you switch between characters. If you're in Edit Mode and select a different character, that character also opens in Edit Mode, so you do not have to switch it again for each one.

The character sidebar displays your full character list with controls for sorting and organizing your cast. The sidebar can be collapsed, shown at default width, or expanded to take up most of the screen.

The sidebar has three widths that you can switch between by hovering over the vertical divider between the sidebar and the character details area on the right. Control icons appear on hover: Collapsed: Hides the character list, giving maximum space for character details. Click a small arrow pointing right (>) to expand to default width. Default: Shows the full character list at a comfortable width. Click a small arrow pointing left (<) to collapse, or a small arrow pointing right (>) to expand to fullscreen. Expanded: Takes up most of the screen, displaying characters in multiple columns, side by side. Perfect for organizing your cast, adding multiple characters, or reviewing your full list at a glance. Click a small arrow pointing left (<) to return to default width. Tip: When the sidebar is expanded and you select a character, it automatically returns to default width so you have enough room to view character details.

Click the Sort button at the top of the character list to choose how your character list is organized. You can also right-click anywhere in the character list to access sort options directly. Penpoint offers three sort methods: Date Added: Characters appear in creation order. Choose Oldest first or Newest first. This is the default sort. Alphabetical: Characters appear in alphabetical order. Choose A to Z or Z to A. Importance: Characters are grouped by importance level (Primary, Secondary, Background) with alphabetical sorting within each group. Most important first puts your main cast at the top; Least important first flips it. Your sort choice is saved — it'll still be there next time you open your book. Tip: Sort alphabetically when you need to find a specific character by name quickly, especially with large casts. Sort by importance when you want to prioritize your main characters.

Click any character's name in the sidebar to select that character and display their details in the character details area on the right. You can also use left and right arrow keys to navigate between characters in the sidebar without using your mouse. Arrow key navigation is disabled when you're in edit mode (see View Mode vs Edit Mode) or typing in any text box.

Blocks are the individual sections on your character sheet: things like text areas, number fields, and trait lists. Each block type serves a different purpose, from simple text fields to complex relationship mapping. Your layout (the arrangement of sections on every character's page) applies to all characters in your book. When you add a number block and name it "Height", every character gets a height field; each character has their own unique value. Changing your layout doesn't delete any information you've already entered. You can add new blocks at any time, and all your characters will retroactively get the new block applied to their character sheet. You'll just have to go back through and update them with the new content. Tip: Focus on blocks that help you write better characters. You don't need to track everything - just what matters for your story.

General-purpose fields you can add multiple times to your layout: Text Block - Single-line text input Paragraph Block - Multi-line text area Number Block - A field for numbers like age, height, or weight Divider Block - Visual separator line Calculate Block - Perform calculations between number fields Image Block - Upload and display a reference image (portraits, maps, mood boards) Notebook Block - Show a note, folder, or set of tags from your Notebook right on the character sheet

Specialized blocks that connect to other parts of your book. Most of these you can only add one per character sheet: Trait Block - A list you can pick from, based on the traits you've set up for your book (can add multiple) Tags Block - Labels you can attach to characters to group and organize them (you can only add one per character sheet) Relationships Block - Character-to-character connections (you can only add one per character sheet) Items Block - Track items/objects owned (you can only add one per character sheet) Locations Block - Link characters to places (you can only add one per character sheet) Chapters Block - Track chapter appearances (you can only add one per character sheet) Events Block - Key moments this character is part of, that also appear on the items and locations involved (you can only add one per character sheet) Character Arc Block - A visual chart showing how a character's fortune rises and falls through the story (you can only add one per character sheet)

Blocks display differently depending on your current mode: View Mode: Clean, readable format where links to related characters, locations, items, and chapters are clickable Edit Mode: Editable forms with input fields that auto-save as you type, so you never have to worry about losing your work Learn more about switching between modes in View Mode vs Edit Mode.
Add, remove, or configure blocks in Settings > Character Sheet Setup (the gear icon in the navigation bar). For detailed guidance, see Customizing Character Layout.

A short text block (a section on your character sheet) for brief character information like nicknames, titles, roles, and more. Click any text block to edit it, or view its contents at a glance. Ideal for quick blurbs that don't need formatting like bold, italic, and lists. Text Blocks also work on the Chapters page — drop one into a scene's layout for per-scene snippets like a working title or one-line summary. See Chapter Block Types.

Nicknames: What other characters call this person Titles: Formal titles, ranks, or positions Roles: Story role (Protagonist, Mentor, etc.) Pronouns: Preferred pronouns Species/Race: In fantasy or sci-fi stories Quick descriptions: "grumpy blacksmith" or "cheerful thief" Tip: If you are commonly using a group of attributes that apply to more than one character, you might consider using a Trait Block instead. The Trait Block has preconfigured, selectable text options that can be reused across multiple characters.

To configure a Text Block, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup and click on the block to reveal its settings panel. Block Title: Custom title for this text block (e.g., "Nickname", "Title", "Pronouns") Include in Quick Create: When checked, this block appears in the Quick Create menu (the streamlined form for adding new characters quickly) for faster character creation Tip: Running out of room or want to add formatting like bold, italic, and lists? Use a Paragraph Block instead.

A multi-line text field with formatting support for detailed character information like backstories, physical descriptions, and personality notes. Paragraph Blocks aren't just for character sheets — you can also add them to chapter scenes for descriptions, notes, or any longer-form text per scene. See Chapter Block Types.

Use the toolbar buttons to format your text: Bold, italic, underline, strikethrough Block styles via the Style dropdown: Paragraph, Quote, Heading 1, Heading 2, Heading 3 Bulleted and numbered lists Indent and decrease indent (move text back to the left) Hyperlinks to external websites Inline images Horizontal line (a divider across the block) Undo and redo

Physical descriptions and mannerisms Backstory and history Personality and quirks Motivations and goals Relationship descriptions Tip: Create separate Paragraph Blocks for different aspects (one for appearance, one for personality, one for backstory) rather than one massive block.

Type @ to create clickable links to other characters, locations, items, chapters, notes, or arcs. This makes it easy to navigate between related content directly from your character sheets. When you type @, a dropdown menu appears with search results. Use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate through the options, then press Enter to select. A clickable link is automatically inserted into your text. Tip: The @ mention system works in any Paragraph Block throughout Penpoint (and well beyond; see @Mentions for everywhere it works). Write "Trained under @MasterKai before joining @Sarah's rebellion" to create quick links to other characters. Note: Paragraph Blocks don't appear in Cards View (a compact visual layout for your character list). Use Text Blocks for brief info that should display on cards.

To configure a Paragraph Block, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup and click on the block to reveal its settings panel. Block Title: Custom title for this paragraph block (e.g., "Physical Description", "Backstory", "Personality") Include in Quick Create: When enabled, this block appears in the Quick Create form (the streamlined form for adding new characters quickly)

A section that holds a number. You can set minimum and maximum limits, and use small arrow buttons to count up or down. Number Blocks also work on chapter scenes — useful for things like word-count targets or per-scene tracking. See Chapter Block Types.

Age: Character ages Height/Weight: Physical measurements Stats: Strength, intelligence, etc. Ratings: 1-10 scales for skills or influence Dates: Birth year, year of death Counts: Books written, battles fought, years of service

Set minimum and maximum values to catch unrealistic entries. Values outside the range turn red. Age: min 0, max 120 Rating scale: min 1, max 10 Stats: min 1, max 100 Tip: Use min/max validation to catch data entry errors. If you accidentally type -5 for age, the red color alerts you immediately.
Number Blocks can be used in math formulas with Calculate Blocks: Current year minus "Birth Year" = Age "Strength" + "Intelligence" = Total stats See Calculate Block for more on formulas.

To configure a Number Block, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup and click on the block to reveal its settings panel. Block Title: Custom title for this number block (e.g., "Age", "Strength", "Height") Minimum: Optional minimum value. Values below this turn red for validation Maximum: Optional maximum value. Values above this turn red for validation Include in Quick Create: When checked, this block appears in the Quick Create menu for faster character setup Add and configure Number Blocks in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. Number Blocks can be placed side-by-side using the half-width option in Settings > Character Sheet Setup for compact stat displays.

A visual separator you can place between blocks on your character sheet. You'll find Divider Blocks in Settings > Character Sheet Setup, where you can add and configure them alongside your other blocks. Dividers are purely decorative: they just help organize your character sheet visually. Divider Blocks also work on the Chapters page detail panel for the same purpose. See Chapter Block Types.

To configure a Divider Block, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup and click on the block to reveal its settings panel. Divider Style: Choose from Quill, Full, Half, Tiny, Dot, Circle, Fade, Double, or Book Intensity: Strong (darkest), Medium, or Light (faintest) Apply to All: Match the style and intensity across all dividers in your layout Tip: Use dividers to break up long pages into scannable sections. Place one wherever you want a natural break between your grouped blocks for easier navigation. Add and configure Divider Blocks in Settings > Character Sheet Setup.
Here are all available divider styles. Each style creates a different visual separation effect to match your character layout aesthetic.

Performs math operations using Number Block values (values from Number sections on your character sheet) or fixed numbers. Perfect for auto-calculated ages, combined scores, or tracking time elapsed. Calculate Blocks also work on the Chapters page, where they can crunch numbers from other Number Blocks on the same scene's layout. See Chapter Block Types.

Input 1: Select a Number Block OR enter a fixed number Operation: Add, Subtract, Multiply, or Divide Input 2: Select another Number Block OR enter a fixed number Result: Updates automatically when source values change

Age: Current year as a fixed number (e.g. 1873) − "Birth Year" block Combined Score: "Skill" + "Experience" Years of Service: "End Year" − "Start Year" Percentages: "Chapters Completed" ÷ "Total Chapters" Tip: Both inputs can be either a fixed number or a Number Block. Use fixed values for constants (like current year) and Number Blocks for character-specific values (like birth years).

To configure a Calculate Block, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup and click on the block to reveal its settings panel. Block Title: Custom label (default: "Calculate") Input 1 Type: Choose "Fixed Number" for constants or "Number Block" for a character field Calculation Type: Add (+), Subtract (-), Multiply (×), or Divide (÷) Input 2 Type: Choose "Fixed Number" for constants or "Number Block" for another field Round to whole numbers: Enable for ages or counts. Otherwise shows up to 2 decimal places Add and configure Calculate Blocks in Settings > Character Sheet Setup.

Trait sections give you lists of options you can pick from for common character details — things like eye color, personality type, or alignment. You can select multiple values at once using checkboxes. For example, you might have an Alignment trait with options like Lawful Good, Chaotic Evil, and True Neutral, or a Community trait for groups within your world like Fire Nation, Water Tribe, and Earth Kingdom. First, you set up your list of options in Settings > Traits (for example, a list of eye colors). Then you add a Trait section to your character sheet in Settings > Character Sheet Setup and connect it to that list. You can then use the Glorious Searchbar (the search bar at the top of the screen) or the Character Filter (the filtering options on the Characters page) to find characters who share a specific trait.
Create trait definitions in Settings > Traits, then link Trait Blocks to them in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. See Managing Traits for details on creating and organizing trait definitions.

Eye/Hair Color: Blue, Green, Brown, etc. Personality Type: Introvert, Extrovert, Ambivert Role: Protagonist, Antagonist, Supporting Alignment: Lawful Good, Chaotic Neutral Species/Race: Human, Elf, Dwarf Tip: Add multiple Trait Blocks - one for each categorical attribute. Each links to its own trait definition with its own dropdown options.

To configure a Trait Block, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup and click on the trait section to see its options. Select Trait: Choose which trait definition this block links to. If you don't see a trait here, it just means it's already being used in another section Include in Quick Create: When checked, this trait block will appear in the Quick Create menu for faster character setup Learn more about creating trait definitions in Managing Traits.

Tags are color-coded labels you can assign to characters, locations, items, chapters, and notes. Think of them as a powerful organizational system that works everywhere. The Tags Block also lives on the Chapters page, where you can attach tags to the whole chapter and to individual scenes. See Chapter Block Types. The Tags Block appears differently depending on whether you're in View Mode or Edit Mode. In View Mode, tags are shown as plain labels you can't change. In Edit Mode, you can add or remove them. See View Mode vs Edit Mode for details. Once tagged, all your related content can be viewed together in the Tags Viewer, making it easy to see all characters, locations, and other elements that share a tag. This makes tags essential for finding like-content across your entire book.

If you've filed your tags into Tag Groups, the list of available tags is split into sections with a heading for each group, and anything unfiled sits under Ungrouped at the bottom. Clicking a heading folds that group away, and it stays folded everywhere else you pick tags until you open it again, so a category you're not using today keeps out of your way. A group can also carry a color, which takes over the display of every tag inside it; your own tag colors are kept, and removing the group color brings them straight back. Groups are made and organized on the Tags Manager, in Settings > Tags.

Roles: Protagonist, Antagonist, Supporting Status: Alive, Dead, Unknown Affiliation: Team A, Team B, Neutral Abilities: Magic User, Fighter, Healer Development: Needs Work, Complete Cross-content markers: "Act 1", "Needs Revision", "Important Plot Point" Tip: Tags work across your entire book. A tag created for characters is automatically available for locations, items, chapters, and notes.

To view the Tags Block settings, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup and click on the Tags section. The Tags Block's only setting is Include in Quick Create.
