Quick Create is the short form you get when adding a character in a hurry; turn this on and the Tags Block appears on it. Everything else about tags (creating, renaming, deleting, colors, and groups) is handled in one place, on the Tags Manager. Manage all tags in Settings > Tags. Learn more about creating and managing tags in Managing Tags. Note: Only one Tags Block allowed per character layout.
Managing Tags - Create and manage tags in Settings Tags Viewer Page - View all content associated with a specific tag

Manages character-to-character relationships. Supports two-way (reciprocal) relationships, so you can track family ties, friendships, rivalries, and any other connections between your characters from both sides. All relationships are visualized in the dynamic Map page, where you can see your entire character network as a visual map showing connections between characters.

To add a new relationship in Edit Mode (see View Mode vs Edit Mode): 1. Click "Add New Relationship" - A small form appears right there on the page 2. Select a character - Choose from existing characters, or use "Create New Character..." to create one on the spot 3. Enter relationship type - Type a label like "Friend", "Sister", or "Rival". Autocomplete suggests types you've used before 4. Optional: Enable two-way - Click the circular arrow icon (two arrows forming a circle) to create a two-way relationship with different labels for each direction. For example, what this character calls the relationship might be "Mentor", while what the other character calls it might be "Student" 5. Click "Apply" - Saves the relationship Tip: Use the two-way option for asymmetric relationships where each character views the connection differently. For example: Character A sees the relationship as "Admires", but Character B sees it as "Mentors".

In Edit Mode, hover over any relationship to reveal action buttons. Click the pencil icon to edit the relationship type or turn two-way on or off. Click the trash icon to remove the relationship entirely (both directions are deleted together).

One-way: "Robin: Sidekick" means this character considers Robin a Sidekick Two-way (same type): A double-headed arrow (↔) appears before the name, e.g. "↔ Robin: Ally" — both characters share the same relationship type Two-way (different types): Shows what this character calls the relationship on the first line, and what the other character calls it on an indented sub-line, e.g. "Robin: Sidekick" with a return arrow (↵) "Batman: Mentor" beneath it Incoming only: If another character has a relationship pointing to this one, it shows up here. For example, if you defined "Mentor" on Gandalf pointing to Frodo, Frodo's page would show an incoming relationship from Gandalf. Tip: In Settings > Character Sheet Setup, the Relationships Block has a "Swap Role Labels" option. When enabled, two-way relationships with different types show each character's name paired with their own role instead of the role assigned to them. This is purely visual and does not change your data. Add and configure the Relationships Block in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. Only one Relationships Block allowed per layout.

The Items block (a section on your character sheet) tracks items connected to the character. Items display with custom icons and item types. Click any item's name to see its full details on the Items page. Items are created and assigned to characters in the Items page. You can customize item icons and types in Settings > Items.

In Edit Mode, click "Add Item" to search for and assign items, or create a new item right from the dropdown. You can remove an item by hovering over it in Edit Mode and clicking the trash icon — this only unassigns the item from the character, and the item itself is not deleted.

Weapons and armor Magical artifacts Personal belongings Tracking possessions and meaningful objects Manage items in Items. Add and configure the Items Block in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. You can only have one Items section per character sheet.

The Locations block (a section on your character sheet) links characters to specific places in your story world. Track hometowns, workplaces, hideouts, or any location associated with a character. Each location displays with a custom icon and location type. You can add and configure the Locations block in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. Create and manage all locations in the Locations page. For more details, see the Locations help article.

To assign locations to a character in Edit Mode (the pencil toggle that lets you make changes, as opposed to View Mode): 1. Click "Add Location" - a search box appears 2. Search and select a location - Type to search existing locations by name 3. Location is assigned - Selecting a location immediately assigns it to this character If the location you need doesn't exist yet, select "Create New Location..." from the dropdown to create one without leaving the character page.

To unassign a location (without deleting it), hover over it in Edit Mode and click the trash icon on the right side. This only removes the association — the location itself stays in your book and can be reassigned at any time. Tip: Clicking any location name takes you directly to that location's detail page. Manage locations in Locations. You can only have one Locations section per character sheet.

Displays all chapters where this character appears. Track character appearances throughout your story and identify POV chapters at a glance. Each chapter is clickable and navigates to the full chapter details. Create and manage chapters in the Chapters page. For more details, see the Chapters help article. You can add and configure the Chapters section from Settings > Character Sheet Setup. Note: If you haven't created any chapters yet, this section will be empty. Head to the Chapters page to get started.

Chapters where this character has a point-of-view (POV) are marked with an eye icon. This makes it easy to see which chapters are told from this character's perspective. Tip: To mark a character as the point-of-view narrator for a chapter, go to the Chapters page and set it there. POV status helps track narrative perspectives across your story.

To assign a character to chapters, switch to Edit Mode (see View Mode vs Edit Mode): 1. Click "Add Character to Chapter" - A search box appears 2. Select a chapter - Choose from available chapters in your book, or select "Create New Chapter..." to add one on the spot 3. Character is assigned - Selecting a chapter immediately assigns this character to it Remove a chapter - Hover over an assigned chapter and click the X button to unassign this character from it. This only removes the character from that chapter — it doesn't delete the chapter or any of your writing. You can always re-add them. Note: You can also assign characters to chapters from the Chapters page itself. Manage chapters in Chapters. You can only have one Chapters section per character sheet.

Displays a compact version of a character's fortune curve (a visual chart showing how a character's circumstances rise and fall through the story) directly on their character sheet. The arc visualizes how a character's circumstances rise and fall across key story moments, with diamond-shaped turning points (called keyframes) marking each shift. Character arcs are created and managed on the Arcs page. For a full guide to fortune curves, turning points, and modifiers, see Character Arcs.

The block offers two ways to view a character's arc: Curve View: A fortune curve with turning point diamonds and labels. This is the default view. List View: Turning points listed with icons showing whether fortune is rising or falling, along with descriptions. Useful when you want a quick text summary of the arc. Switch between views using the Curve/List toggle in the top-right corner. Penpoint remembers which view you picked, even after you close the app.

Click any turning point diamond or the curve itself to jump directly to that character's full arc view on the Arcs page. From there you can edit turning points, adjust fortune modifiers, and compare arcs between characters. Tip: If a character doesn't have an arc yet, the block shows an empty state. In Edit mode (as opposed to View mode, which is for reading only), a button appears to navigate to the Arcs page where you can create one. Add and configure the Character Arc Block in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. You can only have one Character Arc section per character sheet.

An Image Block lets you attach a single picture to a character or scene (a portrait, a piece of concept art, a map, a reference photo, anything visual that helps you write). Each character (or scene) keeps their own picture, even though the block design itself is shared across every character (or scene) in your book. Image Blocks work on the Chapters page too. Drop one into your scene layout for scene-by-scene reference art, location photos, or map fragments. See Chapter Block Types.

Character portraits: Commissioned art, AI references, or real-life inspirations Reference photos: A face you want to capture, a costume, a setting Location concept art: Maps of cities, sketches of landmarks, mood boards Item visuals: Sketches of weapons, jewelry, or other story-relevant objects Scene mood boards: Set the visual tone for a chapter while you write

Click the dashed rectangle in the empty block (it shows an upload arrow and the words "Click to upload an image") to pick a file from your computer. Penpoint accepts JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, and BMP up to 20 MB. Once uploaded, hover over the image while you're in edit mode (see View Mode vs Edit Mode) to find the Replace and Remove buttons. Replace swaps in a new picture (the old one is removed from this character or scene), and Remove always asks you to confirm first — your portrait won't disappear from a stray click. Click any uploaded image to open it in the lightbox (a big pop-up viewer for zooming in on the picture), where you can zoom and pan to inspect detail. Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) the image to Export Image…. Penpoint opens the standard Save window with the character or scene name already filled in, so the file is recognizable even if you're saving several at once. Tip: Use the Block Title for the role ("Portrait", "Map") and the caption for what's actually in the picture ("Lady Mirabel, age 27"). Each picture has its own caption (added below or above the picture, depending on how you've configured the block), while the Block Title (set in your layout) is shared across every character or scene.

To configure an Image Block, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup (or Settings > Chapter Layout for scenes) and click on the block to reveal its settings panel right below it. Block Title: The heading shown on every character or scene that uses this block (e.g. "Portrait", "Reference", "Map"). Image Fit: Contain (the default) keeps the picture's natural shape: a tall portrait stays tall, a wide landscape stays wide, and the block grows to match. Cover crops the image into a fixed widescreen (16:9) frame so every character's block has the exact same shape, useful when you want a tidy, uniform layout. Heads-up: tall portraits may lose their tops or bottoms in Cover mode, since the picture is cropped to fit the wide frame. Caption Position: Where each picture's caption appears. Below or Above shows the caption as a small line of text outside the picture. Overlay places it as a dark bar at the bottom of the image itself. None hides captions entirely (you can still add one from the lightbox). Tip: For a library of unattached reference images organized into folders, use the Images in the Notebook feature instead. The Image Block is for visuals that belong to a specific character or scene; the Notebook is for everything else.

The Events block (a section on your character sheet) lists the key moments this character is part of. Events are shared, so the same moment can appear on several characters, items, and locations at once. For how events work across your whole book, see Events.

Add the Events block from Settings > Character Sheet Setup using Add Block. You can only have one Events section per character sheet. Note: Don't see an Events section on your character sheet? You can add one yourself in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. See Customizing Character Layout if you'd like a walkthrough.

In Edit Mode, click Add event to add an existing event or create a new one with just a title. To take an event off this character without deleting it, open the event and choose Remove from this character. That leaves the event intact for everyone else it involves.

The block's settings include one option: Show numbers before each event, on by default. It puts a small position number to the left of each event. It's purely visual and doesn't change anything about the events themselves. Manage your full layout in Settings > Character Sheet Setup.

A Notebook Block pulls a note (or a whole group of notes) from your Notebook straight onto a character sheet or a scene. It's a live link, never a copy: think of it as a window onto your Notebook, not a photocopy. Whatever you write in the Notebook shows through here, and any change you make to a note keeps every block showing it in sync. You do your editing in the Notebook itself; the block just displays it. Write your lore once, and it appears wherever you need it. The Notebook Block works on both character sheets and the Chapters page, so you can show the same reference on a character and on the scenes where it matters. To learn about the Notebook itself, see Notebook.

Each block shows notes from one of three sources. You pick the source, and what shows up: A single note: the note's full contents appear right on the page for reference (you make your edits over in the Notebook itself), with an Open in Notebook button to jump to the original. Best for one focused piece of writing you want front and center: a character's backstory, a scene's beat sheet, a passage of worldbuilding lore. A folder: a live list of every note in that folder, each one a clickable link. Best when a topic is spread across several notes and you want them gathered in one spot. Point a character's block at a "Character Work" folder and every note you file there shows up automatically, with no re-linking needed. One or more tags: a live list of every note carrying any of the tags you choose. Best for pulling together notes that live in different folders but share a theme. Link the "Magic System" and "Prophecy" tags to your wizard, and any note with either tag appears, wherever you filed it. Tip: Folder and tag links stay current on their own. Add a new note to a linked folder, or put a linked tag on a note, and it shows up in the block the next time you look. You never have to come back and update the list.
Linking a Note, Folder, or Tags

Think of it in two halves. The block's name is part of your page design, shared by every character or scene. But what each one actually shows is personal to them: each character and each scene picks its own note, folder, or tag, right on its own page in Edit Mode. That's how the same block can show a different note for every character. Open the character or scene, switch to Edit Mode (the Edit button at the top of the page), and find the Notebook Block. See View Mode vs Edit Mode if you need a refresher on switching modes. Under Show notes from, choose Folder, Tag, or Note. For a folder or note, pick one from the list that drops down. Once chosen, it shows a summary with Click to change underneath if you want to swap it later. For tags, click each tag you want from Available Tags to move it up to Selected Tags. Click a selected tag's X to remove it. Choose as many as you like. For a folder or tags, Open notes in decides what happens when you click a note in the list. See below. Your choice saves on its own; there's no Save button to hunt for. Switch back to View Mode to see the notes in place. Changed your mind entirely? The trash icon beside the selection empties the block, leaving it blank and ready for a fresh choice. Like everything else here, that applies only to the character or scene you're on, and it never touches the note, folder, or tag itself.
Reading a Note Without Leaving the Page

When a block is linked to a folder or tags, it shows a list of notes. Clicking one opens it right there in the block, with the full note to read and a Back button to return to the list. You stay on your character sheet or scene the whole time, so you never lose your place mid-thought. Beside the Back button sits Open in Notebook, for when you'd rather go to the note itself. The block remembers where you were. Leave a note open, close Penpoint, come back tomorrow, and that note is still open, waiting where you left it. The Minipen sidebar keeps its own place, so reading a note there while you write doesn't move the character page you left behind. Would you rather a click take you to the Notebook? In Edit Mode, set Open notes in to Notebook and that's what a click does. This is a per-character (and per-scene) choice, the same as the folder or tags a block points at, so changing it on one character leaves the rest alone. Note: The Notebook is still where you write. A note opened inside a block is there for reading and reference; to edit it, use Open in Notebook.
When a Linked Note Goes Away

Your notes are always safe. A block is only a window onto your Notebook, so emptying the block, removing it, or pointing it somewhere new never deletes the note itself. The note stays right where it lives in the Notebook. If a note, folder, or tag a block was showing later gets deleted, the block won't show an error or disturb anything else on the page. It simply says the link is gone and offers to let you pick a new one in Edit Mode. Writing a series of books? Your Notebook is shared across every Book in the series, so a block keeps showing the note you linked no matter which Book you are working in.

The Notebook Block's only setting is its title. To change it, go to Settings > Character Sheet Setup (or Settings > Chapter Layout for scenes) and click the block to open its settings. Name it something that fits what you keep there: "Lore", "Research", "Backstory". Note: The title is the only thing set in Settings. The folder, tag, or note each block shows is chosen per character and per scene, on the page itself, in Edit Mode. Tip: To add or remove this block from your layout, see Customizing Character Layout for characters, or Customizing Chapter Layout for scenes.

Notebook - Your workspace for notes, folders, and reference material Folders and Smart Folders - Organize notes into folders you can link to Managing Tags - Create the tags you link to in tag mode Tags Block - Attach tags to a character or scene (a different block)

The Items page helps you track objects in your story: weapons, artifacts, documents, vehicles, or any other significant items your characters interact with. Whether you're managing a fantasy hero's legendary sword collection or tracking clues in a mystery novel, Items keeps everything organized and connected to your characters.

On the Items page, you can: Create items with custom types that match your story's needs View items in three display modes (Cards, Compact, or Standard) Filter by type, character, importance, tags, and more Sort items alphabetically, by creation date, or by importance Assign items to characters and add relationship notes Set single-character restrictions for unique items Assign items to locations and chapters to track where they appear Add descriptions, tags, and other details to each item Note: Writing a series? Items are shared across every Book. Presence: Which Books a Character Is In controls where each one appears, and the This Book vs All Books view narrows this list.

Every item has a type that defines what category it belongs to. Penpoint templates include default types like Personal Effects, Documents, Weapons & Armor, and more, but you can create your own custom types with unique icons. To manage your item types, visit Settings > Items. You can add, remove, reorder, and customize types to match your story's genre and needs.
This guide covers creating, managing, and deleting items in Penpoint. All item data auto-saves as you type.

Click the Add New Item button in the Items page toolbar. Enter the item's name (up to 50 characters) and select its type. Click Create Item to add it to your project. New items are automatically created with Primary importance. After creation, the item opens in the detail panel in edit mode, ready for you to add descriptions, characters, and tags. Tip: Choose item types that match your story's genre. Fantasy stories might use Weapon and Artifact, while modern mysteries might use Document and Evidence types.

Give your items a visual identity by adding a profile picture. In Edit mode, click the placeholder to upload an image, then crop it to fit. You can also drag and drop an image file directly onto the placeholder. Hover over an existing picture to see options for changing or removing it. Profile pictures appear on item cards in Cards and Standard views. In View mode, clicking a profile picture opens a full-size lightbox. If no picture is set, the item's type icon is shown instead.

Organize your items with three importance levels: Primary (significant items central to your plot), Secondary (items with moderate importance), and Background (minor items with occasional mentions). Change an item's importance level in Edit mode using the dropdown in the detail panel. Use importance to sort your item list, keeping plot-critical items at the top for quick access. In a series, importance is kept separately for each Book, so an item that drives the plot of Book 1 can sit in the background of Book 2. See Importance Across Books.

To delete an item, select it, switch to Edit mode, scroll to the bottom of the detail panel, and click Delete Item. A confirmation dialog shows what will be removed before you confirm. Note: Deleting an item permanently removes all its data: character assignments, tags, location assignments, chapter appearances, and timeline positions. This action cannot be undone. For more information about editing item details, see Editing Item Details.
The Items page offers three display modes to match your workflow: Cards, Compact, and Standard. Switch between them using the view mode menu in the toolbar.

The default grid layout with comfortable spacing. Each card shows the item's icon (or profile picture if one is set), name, type, and importance level. The layout adjusts to show more items when you collapse the filter sidebar. Items with the single-character restriction display a icon in the bottom right corner of the card, indicating that only one character can be assigned to this item at a time. Best for: Visual browsing, smaller inventories, or when you want to see item icons at a glance.

A dense list view with minimal spacing. Shows the item icon, name, and type badge in compact rows, allowing you to see more items on screen at once. Best for: Large inventories, quick scanning, or when screen space is limited.

A full-width list with comfortable spacing between rows. Each row displays the item icon (or profile picture), name, and type on the first line, with importance shown below. More breathing room than Compact view makes scanning easier. Best for: Focused work, detailed browsing, or when you prefer a traditional list layout.

When some of your items have a picture and others don't, the ones without one show a framed placeholder in its place, so your list stays lined up instead of leaving gaps. Items with a real picture always show it as normal. This is on by default. To hide the placeholders, open the view options (gear) menu and uncheck "Show blank item icons." The same setting controls the placeholders on your Characters list too, so turning it off in one place turns it off in both.
The filter sidebar on the left helps you narrow down your item list to find exactly what you're looking for.
Filter by item type. Select one or more types to show only items of those types. Clear the filter to see all items again.
Filter by importance level: Primary, Secondary, or Background. Useful for focusing on plot-critical items or finding minor background items.
Check this box to show only items with the single-character restriction enabled. This helps you quickly identify unique items that can only belong to one character at a time.
Filter by character. Select one or more characters to see all items connected to them. Perfect for tracking a specific character's inventory or belongings.
Filter by one or more tags. You can select multiple tags to narrow your search. Items matching any of the selected tags will be shown. Tag filters display colored dots for visual identification.
Filter by chapter assignment. Select one or more chapters to show only items that appear in those chapters. Each option shows the chapter number and title.

When any filter is active, a Clear button appears at the top of the filter sidebar. Click it to reset all filters and show your complete item list. Tip: Combine multiple filters to create powerful searches. For example, filter by Character and Type together to see all weapons connected to a specific character.
Your filter settings are saved automatically. When you return to the Items page, Penpoint restores your active filters exactly as you left them.
Control how your items are ordered using the sort menu in the Items page toolbar. Choose both the sort method and direction to organize your list exactly how you need it.
Sorts items by name. Choose A to Z or Z to A. The default sorting method for finding items by name quickly.

Sorts items by when they were created. Choose Oldest first or Newest first to put your most recently created items at the top. Useful for tracking what you added recently or finding items created early in your project.

Sorts items by importance level. Most important first shows Primary items, then Secondary, then Background. Choose Least important first to see background items at the top. Switching to Importance from another method starts with Most important first. Perfect for keeping plot-critical items at the top of your list for quick access during writing sessions.
Your sort preferences are saved automatically. When you return to the Items page, Penpoint restores both your sort method and direction exactly as you left them.
When you select an item from the list, its detail panel appears on the right side of the screen. In View mode, you can read all the item's information. Switch to Edit mode to make changes.

The top of the panel shows the item's profile picture (or type icon if none is set) alongside the name. If the item has the single-character restriction enabled, a "Single Character" badge appears below the name. Click a profile picture in View mode to open it full-size. Use the Edit/View toggle button in the header to switch between reading and editing modes.
Displays the item's type with its icon. This section shows what category the item belongs to, based on the types you've configured.
Shows the item's importance level: Primary, Secondary, or Background. This helps you track which items are central to your plot versus minor background details.

The description section displays rich text content about the item. You can include detailed information about the item's appearance, history, powers, or significance to your story. In View mode, the description is displayed with all formatting intact. If no description has been added, you'll see "No description provided"

Lists all characters connected to this item. Each character is shown with their name (clickable to navigate to that character) and their importance level badge. If a relationship note has been added, it appears in italics beneath the character's name — for example, "forged it" or "guards it." The section header shows the count: "Characters (2)" for example. If the item isn't assigned to any characters, you'll see "Not assigned to any characters." Tip: Click a character's name to jump directly to their detail panel, making it easy to explore connections between items and characters.

Shows which chapters this item appears in. Each chapter displays its number and title, and is clickable to navigate directly to that chapter. In Edit mode, use the Add to Chapter button to assign the item to additional chapters.

Lists the key moments this item is part of, like the night it was stolen or the duel it was drawn in. The same event can also appear on the characters and locations involved: it's one event in several places, not a copy. In Edit mode, use Add event to add an event you've already made, or create a new one. Removing an event here only takes it off this item; it stays on everyone else it involves. For how events work across your book, see Events.
Shows which locations this item is found at. Each location is clickable to navigate directly to it. In Edit mode, use the Add to Location button to assign the item to additional locations.

Displays all tags assigned to the item with their colored dots for visual identification. Tags help you categorize and filter items across your project. For more information about creating and managing tags, see Managing Tags. Tip: Press Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on Mac) to quickly toggle between View and Edit modes without reaching for the mouse.
Edit mode lets you modify all aspects of an item's information. Press Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on Mac) or click the Edit button in the detail panel header to enter edit mode.
All changes save automatically as you type. No need to click a Save button; your edits are preserved instantly. You can see save progress in the top bar of the application.
Click into the name field to edit the item's name. You can use up to 50 characters. A character counter appears below the field once you pass 25 characters.

Click the placeholder next to the item name to upload a profile picture, then crop it to fit. You can also drag and drop an image directly. Hover over an existing picture to see options for changing or removing it.
Use the Type dropdown to change the item's type. Select from any of your configured item types.
Use the importance dropdown to set the item's priority level: Primary, Secondary, or Background. Changes apply immediately.

Enable the Single Character checkbox (with lock icon) to restrict this item to only one character at a time. Useful for unique items like legendary weapons or one-of-a-kind artifacts that can't be shared. When enabled, you'll see a yellow lock icon warning if a character is already assigned, and you won't be able to add additional characters until the first one is removed. Tip: Use single-character restriction for items that are central to character development or plot progression, ensuring they can't accidentally be assigned to multiple characters.

The description field is a full rich text editor supporting markdown formatting. You can add bold, italics, lists, and more to format your item's description. Use the @ symbol to create mentions that link to characters, other items, locations, or chapters. Start typing after @ to see available options. The rich text editor works the same as the Paragraph Block. See Paragraph Block for formatting details and @Mentions for everything you can link to.

In edit mode, you can add or remove characters. Click the Add Character button to assign the item to a character. A dropdown appears with all available characters; start typing to filter the list. Below each character, you can type a short relationship note describing how they connect to the item, for example, "created it," "guards it," or "inherited from grandmother." Notes are limited to 100 characters and appear in italics in View mode. To remove a character, click the trash icon next to their name. The item will be unassigned from that character immediately. If the item has single-character restriction enabled and already has a character, the Add button will be disabled until you remove the existing character.

In edit mode, you can assign this item to chapters where it appears. Click the Add to Chapter button to search for and select a chapter. To remove an assignment, click the trash icon next to the chapter.

In edit mode, you can assign this item to locations where it's found. Click the Add to Location button to search for and select a location. To remove an assignment, click the trash icon next to the location.

In edit mode, you can add and remove tags by clicking on the tags section. Tags help you categorize items and filter them across your project. For more information about creating and managing tags, see Managing Tags.

At the bottom of the edit panel, you'll find the Delete Item button. Click it to permanently remove the item from your project. Note: Deleting an item is permanent and cannot be undone. A confirmation dialog will show you what will be deleted before you confirm.
Press Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on Mac) or click the View button in the header to exit edit mode. You'll see your latest changes reflected immediately in view mode.

Item types define categories for your items. Customize them in Settings > Items to match your story's genre and needs. Penpoint includes default types like Weapon, Artifact, Document, and Vehicle, but you can create custom types for any category: Evidence for mysteries, Spell Components for fantasy, Tech Gadgets for sci-fi, or anything else your story requires.

Click Add Item Type to create a new item type. Enter a name and choose an icon from the available options. Your new type appears immediately in the list and becomes available when creating items. Note: You can have up to 50 item types per book. The button will show "(Maximum reached)" when you've hit the limit. Tip: Choose icons that visually represent your item categories. With 60+ icons available (from swords and shields to phones and rockets), you can find something that fits most genres.

Click the edit button next to any item type to modify its name. Click the icon to change it. Changes apply immediately to all items using that type. The icon helps you quickly identify item types at a glance in the Items page, making it easier to scan your inventory visually.

Use the up and down arrow buttons to reorder your item types. The order affects how types appear in dropdown menus when creating or editing items. Put your most frequently used types at the top for quicker access.

Click the delete button next to an item type to remove it. A confirmation dialog will warn you that any items using that type will need a new type assigned. Note: Deleting an item type doesn't delete the items themselves; they'll remain in your project, but you'll need to assign them a different type.

Penpoint's Standard template includes ten default item types: Personal Effects, Documents, Clothing & Accessories, Tools & Equipment, Weapons & Armor, Vehicles, Consumables, Technology, Artifacts, and Miscellaneous. Other templates include their own genre-specific types. Feel free to modify, delete, or replace these defaults to match your story's needs.

The Locations page helps you organize the places in your story. You can nest locations inside each other: for example, a kingdom containing cities, each city containing buildings. Whether you're building a sprawling fantasy world or tracking a few key settings, the Locations page gives you complete control over how you structure and visualize your story's geography.

On the Locations page, you can: Create locations with importance levels (labels like Primary, Secondary, or Background that help you track how significant a location is) and customizable types Put locations inside other locations: cities inside kingdoms, rooms inside buildings, and so on Show or hide the locations inside another location by clicking the small arrow next to it Sort locations by creation date, alphabetically, or by type Drag and drop to reorganize where locations sit in the list; changes are saved automatically, and you can always drag things back if you change your mind Track which characters and items are at each location Navigate using breadcrumb trails that show a location's full nesting path Note: Writing a series? Locations are shared across every Book. Presence: Which Books a Character Is In controls where each one appears, and the This Book vs All Books view narrows this list.

Every location can have a type (City, Region, Building, etc.) that you customize to match your story's needs. You decide what types exist and how they're ordered. Manage your location types in Settings (the gear icon in the sidebar) under Location Types. You can create, edit, delete, and reorder types to match your world-building system. Tip: If you delete a type, any locations using it will just show "No type selected" — the locations themselves are not deleted.
This guide covers creating, managing, and deleting locations in Penpoint. All location data auto-saves as you type.
There are three ways to create a new location:
Click the Add New Location button at the top of the hierarchy (the location list on the left side of the screen) to create a top-level location that isn't nested inside anything.

Click the + button next to any location to create a child location underneath it. This is the fastest way to build your hierarchy as you go. Type the location name, then press Enter to create or Escape to cancel. The character counter changes color as you type — it turns yellow above 30 characters and red at 35, because 35 characters is the maximum length.

Press Ctrl+N (or Cmd+N on Mac) from anywhere in the app to open the Quick Create menu, then select Location to create one quickly. Tip: Build your hierarchy as you write. Start with broad regions, then add cities, districts, and specific buildings as they appear in your story.

Like characters, locations have three importance levels: Primary (major settings where key events happen), Secondary (supporting locations with moderate presence), and Background (minor locations mentioned occasionally). Change a location's importance level in Edit mode (click the pencil button at the top of the detail area to switch) using the dropdown in the detail panel (the area on the right side of the screen showing the location's information). In a series, importance is kept separately for each Book, so a location central to Book 1 can fade into the background of Book 2. See Importance Across Books. For more information about editing location details, see Location Detail View.

To delete a location, select it, switch to Edit mode, scroll to the bottom of the detail panel, and click Delete Location. If the location has sub-locations (the locations nested inside this one), Penpoint shows a confirmation dialog before anything is removed. You'll see two deletion options: Delete & Preserve Children: Removes this location but keeps all the locations inside it. They move up one level: if the deleted location had a parent, they become children of that parent; if it was a top-level location, they become top-level locations themselves. Delete All: Permanently removes this location and all the locations inside it, including all their data: tags, character assignments, item assignments, and chapter appearances. This action cannot be undone, so Penpoint asks you to confirm before proceeding.

Tip: Penpoint remembers which locations you had expanded or collapsed. When you close and reopen Penpoint, the location list will look exactly the way you left it. Unlike characters, which appear in a simple list, your locations are organized in a nested list where locations can contain other locations. This mirrors how places work in real life: a continent contains countries, countries contain cities, cities contain districts, and so on. To nest one location inside another, drag it onto the location you want to use as a container, or click the + button on any location to create a new location inside it.

The location list shows which locations are inside which other locations. Tree lines connect inner locations to the ones that contain them, making the structure easy to understand at a glance. Tip: Most stories use 4-5 levels of nesting (continent, country, city, district, building, for example). Penpoint supports up to 25 levels deep if you need them.

Click the small arrow next to any location to show or hide the locations inside it: A downward-pointing arrow - The location is expanded, showing everything inside it A right-pointing arrow - The location is collapsed, hiding what is inside No arrow - The location has nothing inside it Use the Expand All / Collapse All button at the top of the location list to quickly show or hide everything at once.
When you select a deeply nested location, Penpoint automatically expands all the locations above it to show the full path. This ensures you can always see where a location sits in the list.

At the top of the detail area on the right side of the screen, Penpoint shows a location path from the outermost location down to the one you have selected. Click any location in the path to jump directly to it. This is the fastest way to navigate up through several levels.

For deeply nested locations (more than 5 levels), the path shows the first 2 locations, then "...", then the last 2 locations. This keeps the path readable while still showing the most important context.
Penpoint gives you several ways to organize your location list: sorting modes and drag-to-reorder for rearranging your nested locations.
The sort dropdown in the bar at the top of your locations list offers three ways to order your locations:
The default sort mode. Locations appear in the order you created them, which often matches the order they appear in your story or outline.
Sorts all locations alphabetically by name, making it easy to find a specific place when you have many locations.

Sorts locations by their type (City, Region, Building, etc.), then alphabetically within each type. The type order follows the custom order you set in Location Types settings (found under Settings > Item & Location Types). Note: Sorting only changes how your locations are listed — it doesn't move them in or out of their groups.

Click the Edit button in the bar at the top of the list to enter drag-to-reorder mode. This lets you rearrange your locations by dragging them to new positions. When you're done, click Edit again to leave the mode.

Click and hold on any location, then drag it to a new position. You'll see guides showing where the location will land: Drop on another location - Places the dragged location inside the target location Drop at the top or bottom edge - Makes the dragged location a top-level location (not nested inside anything) Drop target highlight - A colored ring appears around a location to show it will become the new parent

Penpoint prevents moves that wouldn't make sense: You can't nest a location inside one of its own sub-locations: that would create a loop. Locations can be nested many levels deep, but Penpoint caps it at 25 to keep things practical. Tip: Drag-to-reorder works across all sort modes. You can switch to alphabetical sort to find a location easily, then switch back to creation date to reorder it.

The detail panel (the area on the right side of the screen where your location's information appears) shows everything about the selected location. Like the Characters page, you can switch between View mode (for reading your location at a glance) and Edit mode (for making changes to any field). Learn more about the difference between these modes in View Mode vs Edit Mode.
The header shows the location's path, icon, name, and the View/Edit toggle.

The location path displays the full hierarchy from the root to the current location. Click any location in the path to navigate directly to it. See Location Hierarchy for more details about location path navigation.

Each location has a customizable icon. In Edit mode, click the icon to open the icon picker and choose from categorized icon sets (Buildings, Nature, Regions, Infrastructure). Learn more in Location Icons.
In Edit mode, the name becomes an editable field. Names can be up to 35 characters and auto-save as you type.

Locations can have a profile picture, just like characters. In Edit mode, click the image area to upload a photo, or drag and drop an image file onto it. You can crop and reposition the image before saving. In View mode, click the picture to see it full-size. To change or remove an existing image, switch to Edit mode and hover over the image to reveal edit and remove buttons.
Two side-by-side dropdowns let you set the location's type and importance level.

Select a location type from your customized types (City, Region, Building, etc.). Types help you organize and sort locations. If you don't see a specific type or want to modify them, manage types in Settings > Location Types.

Like characters, locations have three importance levels: Primary (major settings), Secondary (supporting locations), and Background (minor locations). Note: All fields auto-save as you work: name, description, type, importance, and icon. There is no save button; your changes are preserved automatically.

The description field uses a text area that supports formatting like bold, italic, and links. You can also type @ followed by a name to create a clickable link to another character, item, or location. The description editor works the same as the Paragraph Block: you can use bold, italic, and @Mentions to create clickable links to your characters, items, and locations. In View mode, the description appears as formatted text with @ mention links. Click any mention to navigate directly to it.

This section shows which characters are currently at this location (useful for tracking who is where in your story). In View mode, click any character to navigate to their detail page. In Edit mode, the dashed Add character row at the bottom of the list opens an inline search that suggests characters not already placed here. Hover any assigned character to reveal the trash icon — removing only unlinks them from this location; it does not delete the character itself.

The Items section works identically to Characters, but for items at this location. Each item shows its archetype icon next to the name, and clicking it in View mode navigates to the item's detail page. In Edit mode, use the dashed Add item row to assign an existing item, or pick Create New Item… from the search dropdown to create one on the fly.

Lists the key moments that happen at this location. The same event can also appear on the characters and items involved: it's one event in several places, not a copy. In Edit mode, use Add event to add an event you've already made, or create a new one. Removing an event here only takes it off this location; it stays on everyone else it involves. For how events work across your book, see Events.

If a location has children, the sub-locations section appears showing the locations directly inside it in a grid layout. Each sub-location displays with its icon and name. Click any sub-location to navigate to it instantly. Tip: The sub-locations grid only shows the locations directly inside it, not locations nested further down. This keeps the view focused and uncluttered.

The tags section works identically to character tags. Tags are universal across characters, items, chapters, locations, and notes; a tag created for a location is available everywhere. Learn more about creating and managing tags in Managing Tags.

In Edit mode, a Delete Location button appears at the bottom of the panel. Clicking it opens a confirmation dialog that explains exactly what will be removed and asks you to confirm before anything is deleted. If the location has sub-locations, the dialog gives you the option to preserve them or delete them along with the parent. This action cannot be undone, so review the confirmation carefully.

Every location has an icon you can change. It appears in the location list on the left side of the screen, the top of the detail area (the right side of the screen where your location's information appears), and the grid of locations nested inside the current one. Icons provide quick visual identification and make your locations easier to tell apart at a glance.

Switch to Edit mode (click the pencil button at the top of the detail area), then click the location's icon at the top of the detail area to open the icon picker. The picker shows icons organized into four categories: Buildings - Homes, churches, schools, warehouses, monuments, and other structures Nature - Trees, mountains, water, weather, and natural phenomena Regions - Globes, maps, compasses, flags, and geographic markers Infrastructure - Roads, bridges, transportation, and civic facilities Click any icon to select it. The currently selected icon shows a colored ring highlight. Click Select Icon to apply your choice, or Cancel to keep the current icon. Tip: Choose icons that match the location's function or type. A city might use a globe or map marker, while a specific building could use a home, church, or warehouse icon.

New locations start with the marked map icon (a map with a pin on it). You can change this at any time — icons are just for looks, and changing them doesn't change how your location works. To go back to the default, pick the marked map icon from the Regions category.

The Chapters page is where you organize your book's structure. It pairs an outline of chapters and scenes on the left with the right side of the screen, where chapter details appear. Scenes are where you fill in details like dates, characters, locations, and more. The same scenes are written in Manuscript Mode. It helps to keep two things straight as you work here. Chapters hold your scenes: they carry the chapter number, title, and overall identity readers will see. Scenes are where your actual Worldbuilding content lives. A scene holds its own details (dates, characters present, locations, items, and so on) and corresponds to a stretch of prose you'll write in Manuscript Mode. Every chapter has at least one scene, even if you never give it a name. Essentially, in a single-scene chapter, the chapter itself is the scene. So even if you never use individual scenes in Penpoint, for the sake of clarity, the root chapter itself is considered a 'single-scene chapter.'

Most of your time on this page starts in the outline. Click a chapter or scene there, and its details appear on the right. The Chapter Outline: the tree on the left side of the page. The Corkboard: a second view that lays your chapters out as index cards. Placeholder Cards: sticky notes for chapters you haven't written yet.

Everything you can do to add, rename, rearrange, combine, or remove chapters and scenes lives in these articles: Creating Chapters and Scenes: adding new chapters or scenes. Editing Chapter and Scene Details: filling in the details on the right side of the screen. Reordering and Organizing Chapters: moving items earlier or later, or between chapters. Chapter Groups (Folders): gathering related chapters into acts or parts. Merging and Deleting: combining items, or removing them safely.

The right side of the page is built from blocks (small sections like a date field, a character list, or a notes field). You decide which blocks appear and in what order, then fill them in for each scene. Customizing Chapter Layout: adding, removing, and reordering blocks. Chapter Block Types: what each block is for and when to use it. Calendar Block: placing scenes on your book's timeline. Assigning Things to Scenes: connecting characters, locations, and items to a scene.

Chapters don't live in isolation. These articles cover how the page connects to the rest of your book: Open in Manuscript: jumping straight from a scene to the prose you're writing. Calendar Settings: configuring the book-level calendar that scene dates use. If this is your first time on the page, start with The Chapter Outline. Once the outline makes sense, everything else follows naturally.

The Chapter Outline is the tree on the left side of the Chapters page. It shows every chapter in your book (and every scene inside each chapter) as a single, scannable list. This is your primary way to move around the Chapters page: click a chapter or scene here, and its details appear on the right. The outline stays where it is no matter which view you're in, so it works the same way when you switch the right side over to The Corkboard.

Chapters are listed in the order they appear in your book, with their chapter number alongside the title. When you've assigned a color to a chapter or scene, the row shows that color as a small square: a quick visual cue you can use however you like (point of view, mood, draft state). Chapters that contain more than one scene have a small triangle (called a chevron) on the left. Click the triangle to show or hide that chapter's scenes. Scenes appear tucked slightly to the right under their chapter, so it's always clear what belongs to what. You can also organize chapters into groups: folders that hold a stretch of related chapters, like an act or a part. Groups have their own triangle and behave the same way: click to open or close the folder. For everything you can do with groups, see Chapter Groups (Folders).

Click any chapter or scene to select it. Its details load into the right side of the screen, where you can read or edit them — covered in Editing Chapter and Scene Details. To rename a chapter, scene, or group without leaving the outline, double-click its title. An inline text field opens right where the name was. Type the new name and press Enter to save, or Escape to cancel. Tip: Scene titles are optional. If you leave one blank, the outline shows the scene's opening words in italics instead, or "Empty scene" if you haven't written anything yet. The right side of the screen falls back to "Untitled Scene".

Alongside your chapters you may see rows with a dashed edge and a small "Placeholder" label. These are sticky notes for chapters you haven't written yet: they hold a spot in your outline but stay out of your manuscript entirely. Everything you can do with one is on its right-click menu. See Placeholder Cards.

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any chapter, scene, or group to open a context menu with everything you can do to that item: insert a new chapter before or after, change a status color, create a group, merge with the previous item, delete, and more. Right-clicking empty space in the outline opens a smaller menu for creating a new chapter or group from scratch. Each menu has its own dedicated article so you don't have to hunt for what each option does: Creating Chapters and Scenes: adding new chapters or scenes from the outline. Reordering and Organizing Chapters: moving items earlier or later. Chapter Groups (Folders): creating, naming, and using groups. Merging and Deleting: combining items or removing them safely.

The outline has a resize bar along its right edge. Click and drag it to make the outline wider or narrower (useful when chapter titles get long, or when you want more room for the details on the right). Your chosen width is remembered the next time you open the app, so you set it once and it stays.

When you want maximum room for chapter and scene details, you can hide the outline entirely. Click the Collapse outline icon (a small icon at the top of the outline header that looks like a panel with an arrow pointing left). The whole tree slides away and leaves a thin strip down the left side. Click the icon on that thin strip to slide the outline back out at its previous width. Tip: The Chapters page and Manuscript Mode each remember their own outline width and collapsed state, so you can keep the outline wide for planning and slim for writing without one bleeding into the other. For broader navigation tips across Penpoint, see Sidebar & Navigation.
Chapter View Modes: By Group or By Scene
Chapter View Modes: By Group or By Scene

Sometimes you want to compare one thing across a whole chapter. Other times you want everything about a single scene in one place. When a chapter holds several scenes, Penpoint can arrange it either way: By Group, which is the default, or By Scene. The button that swaps between them sits on the strip across the top of the chapter page, beside New Scene and Edit. It has a small icon of two stacked rows and reads View Mode: Group or View Mode: Scene, naming the view you're in.

The default arrangement groups content by block. Blocks are the boxes that make up a chapter page, and your layout is the set you've chosen for every chapter. One Description block holds every scene's description, one Characters block every scene's cast, and so on, each broken down by scene inside. Reading four descriptions one after another tells you whether a chapter's shape is working, and a scene you haven't filled in yet sits there as a blank line, which is exactly what you want when you're checking what still needs doing.

Here each scene gets its own section, with your layout repeated inside it. Use it when you want to know what happens in a given scene without hunting for the pieces. It reads the way the chapter reads: this happened, then this happened, then this happened. Note: Both views show the same information and use the same layout you set up. Nothing is hidden in one and shown in the other, and switching between them changes nothing about your book. Pick whichever suits what you're doing right now. On a chapter with only one scene, or when you've picked a single scene from the outline (the chapter list down the left), both arrangements look identical, so the page won't appear to change. The button stays put, ready for the moment you add a second scene.

Story Arcs (the plot threads you follow across a book) and tags pinned to the chapter belong to the whole chapter rather than to any one scene. By Scene gathers them into a Whole Chapter section above the first scene; By Group keeps them under a Whole chapter heading inside the Story Arcs and Tags blocks. Tags on individual scenes stay with their scene. Tip: In By Scene, click a scene's heading to fold it away, and click again to open it back up. Nothing inside is lost while it's folded, and Penpoint remembers which sections you left folded.

At the right-hand end of that strip is a gear icon (hover it and it says View options) holding a Hide empty blocks option. Switch it on and blocks you haven't filled in drop out of sight: nothing is deleted, and switching it off brings them straight back. Story Arcs always stays, as does Calculate, which works a number out from two others and so always has something to show. Everything reappears the moment you press Edit, so there's never a block you can't get at to fill in. In By Group a block only goes if it's empty for every scene, and empty lines inside a surviving block are tucked away too. In By Scene an empty scene keeps its heading and says so.

Both are display settings: they change how things look, never what's inside a book. Penpoint carries them across every book you open and shares them with the Minipen (the reference sidebar beside your prose in Manuscript mode). The Minipen has no room for the button, so both settings live under its gear icon. Which blocks appear in the first place is up to you: see Customizing Chapter Layout.

The Corkboard is a second way to look at the Chapters page. Instead of reading your book as a list, you see every chapter as an index card laid out across the screen, the way you'd spread notecards on a table. It's built for the moment when you're not writing yet: you're deciding what happens, and in what order.

At the very top of the Chapters page are two buttons: Chapters and Corkboard. Click Corkboard and the right side of the screen becomes the board. Click Chapters to go back to the usual chapter details. Penpoint remembers which view you were last in, so the board is still there when you reopen your book. The outline (the list of every chapter and scene down the left side of the page) stays put in both views, so you never lose your place. See The Chapter Outline.

Each card shows the chapter title and a short summary. Penpoint writes the words in which at the start for you and you supply the rest, so the finished line reads like a classic chapter heading: in which the letter arrives too late. It's the same summary you'd fill in on the Chapters page. Numbered chapters also carry their number in a small box beside the title; a chapter you've set as unnumbered (a prologue, say) simply shows its title. Underneath, a small line of extra detail shows things like the draft status and whose point of view the chapter follows. A chapter with a color shows it as a small ribbon in the corner of the card, so you can sweep your eye down the board and see your color-coding at a glance.
Writing Summaries Right on the Board

Click the summary area of any card and it turns into a text box you can type in, prompting you with What happens in this chapter…. This is the heart of the Corkboard: you can sit down with an empty board and write one sentence per chapter until the shape of the book appears. Your typing saves on its own after a short pause, and again the moment you click away. There's no save button to hunt for.

Look for a small gear (cog-shaped) button in the strip of buttons sitting directly above the cards (marker 3 in Figure 1). This is a different row from the Chapters and Corkboard buttons at the very top of the page. Click the cog and the first thing you'll find is Card Size, with three choices: Compact: small cards showing the first three lines of each summary, so you can see far more of your book at once. Good for getting the shape of the whole thing. Standard: four lines of summary. The everyday size, and what you start with. Large: roomy cards with up to eight lines on show. Good for actually reading what you wrote. A smaller card only shows you less; it never shortens anything. Your full summary is safe, and all of it comes back when you pick a bigger card. If a summary runs past what the card can show, it simply trails off with a "…". Your size choice is remembered, and it applies to every book you open rather than just this one. Because Compact cards are short, they're best for scanning and reordering: if you want to sit and rewrite your summaries, Standard or Large gives you more room to type into.

Underneath the size choices, the same cog gives you Show on Cards: a short list of details you can switch on or off. Subtitle: the smaller line under the chapter title. Status: the chapter's status label (Draft, for instance), the same one you set elsewhere in Penpoint. Point of view: which characters the chapter follows. First line of prose: the opening words of what you've actually written. Off to start with. Chapter notes: the chapter's Chapter Notes field, the same rich text you see on the chapter page. Click it on a card to write in it directly; bold, italics, and the other keyboard shortcuts all work. The summary line stays a quick one-liner; this is where the longer thinking goes. The summary line is always shown and can't be switched off. Your choices are remembered for next time. Compact cards are too small to fit the subtitle, the first line of prose, or the chapter notes, so those go gray while you're using that size. You'll notice their ticks stay put: that's deliberate. Nothing has been switched off or forgotten, the card simply hasn't the room right now, and they come straight back the moment you pick a bigger card. Tip: Turning on First line of prose turns the board into a quick way to see which chapters you've actually started. Cards with nothing written stand out immediately.

Chapters with more than one scene show a small strip of scene cards tucked underneath. A chapter with a single scene doesn't show one, because the chapter card is that scene. Click a scene card to open it up and see more: its status, its point of view, and how many words you've written in it. The same Show on Cards choices apply here, so a detail you've switched off won't appear on the scene cards either. Click again to close. You can leave as many scene cards open as you like, and they'll still be open the next time you come back.

Dragging a card reorders your actual book, not just the picture on the board. When you move a chapter, the whole chapter travels with it: its summary, its scenes, and every word you've written inside them. Nothing is deleted; the order is the only thing that changes. Pick up any card and drag it. A bright line shows where it will land. Changed your mind halfway? Press Escape before you let go and the card springs straight back to where it started. When you do let go, the surrounding cards fade out, shuffle, and fade back in. Numbered chapters renumber themselves automatically. Chapter cards can be dropped anywhere on the board. Scene cards can be dragged within their chapter, or dropped into a different chapter's scene strip. Note: Once you've dropped a card, the move can't be undone with Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac); you'll need to drag it back yourself.

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) a chapter card and you'll get the same menu the outline gives you: rename it, insert a chapter before or after, change its color or status, or add a scene. Right-click empty space on the board to create a new chapter or a new placeholder right there. That menu also holds merging and deleting. Those two reshape your book rather than just tidy it, so they have an article of their own that walks through what happens to your writing first: Merging and Deleting.
Cards for Chapters You Haven't Written

The board also holds a second kind of card. A placeholder is a sticky note for an idea you're not ready to commit to: it sits on the board and in your outline, stays out of your manuscript, and turns into a real chapter whenever you say so. You can tell them apart by their dashed edge. See Placeholder Cards.

Placeholder Cards: sticky notes for chapters you haven't written yet. The Chapter Outline: the list down the left side, shown in both views. Reordering and Organizing Chapters: moving chapters from the outline instead. Editing Chapter and Scene Details: the full detail view behind each card.

Sometimes you know something happens between Chapter 4 and Chapter 5, but not what yet. A placeholder is a sticky note for exactly that: it holds the spot and the idea without becoming a real chapter. When the idea firms up, you turn it into one. Placeholders live in your chapter outline and on the Corkboard, the index-card view of your book. See The Corkboard.

This is the point of the whole feature. A placeholder never appears in Manuscript Mode (the side of Penpoint where you write your prose), never lands in an export, never shows up in search, and never adds to your word count. It holds no scenes, links to no characters or items, and takes no chapter number, so your Chapter 5 stays Chapter 5 no matter how many placeholders sit around it. Scatter as many as you like; none of them touch your real book. All of that holds right up until you promote the card. That's the moment it becomes a real chapter, with everything that comes with it.

Add a placeholder with the + Placeholder button above the Corkboard, by right-clicking (or Ctrl+click on Mac) empty space on the board, or from the + button at the top of the chapter outline. It lands just after the chapter you had selected, and you can drag it elsewhere anytime. A card has a title and a note. Click either one and type; both save on their own. In the title, Enter finishes and Tab jumps down to the note. Whatever you write carries over when you promote.
Turning a Placeholder Into a Real Chapter

When you're ready to write it, promote the card. Penpoint confirms first, because this reshapes your book: the new chapter takes the placeholder's spot, and every chapter after it moves up a number (the one that was 5 becomes 6, and so on). The confirmation window shows the number it will take and lets you tidy the title and details first. Everything you'd written, color included, is already filled in. The placeholder is removed, and you land on the new chapter. Note: Promoting can't be undone. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) won't bring the placeholder back, so check the confirmation window before you click through it. From there it's an ordinary chapter with an empty scene, ready to write in. See Editing Chapter and Scene Details.

Select a card to reveal buttons for its color, promote, and delete along the bottom edge. Right-clicking the card, or its dashed row in the outline, offers the same actions plus Rename, Move Earlier, and Move Later. Dragging sets where the card sits in your book's order; it travels with the chapter above it. If you delete or merge away that chapter, the card stays where the chapter was, right after the chapter that came before it (or at the start of its folder, or the top of the book if nothing came before). Note: Deleting a card asks you first and warns that its notes will be lost. There's no undo, so read the question before you click through it.

Placeholders can live inside a chapter group, including one that holds no chapters yet. This is what lets you rough out a whole section (say, an empty Act II folder) as a stack of cards before any of it is written. Promote one of those cards and the new chapter appears inside the same folder. Folders live in the chapter outline on the Chapters page, the list down the left side, so that's where you put cards into them. Grab a card by the small handle at the left edge of its row (it appears when you hover it), then drag it onto the folder. A folder with nothing in it shows the words Empty group: drop your card on those and it becomes the first thing in the folder. Once there's a card in there the label is gone, so from then on drop the next one onto a card already inside. Drop a card under one of the folder's chapters instead and it rides along with that chapter. Watch the folder while you drag: it tints and draws an outline around itself when the card is going inside it. If it doesn't light up, the card is landing beside the folder rather than in it. Changed your mind mid-drag? Press Esc to call the whole thing off. A folder's header shows a sticky-note icon and a number for the cards it holds, so you can tell at a glance that a closed folder still has your notes inside. Note: A collapsed folder can't take a dropped card. Expand it first so you can see where the card is going to land. Note: The Corkboard doesn't draw folders, so cards in a folder appear there as part of the ordinary run of cards. Moving one on the Corkboard positions it against the chapters around it, which can take it out of its folder. If you're arranging folders, do it in the outline.

The Corkboard: the index-card view placeholders were built for. Chapter Groups (Folders): the folders placeholders can live inside. Creating Chapters and Scenes: making a real chapter instead. The Chapter Outline: the list where placeholders also appear.

New chapters and new scenes are both born from the Chapter Outline on the left side of the Chapters page. Whether you're starting a fresh chapter or slipping a scene into the middle of one you've already drafted, it all happens with a right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac); for scenes, there's also a quick button at the top of the chapter's detail area on the right.

To add a brand-new chapter, right-click empty space anywhere in the outline and choose New Chapter (the + at the top of the outline works too). The New Chapter window opens, and the chapter you create goes right after the chapter you have selected, inside the same group if it sits in one. With nothing selected, it lands at the bottom of the list with the next available number. The window asks for a few things, all of them optional except your imagination: Chapter Title: what readers see at the top of the chapter. Up to 50 characters. Leave it blank if you only want a number. Subtitle: a smaller line under the title, useful for date stamps, points of view, or epigraphs. Up to 100 characters. In which...: a one-sentence summary in the spirit of classic chapter headings. This is your private note about what the chapter does. Up to 100 characters. Chapter Type: defaults to Standard. Other types (like Prologue or Epilogue) help you classify chapters that sit outside the regular numbered sequence. Numbered chapter: a checkbox controlling whether this chapter shows up in the numbered sequence. More on this below. When you're happy, click Create Chapter. The new chapter appears in the outline, already selected, ready for details.
Inserting a Chapter Before or After

More often, you'll want to drop a new chapter between two existing ones. Right-click any chapter in the outline and you'll see two options near the top of the menu: Insert Chapter Before: opens the New Chapter window with the new chapter aimed at the slot just before the one you clicked. Insert Chapter After: opens it aimed at the slot just after. The window itself shows you exactly where the chapter is going. A pair of Before / After buttons sit at the top so you can flip your mind between them, and a large "Chapter N" preview updates underneath to show the number this chapter will take when you save. Any chapters that came after the insert point get bumped one number higher automatically. Note: Inserting a chapter shifts every later chapter's number. If you reference chapter numbers in notes or scene summaries, those references won't auto-update. Re-read after a big insertion to make sure nothing's stale.
When You're Not Ready to Commit

If you know something belongs between two chapters but you don't know what it is yet, you don't have to make a real chapter for it. A placeholder holds the spot without taking a number, without shifting anything, and without appearing in your manuscript. You can promote it into a full chapter later, and everything you wrote on it carries over. See Placeholder Cards.

Most chapters belong in the numbered sequence: Chapter 1, Chapter 2, and so on. But some don't. A Prologue, Epilogue, or Interlude usually sits outside the count, and forcing it into the sequence pushes every other chapter's number off by one. Uncheck Numbered chapter and the chapter still appears in your outline in its proper position, but it doesn't claim a number. The numbered chapters around it keep their original order undisturbed. You can change your mind anytime: right-click the chapter and turn Numbered Chapter on or off in its right-click menu. Tip: Pair an unnumbered chapter with a custom Chapter Type ("Prologue", "Interlude") to make its role in the book obvious at a glance in the outline.

Every new chapter is born with one scene already inside it. If your chapter is a single uninterrupted unit of prose, that's all you'll ever need. Write it and move on. The outline won't even show the scene as a separate row until a chapter has more than one. When a chapter needs to break into multiple scenes (a viewpoint shift, a time jump, a cut to a different location), you can add as many scenes as you like. There are two ways to do it: Right-click the chapter in the outline and choose New Scene. With the chapter selected, click the New Scene button in the top-right of the wide strip at the top of the chapter view on the right side of the page. Either way, the new scene appears at the end of that chapter's scene list, the chapter auto-expands so you can see it, and the new scene is selected and ready to fill in. Scene titles are optional: leave one blank and the outline labels it "Empty scene" until you start writing, then shows your opening words in italics instead. The right-hand side falls back to "Untitled Scene". Tip: You can always add a scene to a chapter that currently has only one. The first time you do, the outline starts showing the scenes as a small list under the chapter so you can navigate between them. Once a chapter or scene exists, the right-hand side is where you flesh it out. See Editing Chapter and Scene Details.

When you select a chapter or scene from the outline on the left, its details load into the right side of the screen. A slim control bar sits at the very top and stays put as you scroll. Below it is a wide colored strip holding the chapter or scene's identity and its core fields, and below that, additional blocks fill out the rest of the page. This article covers the control bar, that top strip, and the fields you'll edit there most often.
The Top of the Chapter View

Every chapter and scene has its own wide colored strip at the top of the chapter view. On the left sits a small label showing the chapter or scene number, with a colored ribbon if you've assigned a color. On the right is the title and a stack of detail fields.

Above that strip sits a row of controls pinned to the top of the chapter view. It stays there as you scroll, so the buttons are always in reach however deep into a long chapter you go. Once the title itself scrolls up out of sight, the bar quietly shows the chapter or scene's name in its place, so you never lose track of what you're looking at. It holds five controls: View Mode: Group / View Mode: Scene: arranges a multi-scene chapter either by block or one section per scene. The button names the view you're in now. New Scene: adds a new scene to the chapter you're viewing. Edit / View: switches between reading and editing (more on this below). Manuscript: jumps to this chapter or scene in Manuscript Mode so you can write prose. The cog: labeled View options. It opens a short menu holding the Hide empty blocks setting. When a chapter has more than one scene, the blocks below that strip cover every scene in the chapter, so you can read or edit the whole thing in one place. How they're arranged depends on which View Mode you've picked. For what the two arrangements do and when each one helps, see Chapter View Modes: By Group or By Scene.
Switching Between View and Edit Mode

The Edit button in the control bar (a pencil icon) flips into edit mode; once there, the same button becomes View (an eye icon) to flip back. You can also press Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on Mac) anywhere on the Chapters page, as long as a chapter or scene is selected, to switch modes without reaching for the mouse. Both modes work the same way they do everywhere else in Penpoint. For the full breakdown, see View Mode vs Edit Mode.

When a chapter is selected, that strip shows the chapter's identity and details. In edit mode you can change: Title: the chapter title (up to 50 characters). Subtitle: an optional second line under the title. In which: a one-sentence summary of what happens in the chapter. Shown in italics, prefixed with "in which" so it reads like a Victorian table of contents entry. Type: pick from Standard, Prologue, Opening, Transition, Flashback, Interlude, Confrontation, Climax, Resolution, or Epilogue. Anything other than Standard is listed in the details row beneath the title. Standard, Prologue, Epilogue, and Interlude are the familiar writing terms most authors will recognize; the others (Opening, Transition, Flashback, Confrontation, Climax, Resolution) are extra labels you can use if they help you, or ignore if they don't. Status: one of Draft, Revised, Polished, or Final. Scenes use the same four stages. Color: a 12-color palette plus a "no color" option. Your choice appears as a ribbon bookmark on the small label, and in the outline it fills a small square behind the chapter's icon. Is Numbered: switch between Enabled and Disabled.
