Numbered chapters get sequential numbers in the outline and table of contents; unnumbered chapters (prologues, interludes, epilogues) sit in the order without taking a number. Chapter Notes: a rich text field for chapter-level notes that don't belong inside the manuscript itself. Useful for outlines, reminders, or beats you want to hit. These same notes appear on the chapter's index card in the Corkboard view, where you can edit them too. When a chapter has scenes assigned to point-of-view characters, that top strip also lists those POV characters as a read-only summary. To change a scene's POV, select that scene in the outline and edit it there. The strip also carries an Events in this chapter line: every event anchored to the chapter, whether you linked it to the whole chapter or to one of its scenes. In edit mode, the + links an existing event to the chapter and the × beside an event unlinks it (the event itself lives on; only its link to this chapter is removed). Events are created and fleshed out on your character, item, and location pages. To learn how they work, see Events. Tip: Every dropdown here (Type, Status, Color, Is Numbered) saves the moment you pick it; there's no Save button to chase. Typed fields autosave a moment after you stop typing.

Selecting a scene swaps that strip into a slimmer scene view. Under the title, a small location label reads "A scene in [chapter title]" so you always know which chapter the scene belongs to. The small label shows "Scene" and the scene's number within the chapter. Scenes carry a smaller set of fields than chapters: Title: the scene title. Optional; blank scenes show "Untitled Scene". Status: same four-tier progression as chapters (Draft, Revised, Polished, Final). Color: same 12-color palette as chapters, used for the scene's ribbon and for a small colored square beside the scene in the outline. Scenes also display their POV characters as a read-only summary when you've assigned point-of-view characters to them.

That strip is just the top of the chapter view. Below it sit configurable blocks: calendar entries, related characters, plot points, and more. To add, remove, or reorder those blocks, see Customizing Chapter Layout. For an overview of what each block does, see Chapter Block Types.

Stories rarely arrive in their final order. A chapter that was meant to be sixth turns out to belong third. The Chapter Outline lets you nudge chapters into place one step at a time using the right-click menu. Note: Reordering chapters cannot be undone with Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac). If you move a chapter to the wrong spot, you'll need to move it back manually using the same Move Earlier / Move Later commands.

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any chapter and you'll see two options near the top of the menu: Move Earlier: shifts the chapter up by one position in the outline. Move Later: shifts the chapter down by one position. These options are grayed out when the chapter is already at the top or bottom of the list. There's nowhere further to go. Numbered chapters renumber automatically after each move.

Stepping a chapter one slot at a time gets tedious when it needs to travel a long way. Switch the Chapters page over to The Corkboard and you can pick a chapter up and drop it wherever you want in one motion. The same renumbering rules apply, and the same warning above about Ctrl+Z still holds; but you can press Escape mid-drag to call the move off before you let go.

Sometimes you don't want to move an existing chapter: you want to slot a new one into a specific place. Right-click any chapter and choose: Insert Chapter Before: opens the New Chapter window aimed at the slot just before the chapter you clicked. Insert Chapter After: opens it aimed at the slot just after. The full creation flow (including titles, subtitles, and the Numbered chapter setting) lives in Creating Chapters and Scenes.

Numbered chapters keep themselves in order without you having to think about it. Whenever a chapter is moved, inserted, or deleted, every numbered chapter renumbers from the top of the book down. If you slip a new chapter between Chapter 4 and Chapter 5, the old Chapter 5 becomes Chapter 6, the old Chapter 6 becomes Chapter 7, and so on through the rest of the book. Chapters that aren't numbered (a Prologue, an Epilogue, an Interlude) sit out of the count entirely. They keep their position in the outline but don't claim a number, so the chapters around them don't have to shuffle when one is added or removed. The Numbered chapter setting is covered in Creating Chapters and Scenes and Editing Chapter and Scene Details. Tip: If you reference chapter numbers in your scene summaries or notes, those references won't auto-update when chapters renumber. After a big rearrangement, it's worth a quick scan to make sure nothing's pointing at the wrong chapter.

Once a book grows past a handful of chapters, the outline can start to feel like a long scroll. Chapter Groups are simple folders that let you bundle a stretch of related chapters together (an act, a part, a long arc) and open or close them as one. They live entirely inside the outline; nothing about your chapters or scenes changes when you put them in a folder.

A group is a named folder with chapters tucked inside it. You'll see it in the outline with a folder icon and a small triangle (called a chevron): click the triangle to open the folder and reveal its chapters, click again to fold them away. The chapters themselves keep their numbers, their scenes, and everything else; the folder just gathers them under a single label. Common ways writers use them: Act One / Act Two / Act Three for a three-act novel, or Part One / Part Two for a longer book. Groups are entirely optional: if you don't need them, your outline simply stays flat. Note: Groups are for acts and parts within a single book. Writing an actual series? Each volume gets its own Book (with its own chapters and outline) inside one series file. See Writing a Series.

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) anywhere in the outline to start a new group. There are two starting points, depending on where you click: Create Group: appears when you right-click an existing chapter. The new group is created with that chapter already inside it as its first member, so you don't have to file it in afterward. New Group: appears when you right-click empty space below the chapter list. This makes an empty group you can fill by right-clicking chapters and choosing Add to Group. In both cases, the new group lands in the outline ready for naming: type the name and press Enter to save, or Escape to cancel.

To rename a group, double-click its name in the outline. An inline text field opens right where the name was; type the new name and press Enter to save, or Escape to leave it as it was. You can also right-click the group and choose Rename Group from the menu: same result, just a different way in.

Right-click a chapter that isn't already in a group and choose Add to Group. A submenu lists every group in your book — click one and the chapter slides in at the end of that folder. To take a chapter back out, right-click it inside its group and choose Remove from Group. The chapter pops out to the top level of the outline, landing immediately after the group it just left, so you can see exactly where it went. For more on rearranging chapters and groups, see Reordering and Organizing Chapters.
Writing a New Chapter Into a Group

When you're drafting inside one act, you can create the next chapter straight into that folder instead of filing it in afterward. There are two ways in: Pick the folder, then click +: click a group's name to select it (it stays highlighted), then click + at the top of the outline. The menu offers New Chapter in Group. Click anywhere else in the outline to deselect the folder. Right-click the group: choose New Chapter in Group. Either way, the new chapter lands at the end of that folder, after the chapters already inside it. Its chapter number follows along too, so your manuscript and exports read in the same order as your outline. This works in both the Chapters page outline and the Manuscript Mode outline, and it works on empty groups as well: a freshly made Act Three folder can be filled one new chapter at a time.

Each group has a small triangle on its left edge, just like a chapter that contains scenes. Click the triangle to open or close the folder; the chapters inside slide in and out without affecting their order or contents. You can leave the act you're currently working on open and tuck the rest away for a calmer outline.

Note: Group deletion and chapter moves between groups can't be undone with Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac). The chapters themselves are never lost, but if you regret a structural change, you'll need to re-create the group and add the chapters back in one by one with Add to Group. Right-click a group and choose Delete Group to remove the folder. Only the folder is deleted: the chapters inside are not. Every chapter that was in the group is unfolded out to the top level of the outline immediately, in the same order it was in, sitting right where the group used to be. Nothing about the chapters themselves changes; they just stop being filed inside that folder. Tip: Because deleting a group leaves your chapters intact, it's safe to clean up old groups whenever your structure changes. If you decide your three-act split should become a two-part split, delete the old groups first, then create the new ones and add the chapters with Add to Group.

Sooner or later, every writer needs to fold two chapters together, retire a scene that no longer fits, or cut a chapter that the story has outgrown. Penpoint makes these moves easy, and pairs every one of them with a confirmation step, so you always get a chance to back out before anything is lost. Note: Merges and deletions on the Chapters page can’t be undone with Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac). The confirmation window is your safety net, not the keyboard shortcut. If you’re about to make a structural change you aren’t sure about, take a fresh backup first — your peace of mind is worth the extra minute.

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any chapter in the outline and look for Merge with [Chapter N], where the chapter name matches the chapter directly above the one you right-clicked. Merging only ever runs in one direction: the chapter you right-click gets absorbed into the chapter above it. Because of that, the menu item is hidden on the very first chapter in the book; there’s nothing for it to merge into. When you click it, a confirmation window opens explaining what’s about to happen: for example, “Append Chapter 4 to Chapter 3.” Cancel sits right next to the Merge button, so it’s easy to back out the moment you have second thoughts. Confirm only when the direction looks right. Once a chapter merge goes through: The absorbed chapter’s scenes move into the kept chapter, appended after the kept chapter’s existing scenes. Each scene keeps its own prose, blocks, and assignments (the characters, locations, items, and story arc plot points you've attached to that scene). Every scene that was in the absorbed chapter still has the same characters, locations, items, and other details attached, just under the kept chapter now. The absorbed chapter’s description and author notes are appended onto the kept chapter’s description and author notes, separated by a blank line. The absorbed chapter is then removed, and every chapter after it renumbers automatically.

Scenes work the same way, just one level down. Right-click a scene and choose Merge with scene above. The scene above is kept, and the scene you right-clicked is absorbed into it: its prose appended after, its block fields folded in. The menu item is hidden on the first scene in a chapter, since there’s no scene above to absorb it. A confirmation window opens here too, naming the two scenes involved and offering both Cancel and Merge. Once confirmed, the absorbed scene is removed and the chapter’s remaining scenes resequence on their own. Tip: Because merges always pull the lower item up into the one above, the easiest way to plan a merge is to ask yourself, “Which one do I want to keep?” Then right-click the other one and merge it upward.

Right-click a chapter and choose Delete Chapter to remove it. Before anything is actually deleted, a confirmation window opens, and it’s deliberately specific so you know exactly what you’re agreeing to. The window spells out that deleting the chapter will: Remove all character, location, and item assignments tied to that chapter. Renumber all subsequent chapters automatically. Delete all chapter content and notes. At the bottom of the window, Cancel sits beside Delete Chapter. The scary action and the way out are right next to each other on purpose: if any of those bullet points give you pause, click Cancel and nothing changes.

Right-click a scene and choose Delete Scene. As with chapters, a confirmation window opens before anything is removed, listing what the deletion will affect: the scene’s character, location, and item assignments; its content, notes, and field data; and any links between this scene and your story arcs (the plot beats you’ve placed in arcs) will be removed. The arcs themselves stay safe. And, again, Cancel lives right next to Delete Scene. Read the list, decide, and click whichever one fits. There’s no rush, and nothing is gone until you confirm.

Merges and deletions on the Chapters page aren’t reversible after you confirm them. The confirmation windows are designed to be the last clear chance to step back: once you click through them, the change is committed. If you’re about to make a sweeping change (collapsing several chapters, cutting a whole scene you might want back), consider taking a fresh backup of your book first. That way you have a known-good copy to restore from if you decide a few days later that the cut chapter belonged in the book after all. Tip: Deleting a whole group works differently from deleting a chapter: folders can be removed without losing the chapters inside them. See Chapter Groups (Folders) for how that cleanup is handled.

Every book is structured differently, and every writer tracks different things about their chapters and scenes. That's why Penpoint doesn't lock you into a single chapter sheet. You choose which blocks (the individual sections that show up on the right side of the chapter view for every scene) appear, where they live, and how they're configured. Add, remove, reorder, and tune blocks until your layout fits the way you actually plan and write. Open the layout editor at Settings > Chapter Layout.

Your chapter layout applies to every scene in the book. When you add a "Summary" paragraph block, every scene gets a Summary field; each scene fills it in with its own content. Add a new block at any time and it appears on the right side of the chapter view for every scene, ready to be filled in. The same idea is at work on the Characters page. If you've already used Customizing Character Layout, the chapter layout editor will feel immediately familiar: same controls, same flow, just configured per book for chapters and scenes instead of characters. Note: Layout changes are saved as you make them and apply book-wide right away. There is no undo for layout edits, so take a moment before removing a block, though as covered below, removed blocks can be restored, and removing a block never throws away the data inside it.

The chapter view has two columns (Main on the left and Sidebar on the right), and the editor lets you arrange blocks across both. (These columns live inside the chapter detail view, not Penpoint's main app sidebar.) The Main column is the wider area best suited to plot points, summaries, and other long-form content. The Sidebar is narrower and works well for secondary information like the cast, locations, items, and tags for a scene. Every block belongs to one column or the other. Each column has its own Add block to main or Add block to sidebar button at the bottom. New blocks land at the end of the column you added them to. You can drag them somewhere else afterwards.

Click Add block on either column to open the block picker. Blocks are grouped into two categories: Basic blocks (Text, Paragraph, Number, Divider, Calculate) for general-purpose content, and Chapter Data blocks (Tags, Characters, Locations, Items, Story Arcs (Penpoint's way of tracking plot threads across your book), Calendar) that connect each scene to the rest of your book. For a tour of what each block does and how to use it, see Chapter Block Types.

A few block types only make sense once per layout: Tags, Characters, Locations, Items, Story Arcs, and Calendar. If one of these is already in your layout, it appears faded in the block picker and can't be added a second time. The other blocks (Text, Paragraph, Number, Divider, Calculate) can be added as many times as you like.

Each block in the editor has a small row of buttons in the top-left corner that let you manage the block without opening its settings: Drag handle: a vertical row of dots. Click and drag to move the block to a new position, either within its current column or across to the other column. Settings: a small toothed-gear shape. Click to open the block's configuration panel, where you can rename the block and set its other options. You can also click the body of the block itself to open the same panel. Column switch: two arrows pointing in opposite directions (left and right). Click to send the block to the other column without dragging. Handy for quickly rebalancing what's on the main side versus the sidebar. Each block also has a small X icon (a simple cross-shape, like the close button on a window) in the top-right corner that removes it from the layout.

Click any block (or its gear icon) to open its configuration panel right inside the editor. Common options include the block's name and (for number blocks) minimum and maximum values. Changes save automatically as you type, and every option can be changed back later. Tip: The block name you set in configuration is the label every scene in your book will see: for example, naming a paragraph block "Summary" or "What Happens" is what the right side of the chapter view will show.

Drag blocks by the drag handle to rearrange them. As you drag, a highlighted line appears at the spot the block will land on release. You can drop a block anywhere in either column, including across columns to move it from main to sidebar or vice versa.

Removing a block does not delete your data. When you click the X icon on any block, Penpoint asks you to confirm, then hides the block from the right side of the chapter view for every scene; every scene's data for that block is preserved untouched in the background. If you put the block back later, all of that data is still there waiting. Removed blocks aren't gone: they go to the Deleted Blocks list, accessible from the button beneath the layout editor. From there you can click Restore to bring a block back into your layout (along with all of the scene data it was holding), or click Forever Delete to permanently remove the block and everything it contains. Forever Delete asks for one more confirmation before anything is actually erased, and any scene data inside that block is also erased forever. Tip: If you accidentally remove a block, just open Deleted Blocks and click Restore. Your scenes get the block back instantly, and none of their data is lost. For details about each block type, see Chapter Block Types.

Blocks are the small sections (date fields, character lists, notes, etc.) that make up the chapter view. Chapters use the same block system as character sheets: every section in a chapter's detail view is a block, like a paragraph field, a date picker, or a list of characters who appear in the scene. Mix and match blocks to build a chapter layout that matches how you actually plan your story. Your chapter layout applies to every chapter and scene in your book: add a Paragraph block called "Summary" once, and every scene gets its own Summary field. Configure the layout in Settings > Chapter Layout. Tip: You don't need every block type. Start with what helps you plan: a calendar for keeping dates straight, a characters block for tracking who's in each scene, and a paragraph or two for notes is plenty for most writers.

General-purpose fields shared with character sheets. You can add multiples of these to your layout: Text Block - Single-line text input (the same Text Block used on character sheets) Paragraph Block - Multi-line rich text for summaries, notes, and longer prose Number Block - Numeric input with optional minimum, maximum, and step Divider Block - A visual separator to break a layout into sections Calculate Block - Adds, subtracts, or combines numbers from your other Number blocks Image Block - Attach a reference image to each scene (maps, location concept art, mood boards) Notebook Block - Show a note, folder, or set of tags from your Notebook right on a scene

Chapter-specific blocks that connect a scene to the rest of your book. You can only add one of each: Tags Block - Assign tags to a chapter or scene (works on both character sheets and chapters) Calendar Block - Assign in-world dates and times to scenes Assigning Things to Scenes - Covers the Characters, Locations, Items, and Story Arcs blocks — the four ways to mark which entities show up in a scene To add or remove any of these from your chapter layout, see Customizing Chapter Layout.

A Calendar Block is a small date field you drop into a scene to mark when it happens (a single moment, or a stretch of time from one date to another). It's how you tell readers (and yourself) that this scene takes place on Tuesday, September 5th, 2026 at 2:30 PM, or on Day 47 of the voyage, or, if you've built a fantasy calendar, on a date like “Stormwane, Year of the Falling Star” in your invented world. The block adapts to whatever calendar your book is using. The same Calendar Block becomes a real-world date picker, a numeric "Day X" input, or a custom-calendar grid, depending on which mode you've chosen for the book. This article covers using the block on a scene; the calendar itself (modes (required), months / weekdays / eras / moons (all optional)) is configured separately. To add a Calendar Block to a scene, see Customizing Chapter Layout. To choose your book's calendar mode and define its rules, see Calendar Settings. Note: Heads up: switching calendar modes (Gregorian to Day Counter, Custom to Gregorian, etc.) wipes every date inside every Calendar Block. The change can't be undone, so Penpoint pops up a confirmation dialog with a Cancel button before anything happens. Only dates inside the blocks are cleared; your scenes, prose, characters, and notes stay safe. See A Word About Switching Calendar Modes at the bottom of this article for details.
A Calendar Block reads from your book's calendar mode and shows the matching editor. You don't pick the mode on the block itself; it just follows whatever you set in Calendar Settings.

The real-world calendar. The block opens a grid picker with month and year controls at the top, weekday headers, and a 7-column grid of day cells. Click a day to select it. Use the < and > arrows to step a month at a time, the month name to jump months, or the year input to type a year directly. Today's date has a colored ring around it when it's visible in the current month. For historical fiction, you can turn on Epochs (the BCE/CE-style era markers used in historical or fantasy books) in Calendar Settings: once enabled, a Before/After dropdown appears next to the year so you can pick BCE/CE (or BC/AD) without typing negative years. Penpoint follows the historian convention and skips year 0, so 1 BCE and 1 CE sit side by side.

Just a number. The block shows a single field where you type the day: "0", "47", "-12" for a flashback. No months, no weekdays, no calendar grid. Useful when only the passage of time matters, like survival stories or ship logs. Negative numbers are allowed: the editor reminds you of this with a hint right next to the field: Note: Negative values are allowed, like when using flashbacks.

For invented calendars, the block uses a grid picker that respects your custom calendar setup: your own weekday names, month names, hours per day (yes, your fantasy world can have 30-hour days), leap days, and intercalary periods (extra days that don't belong to any week, like a 5-day festival between months). Navigation, selection, and time entry work the same as the Gregorian grid; the structure underneath just matches the calendar you designed. Leap days show up differently to ordinary days. Because a leap day sits between two numbered days rather than being one of them, it takes its slot in the grid as a small star (⟡) instead of a number. Every star on screen is named in the Leap days in view line underneath the grid, so you never have to hover one to find out what it is. If a star belongs to the month either side of the one you're looking at, its name says so: "Stargazing Night (from Emberwane)". If your book uses named eras (set up in Calendar Settings, like "Reign of King Valdris"), a dropdown labeled Era: appears at the top of the picker, above the month and year. Click it to jump to a different era; Penpoint takes you to the start of that era so you can pick a date inside it. The year box shows up as "Year 3" instead of "Year 1503", counting from the start of the era, not the beginning of your whole calendar, so you don't have to do the math in your head. Building a custom calendar (month names, weekdays, leap days, eras) is a worldbuilding job in its own right. See Custom Calendar for the full walkthrough.

By default a Calendar Block stores one date: the scene's start. If a scene spans more than one moment (a long carriage ride, a festival, an overnight watch), click + Add End Date at the bottom of the editor to add an end date. Two tabs appear at the top of the editor: Start and End, and Penpoint moves you to the End tab. It copies your Start date into the End for you, so you only change what's actually different. To go back to a single date, switch to the End tab and click Remove End Date (or just click it from the Start tab; it's available either way). The end date is dropped, and the block returns to single-date mode. Note: When both Start and End are set, Penpoint checks that your end date isn't before your start date as you pick: the End grid won't let you pick a day before Start, and the Start grid won't let you pick a day after End. On Day Counter, an out-of-order day is highlighted in red with a hint about which side is wrong. The data is still saved either way; the editor just flags the mismatch so you can fix it.

Below the date grid is an optional time row with hour and minute selectors. Pick an hour, pick a minute, and the time appears next to the date in View Mode (Edit Mode is what you see when you've clicked into the block to change it; View Mode is how the date appears once you click away). Leave it blank and only the date shows. Time is set on each individual block, so you can have date-only blocks for whole-day scenes and date-plus-time blocks for moment-specific ones. If you'd rather hide the time row entirely on a particular block, the per-block configuration has a switch for that: Include hours and minutes, covered below.

Once a date is set, a Clear All button appears in the bottom of the editor. Clear All only empties the date fields on this one block; your scene, prose, and other blocks aren't touched. If you click Clear All by accident, just pick the date again. Penpoint doesn't remember that the field was empty. Clicking Clear All wipes both Start and End in one step and returns the block to its empty state. Note: Date changes save automatically the moment you make them. There's no Save button. If you click the wrong day, just click the right one. Penpoint always shows you whichever day you picked last.

If your book's calendar has moons configured, every Calendar Block shows the moon phase for the selected date below the editor, and the same phase appears below the date in View Mode. So if your scene takes place on the night of the full moon, the block tells you (and your readers, if you reference moons in prose). Moons are defined in Calendar Settings: name, orbit, starting phase, and color or surface image. Once they exist, they show up automatically on every Calendar Block.

Every Calendar Block has its own visual settings, separate from the book-wide calendar rules. Open a Calendar Block's configuration from the Customizing Chapter Layout flow to find these options: Show calendar grid picker (Gregorian only): Switches between the grid picker (the calendar-style day picker, with month and year controls at the top and a 7-column grid of day cells) and a dropdown editor with separate Year, Month, and Day fields. The grid is faster for browsing; the dropdowns are quicker if you already know the exact date and just want to type it. Custom mode always uses the grid; Day Counter has no grid concept. Include hours and minutes: When off, the time row disappears from the editor and the time portion is hidden from View Mode. Penpoint remembers the time you'd typed, so when you turn it back on, your time comes back. Use 24-hour time (Gregorian only): When on, hours show as "00" through "23"; when off, "12 AM" through "11 PM". Custom calendars don't use AM/PM, since the number of hours in a day is up to you. Show day before month: Switches the date display from "September 3" to "3 September" (common in European date formats). Available on Gregorian and Custom; not relevant for Day Counter.

When your book has moons defined, three more options appear in the per-block configuration: Show moons on this block: Hides moon phases on this specific block, even if the book is showing moons everywhere else. Useful for blocks where the moon phase isn't relevant to the scene. Show names and phase labels: When on, each moon shows its name and current phase next to its picture. When off, only the moon picture appears, and the name and phase are visible on hover. Size: Pick Small, Medium, or Large for the moon icons on this block. Tip: Per-block settings only apply to the one block you're configuring. To change date display across every Calendar Block at once, use the book-wide options in Calendar Settings instead.
A Word About Switching Calendar Modes

Note: Switching your book's calendar mode (Gregorian to Day Counter, Custom to Gregorian, etc.) clears every date in every Calendar Block: only the dates, not your scenes or prose. Penpoint asks you to confirm with a dialog (with a Cancel button) before anything happens. The full warning lives in Calendar Settings.

An Outline Block turns a scene into a living beat sheet: a collapsible list where you sketch your intentions before you write. Indent ideas under a parent heading, then fold that whole section away when you're done planning it. Everything you collapse is still there; it's just out of the way until you need it. To add an Outline Block to your scenes, open Customizing Chapter Layout (the screen where you arrange the blocks on your scenes) and add it from the block menu. You can only add Outline Blocks to your scenes, not to character pages or item pages.

Click inside a scene to enter edit mode: the block becomes editable and your cursor lands in the first bullet. Type your first beat and press Enter to add another at the same level. Press Tab to indent a line one level deeper (making it a child of the line above), or Shift+Tab to move it back out. The outline saves automatically as you type, and Ctrl+Z undoes your typing as you go. Need a second line inside the same bullet (a note, a reminder, a detail) without starting a new item? Press Alt+Enter (Option+Enter on Mac) to add a new line inside the same bullet, rather than starting a brand-new bullet underneath.

Any item that has children beneath it shows a small arrow (a chevron) to its left. Click it to fold those children away; click again to expand them. Items with no children show no chevron. There's nothing underneath them to fold. Collapse state is saved with the scene. Fold a section, close the chapter, come back an hour later. It's still folded. Nothing resets on navigation. Before you've added anything, the block shows a faint "No outline yet" placeholder in view mode. Click inside the scene to start typing and the first bullet appears.

Enter: new bullet at the same level Tab / Shift+Tab: indent or outdent the current bullet Alt+Enter: new line inside the current bullet (instead of a new bullet) Click the chevron: fold or expand a section @: mention a character, location, or item inline

You can switch between bullets (•) and numbers (1, 2, 3…) at any time without losing anything: your indents and folded sections stay exactly as they were. Open the block's settings panel (in Chapter Layout Settings) and pick Bulleted or Numbered to change the whole block at once. The title above the block ("Scene Beats", "Act Structure", etc.) is set in the same panel. Tip: Mentions work inside the Outline Block just like in any other text block (@Mentions). Type the @ symbol to bring up a list of your characters, locations, and items, then pick one to drop a clickable link straight into a beat. Mentions are quick inline references for planning; they don't formally assign anyone to the scene, so use the Characters, Locations, and Items blocks when you want Penpoint to track who's actually in the scene.

Four of the chapter-page blocks let you record who and what shows up in each scene: Characters, Locations, Items, and Story Arcs. They live on individual scenes, not on the chapter as a whole, so a chapter with three scenes can have three different casts, three different settings, three different sets of objects, and three different plot beats. That's the whole point: the real detail of who appears where lives at the scene level. All four blocks share the same shape: a list of what's already assigned, plus a way to add more. Once you've used one, you've used them all. The differences are in what each block tracks and a couple of small extras (a POV indicator on Characters, a two-step picker on Story Arcs). To add any of these blocks to your scene layout, see Customizing Chapter Layout. This article focuses on what each block does once it's there.

Every assignment block lays out the same way. Things you've already assigned appear as a list of rows: each row showing an icon, the name, and (in Edit Mode) a couple of small action buttons on the right. To add something, click the Add button below the list. An autocomplete field appears, and as you type, it suggests matches drawn only from things you haven't already assigned to this scene. Each row has a trash icon you can click to remove the assignment. Removing an assignment never deletes the character, location, item, or plot point itself. It only unlinks it from this particular scene. The entity stays exactly where it lived before, ready to be assigned to a different scene whenever you like. The autocomplete is smart about duplicates. Once you've assigned something to a scene, it disappears from the suggestion list for that scene's block, so you can't accidentally add the same character (or location, or item) twice. To assign the same character, location, or item itself to a different scene, just open that other scene and use its block. Note: Assignments save the moment you make them. There's no Save button on these blocks, and Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) won't undo an assignment — if you remove something by accident, just add it back.

The Characters Block records who's present in a scene. Click Add Character to open the autocomplete (placeholder reads Select character...), pick a name, and they're assigned. The character's name appears in the list, along with their alias if they have one. Adding a character to a scene is also what tells the Timeline page (and other places in Penpoint that count appearances or build timelines) that they were there, so keep this honest if you want timelines and appearance counts to be useful later. In Edit Mode, every row has an eye-shaped toggle button on the right that controls POV. When POV is off, the eye is shown with a line through it; click it to switch POV on for that character (the tooltip reads Set as POV) and the icon turns into a plain open eye. Click it again to switch POV off (Remove POV). When POV is on, a small eye icon stays visible on the row even outside of Edit Mode, so you can scan the list and see who's narrating at a glance. You can mark more than one character as POV in a single scene (useful for ensemble or split-perspective scenes), though most of the time one is plenty. The trash icon on the right removes the character from this scene. The character themselves (their profile, traits, relationships, all of it) is untouched. To create or edit characters themselves, see Working with Characters.

The Locations Block records where the scene takes place. Click Add Location, pick from the autocomplete (Select location...), and the location appears in the list with its custom icon: the same icon you chose when you set the location up. Most scenes have one location, but you can assign as many as you need (a character traveling between rooms, a chase across a city). The trash icon removes the location from the scene. The location itself, with everything you've written about it, stays put on the Locations page. To create or edit locations themselves, see Working with Locations.

The Items Block records the objects that appear in a scene: a sword, a letter, a poisoned glass of port. Click Add Item, choose from the autocomplete (Select item...), and the item appears in the list. The row shows the item's name, with its archetype (its type or category, like "Weapon" or "Document") shown beside it as a smaller label, and an icon drawn from that archetype on the left. Useful for tracking which scene a story-critical object surfaces in, and for catching continuity gaps when an item reappears later. The trash icon removes the item from this scene. The item entity itself is unaffected. To create or edit items themselves, see Working with Items.

The Story Arcs Block is a little different from the other three. You're not assigning whole arcs to a scene: you're assigning specific plot points, which are the individual plot points (the moments you've placed in each story arc) that live inside an arc (the inciting incident, the midpoint reversal, the climax). Linking a scene to a plot point is how you say "this is where that beat actually happens in the book." Click Assign Plot Point and a two-step picker appears. First, pick the arc (Select story arc...); then pick one of that arc's plot points (Select plot point...); finally click Assign to commit. The plot point then appears in the list with the arc name beside it. Click the plot point's name in the list to jump straight to that arc on the Arcs page. The trash icon removes the link between this scene and that plot point; the arc and the plot point themselves are untouched. Tip: If a scene contains beats from more than one arc (a romance thread crossing a mystery thread, say), assign as many plot points as fit. Each one is its own row. For what arcs and plot points actually are, and how to build them, see Story Arcs.

Note: It bears repeating: removing an assignment from a scene never deletes the underlying character, location, item, or plot point. Assignments are just links: clicking the trash icon breaks the link, nothing more. If you're cleaning up a scene that's grown stale and want to start fresh, wiping its assignments doesn't remove the entities themselves.
The Chapters page and Manuscript Mode are two views of the same book. They share the same chapters and scenes, not copies. Use Chapters to plan details and Manuscript Mode to write prose.

Click Manuscript at the top-right of the chapter view. Penpoint opens the selected chapter, or goes directly to the selected scene. You can also right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any chapter or scene in the outline (the chapter-and-scene list on the left), then choose Open in Manuscript.

Both views let you rename and reorganize chapters and scenes or change their status and color. A scene added in Chapters appears in Manuscript Mode. Deleting a scene from either view removes it from both; Penpoint asks you to confirm because deletion cannot be undone. Chapters is the main place for planning blocks such as Calendar, Characters, Locations, Items, and Story Arcs. Manuscript Mode handles prose, formatting, writing tools, and chapter title or subtitle edits. For the full picture of how Manuscript Mode works, see Manuscript Mode. Tip: Planning details and prose are stored separately. Routine changes to blocks, status, or color do not rewrite prose, and editing prose does not replace those details.

In Manuscript Mode, right-click a scene in the outline and choose Scene Drafts. Right-click any chapter and choose View Chapter Drafts. Scene Drafts save one scene's prose. Chapter Drafts save all of the chapter's scenes, names, and order. Before restoring either kind, Penpoint saves your current prose asAuto-saved before restore, which you can restore to return to that writing. Restoring does not replace chapter-level details such as the chapter title. For one-scene versions, see Scene Drafts. For whole-chapter versions, see Chapter Drafts. To compare a saved draft with your current writing, see Comparing Your Manuscript Drafts.

The Arcs page helps you visualize and track the structural and emotional threads running through your story. Whether you're mapping the twists of your main plot or charting a character's rise and fall, arcs give you a bird's-eye view of your narrative.

The Arcs page is divided into two modes, accessible via the tab toggle at the top: Story Arcs: Track your plot structure: main storyline, subplots, and the keyframes that mark each turning point. Character Arcs: Track a character's fortune over time, visualized as a curve that rises and falls with their circumstances. Writing a series? There's a third kind: Series Arcs chart the storylines that span every Book, and your Story Arcs are called Book Arcs there: same tool, one per Book. See Book Arcs and Series Arcs.

Both modes share a three-panel layout: Sidebar (left): Browse your arc hierarchy or character list. Use the divider button to collapse or expand it. Visualizer (top right): An interactive display showing your arcs as curves with diamond-shaped keyframes. Details Panel (bottom right): View and edit the selected arc or keyframe's information.

Each mode has a View/Edit toggle. In View mode you can browse your arcs and read details. Switch to Edit mode to make changes: rename arcs, add or remove keyframes, write plot details, and more. Tip: Press Ctrl+E (Cmd+E on Mac) to toggle between View and Edit mode from anywhere on the Arcs page.

Arcs aren't confined to the Arcs page; they appear throughout Penpoint to keep your story structure visible wherever you're working: Character Arcs appear on character sheets via the Character Arc Block, showing a compact fortune curve you can click to jump to the full editor. Story Arcs appear on chapter detail pages as a mini arc visualizer, showing which plot points each chapter is assigned to. See Editing Chapter and Scene Details for more. Clicking any arc or keyframe in these compact views navigates you directly to the full Arcs page with that arc selected.

Story Arcs let you map the structural backbone of your narrative: the main plot, its subplots, and the keyframes that mark each major turning point. Think of them as the architectural blueprint of your story.

Every book has one main story arc at the top, with subplots nested beneath it. The sidebar on the left shows this hierarchy as a tree. Click any arc to select it and see its details. Subplots are anchored to specific keyframes on their parent arc. For example, a romance subplot might span from your story's "Midpoint" keyframe to its "Climax," showing exactly where that thread weaves through the main plot. Note: In a series, Story Arcs are called Book Arcs (same tool, one per Book), and series-spanning storylines get their own tab. See Book Arcs and Series Arcs.

The visualizer shows your arcs as curves. The main arc sits on top as a broad sweep, with subplots branching below it. Diamond markers along each curve represent keyframes: the major beats of your story. Click any keyframe diamond to select it and view its details in the panel below. Click a subplot curve to expand it and see its own keyframes. Tip: Hover over arcs in the sidebar to highlight them in the visualizer, and vice versa. This makes it easy to orient yourself in complex stories with many subplots.

The gear icon in the top-right of the visualizer opens settings that control what's visible. Toggle Always show labels off when your arcs feel crowded. With it off, labels stay hidden until you hover over (or click) a specific keyframe, giving you a cleaner view of the curves themselves. Tip: Click any empty space on the canvas to deselect the current keyframe and let its label fade away.

Keyframes are the turning points of your arc. Each keyframe has: Label: A short name for the beat (e.g., "Thornfield," "The Revelation"). Type: An optional literary classification such as Inciting Incident, Midpoint, Climax, or Resolution. Tagging keyframes with a type helps you see at a glance whether your story hits the structural beats your chosen framework calls for. Brief Description: A one-line summary of what happens at this beat. Plot Details: A rich text field for longer notes, scene outlines, or draft prose. Chapter Assignments: Link keyframes to specific chapters so you can track where each beat falls in your manuscript. In Edit mode, you can add new keyframes, delete existing ones, and drag to reorder them. Keyframes automatically space themselves evenly along the arc curve.

When creating a new arc, you choose a preset that determines the starting keyframes. Presets give you a narrative scaffold to build on: Three-Act Structure: Setup, Confrontation, Resolution. The classic. Five-Act Structure: Shakespearean dramatic structure with five distinct phases. Hero's Journey: Joseph Campbell's 12-stage monomyth. Save The Cat!: Blake Snyder's detailed 15-beat screenplay structure. Romance Arc: Meeting, Attraction, Obstacle, Resolution. Mystery Arc: Discovery, Investigation, Revelation. Character Growth: Flaw Introduced, Challenge, Growth Moment, Transformation. Simple Arc: Just a Beginning and End. Good for subplots you want to fill in manually. Custom: Two blank keyframes to shape however you like. Note: Presets are starting points, not constraints. After creating your arc, you can rename, add, remove, or reorder any keyframes.

To create a subplot, hover over any arc in the sidebar and click the + button. You'll be asked to: Name the subplot Choose a preset Pick a color Select a Start Anchor and End Anchor: keyframes on the parent arc that define where this subplot begins and ends The start anchor must come before the end anchor in the parent's keyframe sequence. Subplots can themselves have sub-subplots, allowing you to model complex narrative structures. Note: The parent arc must have at least 2 keyframes before you can create a subplot beneath it. If it doesn't, the + button won't appear.

In Edit mode, you can drag and drop arcs in the sidebar to reorder them among their siblings. Grab an arc by the drag handle and move it up or down; a drop indicator shows where it will land. This lets you arrange subplots in whatever order makes sense for your story. Note: Drag handles only appear when an arc has at least one sibling at the same level. The main arc cannot be dragged since it's always at the top of the hierarchy.

When you assign chapters to keyframes, a mini arc visualizer appears on each chapter's detail page showing all your story arcs and highlighting the assigned plot points. Click any keyframe in the mini visualizer to jump back to the Arcs page. See Editing Chapter and Scene Details for more about the chapter-side view.

In Edit mode, every arc (including the main story arc) has a Delete button at the bottom of the details panel. What you see depends on the arc: Main arc: Deleting the main arc is a full reset. It removes the main arc, every subplot beneath it, and all their keyframes. Afterward, the page returns to its empty state and you can create a new story arc from scratch. Subplot with no children: A simple confirmation. The subplot and all its keyframes are removed. Subplot with children: You choose between Delete All (removes the subplot and every nested subplot beneath it) or Keep Subplots (removes only this subplot and promotes its children up one level in the hierarchy). Tip: "Keep Subplots" is useful when you want to restructure your hierarchy without losing the detailed work you've put into child arcs.

Character Arcs track the emotional journey of a single character through your story. Unlike Story Arcs, which map plot structure, Character Arcs visualize fortune: how well or poorly things are going for a character at any given point.

Fortune is the Y-axis of the character arc visualizer. It represents a character's overall circumstances: their happiness, power, safety, or whatever measure matters most to their story. The higher the curve, the better things are going. The lower the curve, the worse. A dashed horizontal line marks the baseline: the neutral point where a character's fortune is neither notably good nor bad. Think of it as "normal life before the story begins." In the example above, Jane begins below the baseline at Gateshead (an unhappy childhood), rises through Lowood and Thornfield as her circumstances improve, crashes when the truth about Bertha Mason is revealed, resets at Moor House, and ultimately rises to her highest point at the reunion.

Each keyframe on a character arc has a fortune modifier that determines how the curve shifts at that point. There are six modifier types: Major Rise (▲▲): A dramatic improvement. Victory, revelation, or breakthrough. Use this for moments like Jane inheriting her fortune or reuniting with Rochester. Minor Rise (▲): A small step forward. A new friendship, a piece of good news, a quiet moment of hope. Neutral (●): No significant change. Status quo, traveling, or setup for what comes next. Minor Fall (▼): A setback or moment of doubt. Not catastrophic, but things are getting worse. Major Fall (▼▼): A devastating blow. Betrayal, loss, or rock bottom. The discovery of Bertha Mason would be a Major Fall for Jane. Reset (◆): A fresh start. The slate is wiped clean and fortune returns to the baseline. This works well for act breaks or moments where a character starts over, like Jane arriving at Moor House. Note: Changing a modifier on an earlier keyframe affects the entire curve from that point forward, so a single change can reshape the whole arc.

When creating a new character arc, you select a character and choose from four preset templates: Positive Change Arc: The character overcomes a flaw and grows. Classic redemption or hero's arc. Starts neutral, falls through struggle, then rises through breakthrough to a new self. Negative Change Arc: The character falls from grace. Corruption, tragedy, or a villain origin. Starts with virtue, then descends through temptation and compromise. Flat Arc: The character stays true to their beliefs while the world changes around them. The steadfast hero. Fortune dips as they're tested but rises when they're vindicated. Custom: Two blank keyframes to shape however you like. Each preset comes with pre-configured keyframes and fortune modifiers that shape the initial curve. You can rename, add, remove, or reorder keyframes after creation.

Each keyframe on a character arc has: Label: A short name for the moment (e.g., "Bertha Revealed"). Fortune Modifier: One of the six types that shapes the curve. Brief Description: A one-line summary. Character State Notes: A rich text field for recording the character's emotional and circumstantial state at this point in the story. Chapter/Scene Assignments: Link keyframes to specific chapters or scenes so you can track where each emotional beat falls in your manuscript. In Edit mode, you can add new keyframes, delete existing ones (minimum of two required), and drag to reorder them.

One of the most powerful features of character arcs is the overlay system. When you select a character as the primary arc, checkboxes appear next to every other character in the sidebar. Check any of them to overlay their fortune curve behind the primary one. This lets you see how multiple characters' fortunes rise and fall in relation to each other. You might notice that one character's fortune rises exactly as another's falls (a hallmark of conflict), or that two allies share similar trajectories (suggesting their fates are intertwined). Use the Select All / Deselect All button at the bottom of the sidebar to quickly toggle every character's overlay on or off. Tip: Click any character's name in the sidebar to make them the primary arc. If they're currently an overlay, they'll swap with the current primary. No need to uncheck and re-select.

The gear icon in the top-right of the visualizer opens settings that control what's visible. These are especially handy when you've overlaid several characters and the canvas gets busy. Show Plot Points: Choose whether keyframes appear for all characters, only the active character, or none at all. Hide them entirely to compare the raw shape of multiple fortune curves without the diamond clutter. Always show labels: Hide every label by default. Hover or click any keyframe to reveal its label on demand. Great for at-a-glance shape comparison across characters. Tip: Click any empty space on the canvas to deselect the current keyframe and let its label fade away.

In Edit mode, drag handles appear next to each character in the sidebar. Grab a handle and drag up or down to reorder the list. This controls the display order of character arcs in the sidebar and when comparing overlays.

In a series, a character arc spans the whole series: one curve from Book 1 to the finale. In the This Book view, keyframes from other Books dim so you can focus on this volume's stretch of the journey. See Book Arcs and Series Arcs and This Book vs All Books.

Each character's fortune curve can also appear directly on their character sheet via the Character Arc Block. This compact view shows the same curve and keyframes; click any keyframe to jump to the full editor on the Arcs page.
Deleting a character arc removes the arc and all its keyframes. The character itself is not affected; only the arc tracking is removed. You can always create a new arc for that character later.

The Timeline visualizes when your characters appear throughout your story. See at a glance who shows up in which chapters, spot gaps in character appearances, and track how your cast weaves through your narrative. Note: Characters only appear on the Timeline after you've assigned them to chapters. You can do this from the Chapters Block on character pages, or from the Chapters page by editing a chapter and assigning characters to it.

Each colored bar represents a character's presence across one or more chapters. Characters are grouped by importance level (Primary, Secondary, Background), making it easy to see how your main cast compares to supporting characters. Chapter headers show the chapter number and how many characters appear in that chapter Continuous bars indicate a character appears in consecutive chapters Split bars show when a character disappears and returns later Importance groups separate Primary, Secondary, and Background characters In a series, the Timeline shows every Book's chapters in reading order, so you can follow a character's presence across the whole series. Clicking a chapter from another Book switches you to that Book. Tip: Click any chapter header to jump directly to that chapter's detail page. Click a character bar to navigate to that character's page.

The toolbar provides several ways to filter and customize the timeline view: Character: Filter to show specific characters, a selection of characters, or all characters Chapters: Narrow the view to a specific chapter range (e.g., Ch 1-5) Importance: Show only Primary, Secondary, or Background characters Spacing: Switch between Comfortable (larger bars) and Compact (tighter rows) Zoom: Scale the timeline from 50% to 300% for more or less detail Sort: Order characters by Presence (most chapters), Alphabetically, or by First Appearance

For single-chapter appearances, you can adjust exactly where within the chapter a character appears. Hover over a bar to reveal drag handles on the left and right edges. Drag these handles to indicate whether a character appears early, middle, or late in a chapter. You can also drag the entire bar left or right to reposition it within the chapter. This precision is useful when multiple characters share a scene and you want to show their relative timing.

Click Chapter Statistics to see insights about your character distribution: Average Density: How many characters appear per chapter on average Most/Least Characters: Which chapters have the highest and lowest character counts Longest Absence: Which character has the largest gap between appearances Most/Least Frequent: Characters who appear in the most or fewest chapters Tip: Use these statistics to identify pacing issues. A character with a long absence might need a reminder scene, while characters that are featured too much might be preventing other characters' development.

Track your protagonist: Filter to your main character and verify they appear consistently Spot dropped threads: Look for characters who appear early then vanish Balance your cast: Use importance groups to ensure Background characters don't overshadow Primary ones Plan story arcs: Visualize when antagonists enter and exit to build tension Check chapter density: Chapters with many characters may need simplifying; chapters with few may lack conflict

An Event is a moment in your story, and you connect it to whoever and whatever it involves. Create "The Duel at Dawn" and link it to the two characters who fought, the sword one of them carried, and the meadow where it happened. That one event then appears on every one of their pages. It's the same event in each place, not a copy, so a change you make anywhere updates it everywhere. You'll find Events as a section on your character, item, and location pages.

In Edit Mode (switch it on with the Edit button at the top of the page), click Add event. A search box opens so you can add an event you've already written. To make a brand new one, choose Create New Event… at the bottom of the list. All an event needs is a title, so you can jot down "The Letter Arrives" and move on. When you're ready, you can give it a date and link it to a chapter, but neither is required. An event you link to a chapter (or to one of its scenes) also appears at the top of that chapter, under Events in this chapter, so a chapter's key moments are visible right where you're working on it.

Because an event is shared, it shows up on the page of everyone and everything it involves. When you open an event's details, the Also involves list shows the rest of its cast: the other characters, items, and locations tied to that same moment. It's a quick way to see who else was in the room.

Your events all share one order that runs through your whole book — or whole series. Each page shows just the events it's part of, but always in that same shared order, so the sequence reads the same no matter where you look. To reorder, switch to Edit Mode and use the up and down arrows beside an event to move it earlier or later. Every event has a single place in that shared order, so if an event is attached to several characters, items, or locations, moving it on one of them moves it for all of them. On those other pages it slides into its new spot among their events too: it's one order underneath, not a separate list kept per page. The upcoming Timeline will bring this whole sequence into one view, so you can see and arrange your story's events from beginning to end.
Removing an Event vs Deleting It

These are two different things, and Penpoint keeps them clearly apart. To take an event off just one page, open it and use the Remove button, which is named for the page you're on (such as "Remove from this character"). The event itself lives on, still connected to everyone else it involves. Delete event is different: it removes the event everywhere at once, from every page it appears on, and this can't be undone. Before anything happens, Penpoint shows you the full list of everywhere the event will disappear from, so there are no surprises, and you can still cancel.

On character sheets, Events are a section on the page. See Events Block for how to set it up. On item and location pages, the Events section is always there, ready to use. Note: Don't see an Events section on your character sheet? You can add one yourself in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. See Customizing Character Layout if you'd like a walkthrough. Note: Every event you add now is groundwork for the upcoming Timeline. More on that when it arrives.

The Relationship Map visualizes your entire cast of characters and their connections in one interactive view. See who's connected to whom, discover clusters of related characters, and explore the web of relationships that brings your story to life. Note: You must have connected relationships in order for the map to populate. If the map is empty or sparsely populated, add relationships using the Relationships Block on the character page and watch your network grow!

Each card on the map represents a character. Lines between cards show relationships, with labels indicating the relationship type (Friend, Nemesis, Mentor, etc.). Characters with many connections naturally appear more central, while isolated characters drift to the edges. The map automatically identifies clusters of closely-related characters. Each cluster appears within a colored circle, making it easy to see factions, families, or social groups at a glance. A character needs at least one direct connection to another group member to be included in its circle: true outliers without any connections within a group are kept separate. Pan and zoom to navigate the map. Click and drag to pan, scroll to zoom in and out. Double-click any empty space to reset the view.
Use the Direction and Importance filters to focus on specific types of connections.

All: Shows all relationships regardless of direction Reciprocal: Only shows mutual relationships where both characters have defined a connection to each other Tip: Reciprocal filtering helps you find mutual relationships. If Captain Courage calls Shadow Strike a "Partner" and Shadow Strike also has a relationship back to Captain Courage, that connection will appear. One-sided relationships are hidden.

Filter by character importance level to focus on your key players: All: Shows all characters Primary: Only shows Primary importance characters Secondary: Only shows Secondary importance characters Background: Only shows Background importance characters Note: Filtered-out characters appear faded rather than disappearing completely, so you can still see the overall structure while focusing on specific groups.

Click any character card to select them. The map highlights their direct connections while fading other characters into the background. A details panel slides in showing all of that character's relationships.

The details panel lists every relationship for the selected character: Character name at the top with their importance level Relationship list showing connected characters and relationship types Direction arrows indicating relationship direction (→ outgoing, ← incoming, ↔ mutual) Click any character name in the list to jump to that character's relationships, navigating through your web of connections. Tip: Hover over a relationship in the panel to highlight that specific connection on the map. This helps you trace complex relationship chains.

Drag any character card to move it wherever you want on the map. The moment you release, the character stays put and a small pin icon appears on the card to show it has been placed. Your arrangement is saved instantly and remembered between sessions, so your mental map of who-knows-who stays exactly the way you left it.
Right-click a pinned character to release it. The pin icon disappears and the character moves back to where it would normally sit based on its connections.

When you have pinned characters, a Reset Positions button appears in the toolbar showing how many characters are pinned. Click it to clear all custom positions at once — you'll be asked to confirm before anything changes. Tip: Drag your protagonist to the center of the map and arrange supporting characters around them to match how you think about your story's social structure.
Click the View Settings button to customize how the map appears.
Controls how curved the relationship lines are. Straight lines (0) create a clean, geometric look. Higher values add more curvature, which can help distinguish overlapping connections.
Toggle whether relationship type labels appear on the lines. Hide them for a cleaner view when you're focused on the overall structure rather than specific relationship types.
Grayscale: All lines appear gray, focusing attention on structure Normal: Lines use colors based on the source character (default) Full: Fully saturated colors for maximum visual distinction

Choose what appears below each character's name: Importance: Shows the character's importance level (Primary, Secondary, Background) Connections: Shows the number of relationships ("3 Relationships") None: Shows only the character name for a minimal view

Map your villain's network: Select your antagonist and explore who they're connected to Find isolated characters: Characters not in any colored circle may need more connections Check for missing mutuals: Use Reciprocal filter to ensure important relationships go both ways Visualize factions: Colored clusters reveal natural alliances and rivalries Track relationship complexity: Switch Card Display to "Connections" to see who has the most relationships Arrange your own way: Drag characters into positions that match your mental model of the story: group allies together, place rivals across from each other Note: The Relationship Map only shows relationships created through the Relationships Block on character pages. To add relationships, navigate to a character's page and use the Relationships Block in Edit mode.

The Tags Viewer is your central hub for discovering connections across your entire book. Select any tag to instantly see every character, item, location, chapter, note, and arc associated with it, all in one unified view.

Tags transcend boundaries. A character, location, and chapter can all share the same tag. The Tags Viewer brings these connections to the surface, helping you: Find related content instantly: See everything sharing a tag without searching multiple pages Track story threads: Follow factions, themes, or arcs across your entire book Spot gaps: Identify which characters or locations need more development Maintain consistency: Review all content related to a specific concept or group

The Tags Viewer lays out all your tags as cards. Each one shows its name, color, and usage count (how many times it's been assigned across your book). Click any tag to view all associated content. Tag Groups: If you've filed your tags into groups, they appear here under a heading for each group, with anything unfiled under a heading called Ungrouped. Penpoint spreads the headings across two columns when there's room for them, keeping each group whole. Clicking a group's heading folds it away, and it stays folded everywhere else you pick tags, including the next time you open Penpoint. Groups themselves are made, renamed and reordered on the Tags Manager, the page in Settings where you look after your tags. Sorting Options: Use the Sort dropdown to organize tags by Usage (most-used first), Alphabetical (A-Z), or Date Created (newest first). There is one tag order shared across Penpoint, so setting it here also sets it on the Tags Manager and everywhere tags are listed. Tip: High usage counts indicate tags you're actively using. Low counts might reveal tags you created but haven't fully integrated yet: perfect opportunities to enrich your content.

After selecting a tag, you'll see all related content organized by type: Characters, Items, Locations, Chapters, Arcs, and Notes. Each section shows cards with names and brief snippets from their descriptions. This page is for looking, not editing: to add or remove a tag, click through to the character, item, location, chapter, note, or arc and switch it to Edit mode. Filters: Use the filter buttons at the top to show or hide specific types. Turn Characters, Items, Locations, Chapters, Notes, or Arcs on and off to focus on what matters for your current task. Collapsible Sections: Click the small arrow beside any section heading to fold that section away. This keeps your view clean when working with tags that have many associated items. Tip: Click any card to navigate directly to that character, item, location, chapter, note, or arc. The Tags Viewer becomes a powerful navigation tool for exploring your book's interconnected structure.

Tag characters with "Rebel Alliance" or "Royal Court," then use the Tags Viewer to see all members at a glance. Add locations and chapters to the same tag to track where the faction appears and which story sections involve them.

Create tags like "Act 1," "Redemption Arc," or "Mystery Thread," then assign them to relevant characters, chapters, and notes. The Tags Viewer shows you everything related to that arc, making it easy to check continuity and pacing.

Use tags like "Needs Development" or "Plot Critical" to mark content requiring attention. Filter by Characters to see which personalities need more depth, or by Locations to identify settings that need fleshing out.

Tag content with themes like "Betrayal," "Redemption," or "Nature Symbolism." The Tags Viewer reveals patterns across your story, helping you strengthen thematic consistency or identify areas where themes could be reinforced.

Back to Tag Selection: Click the "Back to Tag Selection" button to return to your tags and choose a different one Direct Navigation: Click any card to jump straight to that content on its own page (Characters, Items, and so on) Quick Filtering: Turn type filters off to hide sections temporarily without folding them away
Managing Tags - Create, edit, and organize your tags in Settings Tags Block - Assign tags to characters and other content

The Notebook is your personal writing workspace: a place for quick thoughts, reference images, task lists, and links to your characters and locations. It's organized like a file system with folders, so everything stays where you put it.

The Notebook has three sections side by side: Folder list (left): A sidebar on the left showing all your folders. The top level is called the "Binder": it's the main folder that holds everything. Contents (center): Displays the notes, images, shortcuts, and subfolders inside the selected folder. Editor panel (right): Opens when you click a note or image, showing the full editor or image viewer. All three sections are resizable by dragging the dividers between them. The folder list can be collapsed to a thin strip when you need more space.

Notes — Rich text with colors, tags, checkboxes, and @Mentions (type @ to link to a character, location, or other item in your book) Folders: Organize notes into nested groups (up to 5 levels deep) Smart Folders: Create a folder tied to a tag (like "Research" or "Chapter 3"), and every note with that tag shows up here automatically Images: Upload reference photos, maps, or inspiration with names and descriptions Shortcuts: Bookmarks that link to characters, locations, items, chapters, and other parts of your book Tip: Your notes don't have to stay in the Notebook. With a Notebook Block you can show a note, a whole folder, or a set of tagged notes right on a character sheet or a scene, updated live as you write. Great for keeping a character's backstory or a scene's research in view while you work. Tip: Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) anywhere in the Notebook to see what you can create in that spot. The toolbar at the top also has buttons for adding notes, folders, images, and shortcuts.

F2: Rename the selected item Ctrl+A (Cmd+A on Mac): Select all items in the current folder Arrow keys: Move between items Enter: Open the selected item Delete / Backspace: Delete selected items (you'll be asked to confirm first) Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V (Cmd on Mac): Copy, cut, and paste items Escape: Cancel cut, clear selection, or close the editor on the right Ctrl+Shift+N (Cmd+Shift+N on Mac): Create a new folder. You can also right-click and choose "New Folder" if that's easier. Alt+Up Arrow: Go up to the folder that contains this one

Want to go deeper? Here are guides for specific topics: Working with Notes: Creating, editing, and customizing notes Folders and Smart Folders: Organizing your notebook with folders Using Dedicated Book Folders: Keeping notes with a specific book when you're writing a series Images in the Notebook: Uploading and viewing reference images Shortcuts: Linking to characters, locations, and other parts of your book Views and Sorting: Switching views and sorting your content Archiving Notes: Hiding and restoring notes Note Templates: Saving a note as a reusable starting point

Notes are the core of the Notebook: freeform spaces for capturing ideas, dialogue snippets, worldbuilding details, or anything else you want to remember. In a series, your notes are shared across the whole series: one Notebook for every Book.

Click the Note button in the toolbar at the top of the Notebook. A new note is created instantly and opens in the editor on the right side, ready for you to start writing. You can also right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any empty space and choose New Note. Tip: If the Notebook is empty, a "Create your first note" button appears in the center of the page to get you started.

Click any note to open it in the editor on the right side of the Notebook. The editor has three parts: Title: An optional heading at the top (up to 50 characters). Click the title area and start typing to add one. Writing area: The main space below the title, which supports rich text formatting (see below). Color and Tags bar: A row at the bottom of the editor for setting the note's color and tags. Changes save automatically as you type; no save button needed. Click the Close button in the top-right corner of the editor to close it when you're done.

The writing area includes a formatting toolbar with these options: Text styles: Bold, italic, underline, and strikethrough Headings: Three heading levels via the Style dropdown in the formatting toolbar above your note Lists: Bullet lists, numbered lists, and checkbox lists Block quotes: For indented, highlighted passages (useful for letters, excerpts, or quoted text) Links: Insert clickable web links Indent / Decrease indent: Adjust paragraph indentation Images: Insert images from your computer into the note Tables: Insert a table for structured information (magic systems, character stats, comparisons) Horizontal line: Drop a divider across the page to separate sections Undo / Redo: Step back or forward through your edits You can also type @ followed by a name to mention characters, locations, or items from your book. A list of matching names appears as you type; click one to insert the link. Mentions appear as clickable links inside your note, so you can jump straight to that character, location, or item. See @Mentions for the full guide. For a full guide to inserting and working with tables, see Tables.

Use the checkbox list button in the formatting toolbar to add a task list to your note. Check boxes off as you go; notes with checkboxes show how many you've completed on the card (e.g., "2/5 completed"). Great for revision checklists, plot point tracking, or to-do lists.

Click the Color button at the bottom of the editor to open a color picker. Choose a color to add a visual accent: a thick left border and a small square in the top-right corner of the card. Use colors to categorize notes at a glance: purple for worldbuilding, pink for character ideas, blue for plot points. Click the same color again to remove it.

Click the Tags button at the bottom of the editor to see a list of your book's tags. Click any tag to add it to the note; you can assign multiple tags. Tags you've already added to this note are highlighted in the list. Click a highlighted tag again to remove it. Tags appear at the bottom of the note with their color indicator. Tags are managed in Settings > Tags (look for the gear icon at the bottom of the left sidebar).

Right-click a note to see its options: Rename: Edit the note title right where it appears (also triggered by pressing F2; you may need to hold Fn on some Mac keyboards) Change Color: Pick a color accent from a submenu Move to Folder...: Move the note to a different folder Duplicate: Create a copy of the note Save as Template: Save a copy of this note's title, content, and color to your library, so you can reuse it in any book Archive: Hide the note from view without deleting it. Your note is still safely stored and can be restored at any time. Delete: You'll be asked to confirm first. Once deleted, the note is gone for good (if you're not sure, use Archive instead; you can always delete an archived note later). For more on archiving and restoring notes, see Archiving Notes. For reusable note starting points, see Note Templates.

While writing in Manuscript Mode (the prose-writing side of Penpoint), you can pin a note to a specific line of text. The note appears in the page margin beside that line, and the note itself gains a Pinned in manuscript list that jumps back to the spot. See Comments & Pinned Notes.

The folder list on the left side of the Notebook lets you organize your notes, images, and shortcuts into folders within folders (much like folders on your computer). The top level is called the Binder (the top-level folder, labeled "Binder" in the app, that holds everything).

To create a folder, click the Folder button in the toolbar at the top of the Notebook and choose New Folder, or right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any empty space in the folder list and choose New Folder. Type a name (up to 100 characters) and press Enter. You can nest folders up to 5 levels deep. To create a subfolder, right-click an existing folder and choose New Folder.

Right-click any folder to see its options: Rename: Edit the folder name right where it appears (also triggered by pressing F2; you may need to hold Fn on some Mac keyboards) Change Color: Pick a color for visual organization; a color picker will appear with the available options Move to Folder...: Move the folder to a different location in the folder list Delete Folder: Permanently remove the folder and everything inside it. You'll be asked to confirm before anything is deleted, and there is no undo.
