If the folder contains notes you want to keep, move them to another folder first You can also drag folders in the folder list to rearrange them. Tip: Click the arrow next to a folder to expand or collapse it. Your expand/collapse preferences are remembered between sessions.

There are two ways to move items, including notes, images, and shortcuts (quick links to characters, locations, and other items in your book), between folders: Drag and drop: Drag an item onto a folder in the folder list or in the content area on the right Move to Folder...: Right-click an item and choose "Move to Folder..." to pick the destination from a dialog You can move multiple items at once. Select several items by holding Ctrl (or Cmd on Mac) and clicking each one, or hold Shift and click to select a range. Then right-click and choose Move to Folder....

When you go into a nested folder, a breadcrumb trail (a row of folder names at the top showing where you are) appears above the content area. You can click any folder name in that path to jump back to it, or press Alt+Up Arrow to go to the folder that contains this one.

A Smart Folder is a regular folder that's linked to one of your tags (labels you create to categorize items across your book). It automatically creates shortcuts (links to the original items, not copies) to every item with that tag, keeping related content gathered in one place. Deleting a shortcut from a Smart Folder does not delete the original item — it just removes the link.

Right-click in the folder list and choose New Smart Folder. You'll be prompted to pick a tag. The folder is created and named after the tag, and it fills with shortcuts to all items that have that tag. You can also convert an existing folder into a Smart Folder: right-click it and choose Link to Tag (Smart Folder)..., then select a tag. Notes, images, and subfolders already in the folder stay where they are; the tag shortcuts are added alongside them.

To turn a Smart Folder back into a regular folder, right-click it and choose Unlink Smart Folder. The shortcuts that were automatically created will remain and still work; they continue to point to the original items. Any items you added manually also stay in the folder. However, new tagged items won't be added automatically. Note: You can also add tagged items to a regular folder without linking it. Right-click a folder and choose Add Shortcuts from Tag.... This adds them once; it won't automatically update if you tag more items later. Tip: A folder can also appear outside the Notebook. Point a Notebook Block on a character sheet or scene at a folder, and every note inside it shows up there as a live list, updating as you add notes. Handy for a per-character "Character Work" folder. The links below will take you to related articles in this help system. To learn more about shortcuts, see Shortcuts. For tag management, see Tags.
The Notebook lets you upload and organize reference images: character sketches, maps, mood boards, or any visual inspiration for your story.

There are two ways to add images: Toolbar button: Click the Image button in the toolbar at the top of the Notebook and pick files from your computer Drag and drop: Drag image files from your computer directly onto the Notebook page you're currently viewing Supported formats: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, and BMP. Images can be up to 20 MB each. When you upload an image, a dialog appears where you can give it a name (up to 100 characters) and an optional note (up to 500 characters). If you're uploading multiple images at once, you'll work through them one at a time; you can skip any image or use Cancel All to stop adding the rest. Tip: The image name is auto-filled from the filename, so you can skip the naming step if the filename is already descriptive.

Click any image to open a larger view on the right side of the screen. From there, you can: Zoom: Scroll your mouse wheel to zoom in very close or zoom way out. The current zoom level is shown at the bottom of the viewer. Move around: When zoomed in, click and drag the image to move around it Fit to screen: Click the number showing the current zoom level at the bottom-right and choose Fit to see the whole image again, or double-click the image to snap back to the default view Your zoom level and position are remembered for each image, so you can pick up right where you left off.

To change the image's name or description, press Ctrl+E (or Cmd+E on Mac) while viewing an image, or click the pencil icon in the top-right corner of the viewer. Changes save automatically; click the pencil icon again when you're done to leave editing.

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) an image to see its options: Edit Title: Rename the image (also triggered by pressing F2) Move to Folder: Move the image to a different folder (it will be removed from the folder it's currently in) Save to Disk: Download the image back to your computer Duplicate: Create a copy of the image Delete: You'll be asked to confirm first. Deleting an image is permanent and cannot be undone, so use Save to Disk first if you want to keep a copy. If you just want to hide an image, consider moving it to a folder for images you no longer need.

Tables let you organize information that doesn't fit neatly into prose: a magic system's rules, a side-by-side comparison of factions, character stats, or a relationship matrix. They work in any rich text area in Penpoint: notes, paragraph blocks on character and item pages, location pages, chapter author notes, arc details, and more.

Click the table icon (it looks like a small grid of squares) in the row of formatting buttons above the writing area. A small grid appears: hover over it to preview how many rows and columns you want, then click a cell to lock in that size. When you're happy with the selection, click Insert Table. Tables start with a header row (the top row, which is shaded differently: use it for column labels like "Name" or "Location") and can be up to 6 columns wide and 20 rows tall. You can add more rows and columns after inserting (up to the limits).

Click any cell to start typing. Press Tab to move to the next cell, or Shift+Tab to go back. Inside cells you can use: Bold, italic, underline, and links Bullet and numbered lists @Mentions: type @ followed by a name to link to a character, location, or item. Mentions appear as clickable links you can tap to jump straight there.
Adding and Removing Rows and Columns

Right-click any cell (or Ctrl+click on Mac) and hover over Table to see the options. The first four insert a new row or column next to the cell you clicked: Insert Row Above, Insert Row Below, Insert Column Left, and Insert Column Right. Insert options gray out when the table is already at its 6-column or 20-row limit. Below those, Delete Row and Delete Column remove the row or column containing the cell you clicked. These gray out when the table only has one row (or one column) left; to remove the whole table, use the trash icon next to the caption instead.

Every table has a caption above it: Untitled Table by default. Click the caption to type a new name (up to a short sentence). A descriptive name helps you identify the table at a glance and makes it easier to find in exported files. Tip: Undo works for most table edits: typing, adding rows and columns, and even renaming the caption. If you accidentally delete something, Ctrl+Z will bring it back.

Click the trash icon next to the caption. If you change your mind, Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) will bring the table back immediately; the confirmation dialog itself doesn't have an undo button, but the keyboard shortcut works right after you close it. The table and all its contents are removed once you confirm.

Tables don't convert to other formats when you export your work. No matter which format you export to, each table is replaced with a line like: [Table: "Faction Comparison"] At the end of your exported file, you'll find a list of all the tables in the document so you know exactly where to look. If you need the actual table data in another app, you'll need to rebuild it there manually. Note: This is an intentional trade-off. Tables are fully functional inside Penpoint, but because every export format handles tables differently, we show a clear placeholder rather than risk corrupted or mangled output. For more on what gets exported and what doesn't, see Exporting Worldbuilding Data.

Shortcuts are quick links from the Notebook to characters, locations, items, chapters, notes, story arcs, tags, and other parts of your book. Think of them as bookmarks: they point to things in your book without duplicating anything. You can gather related shortcuts in one folder to keep everything organized.

Click the Shortcut button in the toolbar at the top of the Notebook, or right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any empty space and choose Add Shortcut. A search dialog opens where you can find and select anything in your book. Type to search, then use the arrow keys or click to select an entry. Results are grouped by type (Characters, Items, Locations, Chapters, and so on), so you can quickly find what you're looking for.

Click a shortcut to jump straight to the page it points to. For example, clicking a character shortcut takes you to that character's profile on the Characters page. Each shortcut displays the name and an icon indicating its type. Tip: Combine shortcuts with Smart Folders (folders that automatically collect entries sharing a specific tag) to gather everything related to a topic. For example, a "Chapter 1" Smart Folder could contain shortcuts to every character, location, and item tagged with "Chapter 1."

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) a shortcut to see its options: Go to Alice (or whatever the shortcut points to): Jump to the linked character, location, or other page Move to Folder...: Move the shortcut to a different folder Duplicate: Create a copy of the shortcut, useful if you want the same link in multiple folders Delete: Remove the shortcut. This does not delete the original character, location, or other content from your book; it only removes the link to it.

Note: If the thing a shortcut points to has been deleted from your book, the shortcut will show a red "deleted" label next to its name. You can safely delete a broken shortcut; it only removes the link, not anything else in your book.

The Notebook (Penpoint's notes section) offers multiple ways to display and organize your content. Each folder can have its own view mode and sort order, so you can tailor the layout to fit what's inside.

Click the gear icon in the top-right corner of the toolbar above your notes to switch between three view modes: Cards: The default. Items display as cards in a grid that adjusts to fit your screen, showing titles, content previews, color accents (a colored left edge you can assign to notes), and tags. Large Cards: Wider cards with more content visible. Best when you want to read more of each note without opening it. List: Compact horizontal rows with title, tag indicators (small colored squares representing tags), and the date modified. The most space-efficient view for quickly scanning by name. Tip: Each folder remembers its own view mode, so you can use Cards for one folder and List for another.

Click the Sort button (the up-down arrow icon) in the toolbar above your notes to change how items are ordered: Manual: The default. You control the order by dragging items to rearrange them. Name: Alphabetical order Date created: By when items were first created Date modified: By when items were last changed Type: Groups items by kind: folders first, then notes, images, and shortcuts (quick links to other parts of your book) For any sort method except Manual, you can switch between ascending and descending order (A to Z vs. Z to A, or newest-first vs. oldest-first). Note: Drag-and-drop reordering only works when the sort is set to Manual: click and hold an item, then drag it to a new position. With other sort methods, the order is determined automatically.

You can select multiple items to move, archive, or delete them together: Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on Mac): Add or remove individual items from the selection Shift+click: Select a range of items from the last clicked item to the current one Ctrl+A (Cmd+A on Mac): Select all items in the current folder Selecting items doesn't change or remove anything on its own; it just highlights them so you can choose what to do next. Once you have multiple items selected, right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) to see options including: Move to Folder...: Moves the selected items to a different folder. You can reverse this by moving them back. Archive (for notes): Tucks them out of sight without deleting. You can show archived notes again using the "Show Archived" option in the gear menu. Delete: Removes the selected items (you'll always be asked to confirm first). Note: On Mac, Ctrl+click opens the right-click menu, while Cmd+click adds items to your selection. Both shortcuts use the Ctrl key label, but they do different things: use Cmd for selecting, Ctrl for the menu.

Archiving tucks a note out of sight without deleting it; your note is still safely stored in your book. It's perfect for ideas you've already used, old drafts, or notes you might want to reference later but don't need cluttering your workspace.

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) a note and choose Archive. You can also archive multiple notes at once by selecting them with Cmd+click (Mac) or Ctrl+click (Windows/Linux) to pick individual notes, or Shift+click to select a range. Then choose Archive from the right-click menu. Note: Archiving is completely reversible — you can bring any archived note back at any time. When in doubt, archive instead of deleting.

Archived notes are hidden by default. To see them, click the gear (cog-shaped) icon in the top-right corner of the toolbar above your notes and check the Show Archived option. Archived notes appear alongside your other notes but slightly faded so you can tell them apart. This only affects the folder you're in; your other folders won't change.
To bring an archived note back, first turn on Show Archived in the gear menu. Then right-click the archived note and choose Unarchive. The note returns to your active notes immediately.

A note template is a reusable starting point: an interview questionnaire, a scene-planning checklist, a worldbuilding form, anything you fill in the same way over and over. Save one once and it's available from every book and series on this computer, not just the one you saved it from.
Save a note as a template

Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any note and choose Save as Template, or click the template button at the end of the note's formatting toolbar. A copy of the note's title, content, and color is saved on this computer, ready to use in any book. The original note stays exactly where it was. To start one from scratch instead, open the Templates folder, right-click an empty spot, and choose New Template. A few things don't carry over, on purpose, because a template has to work in every book: Tags stay with the note, since other books won't have the same tags @Mentions (the links you make by typing @ and a name) turn into plain text, since the characters and places they point to only exist in one book Pictures are left out

There are three ways to create a note from a template. Each one gives you an ordinary note in your current folder, with the template's title, content, and color. The + Note button in the toolbar above your notes, then From Template... Right-click empty space among your notes and choose Add from Template Right-click empty space in the folder list on the left and choose Add from Template Note: The new note is independent. Editing it never changes the template it came from.

Once you have at least one template, a Templates folder appears in the folder list of the Notebook (the page where your notes live), below your own folders. It can't be renamed, moved, or deleted, and it disappears on its own when you delete your last template. Inside it, templates look and behave like any other notes, including every view mode (Cards, Large Cards, and List), except that each one shows a small template icon beside its title where a note shows its note icon. Opening one shows a banner reading "Template: changes here update the template for every book", because it does. While you edit a template, @mentions and pictures aren't available, for the same reason they're left out when you save one. Right-click a template for Rename, Change Color, or Delete Template. Deleting asks you to confirm first, and removing a template never touches the notes you already made from it.

If you don't use templates, click the gear icon in the top-right corner of the toolbar above your notes and turn on Hide Templates Folder. Penpoint remembers this for every book, so you only set it once. If you sync your settings with Penpoint Cloud, your other computers follow along too. Your templates are kept; turn the option off any time to reach them again.

Minipen (the slim sidebar on the right while you write in Manuscript Mode) shows the Templates folder as the first folder in its list. You can open and edit templates there, create a note from one through the + menu, and hide the folder from Minipen's own gear menu. The template button on a note's toolbar works there too. Renaming or deleting a template is done from the main Notebook.

With Penpoint Cloud, your templates follow you to your other computers. Signing in to a different Cloud account adds this computer's templates to that account, alongside any it already has. Signing out never removes templates from this computer. Templates sync together with your settings, so they stop syncing if you turn off Sync my settings across all my computers in Settings > Penpoint Cloud. Each computer keeps the templates it already has.

Templates don't belong to any one book, so they stay out of a book's search results, @mention suggestions, export, and backup files. They're kept on this computer, and with Penpoint Cloud on your other computers too. If you already keep your own folder named "Templates", it's untouched. The two sit side by side; in the Notebook, the shared one is always the last folder in the list. For everything else notes can do, see Working with Notes.

Manuscript Mode is Penpoint's dedicated writing environment. While Worldbuilding Mode is where you manage characters, locations, and other story details, Manuscript Mode is where you write your prose. It combines scene and chapter organization with Flowstate writing sessions, snapshots, find and replace, and import and export tools.

Click the Manuscript button in the worldbuilding sidebar, or press Ctrl+M (Cmd+M on Mac), to enter. To return to worldbuilding, click the Penpoint button (with the back arrow) in the top-left corner, or press Ctrl+M again. Both modes use the same records in your local book file. Chapters created in worldbuilding appear here, and your prose appears in chapter details. Switching modes does not create a second copy. Tip: When you first open Manuscript Mode in a book with no chapters, a welcome screen will offer to import an existing manuscript or start fresh. You can import .docx, .epub, .rtf, .md, or .txt files.

Manuscript Mode has a three-column layout: The Outliner (left): Shows groups, chapters, and scenes. Resize or collapse it, or select an item to jump there. Right-click (Ctrl+click on Mac) to create, delete, merge, or reorder chapters and scenes. Penpoint confirms deletion and merging. The Writing Area (center): Holds your prose and toolbar. The bottom bar shows the current view's word count and any selection count. Click the word count to show or hide the current Book's total. Minipen (right): A resizable reference sidebar for characters, locations, items, chapters, arcs, tags, and notes.
Every chapter starts with one scene. Press Ctrl+Shift+Enter(Cmd+Shift+Enter on Mac), or use the toolbar button, to insert a scene break. Text after the cursor becomes a new scene.

View and edit your manuscript at three levels: Scene: One scene, with Scene Drafts available. Chapter: One chapter with its scenes joined by dividers, and Chapter Drafts available. Book: See every chapter in the book you are currently writing. In a Series, this means the current Book, not the entire Series. In the Outliner, select a scene or chapter, or select the top open-book icon for the current Book.

Flowstate alternates between timed writing and editingphases. During writing, finished sentences temporarily lock after a short delay and dim by default. Editing unlocks them. The Outliner and Minipen collapse, other toolbar buttons fade but remain available, and your previous sidebar layout returns when you stop. Start Flowstate from the toolbar or press Ctrl+Shift+F (Cmd+Shift+F on Mac). Pause, resume, or stop at any time.

Fullscreen Mode hides the toolbar, sidebars, and header. To exit, press F11 again, or Esc when no menu or dialog is open. Enter with F11 (hold Fn on some laptops), or click Fullscreen Mode in the bottom-left corner of the word count bar. Move to the left or right edge, then click the strip that appears to open the Outliner or Minipen over your text. At the top, click the Toolbar strip to open the toolbar; click Hide Toolbar to close it. In Settings, Start Fullscreen when typing enters Fullscreen Mode after about five seconds of sustained writing. Exit automatically exits after 30 seconds without typing. Sustained writing can enter it again. Tip: Flowstate and Fullscreen Mode are independent. Flowstate collapses the sidebars, but Fullscreen Mode can remain on or off.

Snapshots are read-only copies of a Book's manuscript. In a Series, they cover the current Book, not the Series. Use the toolbar's Versionsbutton to create or browse them. You can read and copy from a snapshot, but not restore it over your manuscript. Scene Drafts save restorable versions of one scene and are available in Scene view. Before restoring one, Penpoint saves the current scene as a safety draft. Chapter Drafts save every scene in a chapter and are available in Chapter view. Before restoring one, Penpoint saves the current chapter as anAuto-saved before restore draft. Tip: Snapshots are read-only records. Scene and Chapter Drafts can be restored.
Press Ctrl+F (Cmd+F on Mac) to open the Find bar, or Ctrl+H (Cmd+H on Mac) for Find & Replace. Matches stay within the Scene, Chapter, or Book in view. Selected text becomes the search term.

Click Settings to choose writing width (narrow, standard, or wide), where reopened chapters begin (beginning, end, or where you left off), paragraph style (standard or novel indentation), scene dividers, chapter-number display, and spellcheck.

Import .docx, .epub, .rtf, .md, or .txt files from the toolbar. Penpoint tries to detect chapter breaks and adds new chapters; it never replaces existing content. You can rearrange or delete imported chapters. Export lets you choose the content, format, and options.
Your writing saves automatically as you type. The indicator at the top shows when it has saved; no manual save is needed.

Note: On Mac, use Cmd instead of Ctrl. The Mac chapter-break shortcut uses Option instead of Alt. Ctrl+M: Switch between Manuscript Mode and Worldbuilding Ctrl+F: Find Ctrl+H: Find & Replace Ctrl+K: Open the Search bar across the open book file. In a Series file, results can include every Book. Ctrl+F stays inside the writing you're viewing. Ctrl+Shift+Enter: Insert a scene break at your cursor Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Enter (Cmd+Shift+Option+Enter on Mac): Insert a chapter break at your cursor. That's a handful of keys, so there's a chapter break button in the toolbar too. Ctrl+Shift+F: Start or stop Flowstate F11: Enter or exit Fullscreen Mode (on some laptops, hold Fn as well) Ctrl+N: Open Quick Create for a character, location, item, chapter, note, or tag. Press Esc to close it without creating anything. Ctrl+Shift+N: Show the chapter you're writing in Minipen

Use these guides when you want more detail: Chapters & Scenes: How chapters and scenes fit together, and how to create and organize them The Outliner: The left sidebar: jump around, reorder, group, and manage your book's structure Scene & Chapter Breaks: Splitting and joining scenes and chapters as your draft grows The Toolbar: Every button in the writing toolbar, explained Manuscript Snapshots: Save and revisit read-only copies of a book's manuscript Scene Drafts: Keep alternate takes of a single scene without losing the original Chapter Drafts: Save and revisit every scene in a chapter together Comparing Your Manuscript Drafts: Compare a saved Scene Draft or Chapter Draft with your current writing Comments & Pinned Notes: Margin notes pinned to your prose, plus Notebook notes kept a glance away Manuscript Settings: Writing-area width, indentation, scene dividers, and other preferences Chapter Scanner: Scan your prose to detect which characters, locations, items, and tags appear in each chapter Minipen: The reference sidebar that brings your worldbuilding into the editor Flowstate: The timed, distraction-free writing mode that keeps you moving forward
In Manuscript Mode, your prose is organized into chapters and scenes. Chapters divide your book into major sections, and scenes divide each chapter into smaller beats of action or narrative.

Chapters are the main building blocks of your manuscript. Each chapter appears as an entry in the sidebar on the left (showing your chapters and scenes) and shows a heading in the writing area with an optional chapter number, title, and subtitle. Chapters in Manuscript Mode are the same chapters you see on the Chapters page in Worldbuilding Mode (the other main section of Penpoint, where you track characters, locations, and other story details). Creating or renaming a chapter in either mode updates it everywhere. This means your chapter outline, character assignments, and prose all stay connected. Title: You can rename a chapter two ways: click the chapter title in the writing area to edit it directly, or double-click the chapter name in the sidebar outline (max 50 characters) Subtitle: An optional line below the title for epigraphs or context (max 100 characters). Click "Add subtitle..." to create one. Numbering: Chapters can show "Chapter 1", "Chapter 2", etc. You can turn numbering on or off for each chapter from the sidebar outline by right-clicking (or Ctrl+click on Mac) and choosing the numbering option. Hiding the header: To make a chapter read as "empty" (like a prologue with no title), right-click its header in the writing area and choose "Hide Chapter Header." The number, title, and subtitle disappear while your prose stays put. Restore it anytime by right-clicking the chapter in the sidebar outline and re-checking "Show Chapter Header."

There are several ways to create a new chapter: Click the + button at the top of the sidebar outline and select "New Chapter" Right-click a chapter in the sidebar outline and choose Insert Chapter to add one directly after it Use a chapter break to split your current content into a new chapter. Click the chapter break button in the toolbar at the top of the writing area (it looks like a two-columns icon, rotated sideways). You can also use the shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Enter (Cmd+Shift+Alt+Enter on Mac). Note: Deleting a chapter removes all its scenes and prose permanently. A confirmation dialog will ask you to confirm before anything is removed. Choose Back Up + Delete to save a version snapshot of your entire manuscript before deleting; you can view it later from the Versions dialog (click the clock-shaped Versions button in the toolbar).

Scenes are the building blocks inside chapters. Each scene holds a portion of your prose and is separated from other scenes by a visual divider (which you can customize in manuscript settings: click Settings in the toolbar at the top of the writing area). Every chapter starts with at least one scene. As you write, you can add scene breaks to create natural story divisions: a change of location, a time jump, or a shift in point of view. Scene titles are optional. If a scene has no title, the sidebar outline shows a preview of the first few words of the scene's text instead. Empty scenes show as "Empty scene" in the sidebar outline. If a chapter has only one scene, the sidebar just shows the chapter; the scene is still there, it just doesn't need its own listing. Once you add a second scene, both appear individually under the chapter. Scenes can be reordered within a chapter by dragging them in the sidebar outline. Scenes can be moved between chapters by dragging them to a different chapter in the sidebar outline.

New scenes are created by inserting a scene break: Click the scene break button in the toolbar (it looks like a rectangle split in two; if the toolbar is narrow, look for it in the "More" dropdown). You can also use the shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Enter (Cmd+Shift+Enter on Mac). The scene break splits the current scene in two. Everything before the break stays in the original scene, and everything after becomes a new scene.

If you want to combine adjacent content, you can merge chapters or scenes: Merge chapters: Right-click a chapter and choose "Merge with chapter above" to combine its scenes into the previous chapter. Chapter merges cannot be undone, so be sure before you merge. Merge scenes: Right-click a scene in the outline and choose "Merge with scene above." Your writing from both scenes is kept: the text from the merged scene is added to the end of the one above it. You can also backspace across a scene divider in the writing area. Penpoint asks you to confirm either way, and Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) undoes a scene merge while you are still in that chapter.

If your book has Parts or Acts, you can use folders (also called groups) to organize chapters under those headings. Folders appear in the sidebar outline as collapsible containers that you can expand and collapse. Create a folder from the + button or by right-clicking a chapter that isn't already in a folder and selecting "Create Group." You can also move chapters into or out of folders using the right-click menu: choose "Add to Group" to file a chapter into an existing folder, or "Remove from Group" to pull it back out. Tip: You can rename a chapter, scene, or folder by double-clicking its name in the sidebar outline. Press Enter to save or Escape to cancel.
The outliner is the left sidebar in Manuscript Mode. It shows your book's chapters and scenes, lets you arrange them, and takes you straight to your writing.

Book: The book-icon row at the top. Click it to show all chapters in the writing area. Groups (Parts / Acts): Optional folders for chapters. The small badge beside a group name counts its chapters. Chapters: Filled page icons have writing; hollow page icons are empty. Scenes: Appear inside an expanded chapter when it has more than one scene.
Click a chapter or scene to open it. The selected row is highlighted. Use a chapter's arrow to show or hide scenes. Use a group's arrow or name to expand or collapse it.

Hover over a chapter, scene, or group and drag its six-dot grip: Chapters can move within, between, or outside groups. Groups can be reordered among other groups and top-level chapters. Scenes can move within or between chapters. A colored line or highlight previews the landing spot. Hold a chapter over the center of a collapsed group to open it. If the drop is wrong, simply drag the item again.
Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any chapter, scene, or group to see its menu.

Open in Minipen: Shows the chapter in the reference sidebar. Rename: Edits the chapter title in the outliner. View Chapter Drafts: Saves the whole chapter or compares a saved draft with current writing. It remains available for chapters with several scenes. Use Scene Drafts on a scene row for that scene alone. Insert Chapter Before / After: Opens the New Chapter window already set to the side you picked, right at this chapter's slot. You can switch Before or After there. The new chapter inherits this chapter's group. Move Earlier / Move Later: Moves one place. A direction is grayed out at that end of the book. New Scene: Adds a scene at this chapter's end. Numbered Chapter: Shows this chapter's number only when Show chapter numbers under the toolbar's Settings is also on. The number appears above the title. Show Chapter Header: Shows or hides the number, title, and subtitle without changing the writing. Use it to restore a header hidden from the writing area. Merge with Chapter 4: Joins this chapter into the one above and keeps both chapters' writing. It appears only when a previous chapter exists and names that chapter by visible number or title. Penpoint confirms first; chapter merges cannot be undone. Create Group / Add to Group / Remove from Group: Shows the grouping choices that apply. Create Group appears only for a chapter outside a group. Change Status: Mark the chapter as Draft, Revised, Polished, or Final. These are organizational labels and do not change your writing. Change Color: Adds a small color square to the row. Scan Chapter for Content: Finds character, location, item, and tag names. You choose which suggestions to add, and scanning never changes your prose. It is grayed out for an empty chapter. Delete Chapter: Permanently removes the chapter and all its scenes after confirmation. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) cannot restore them. The confirmation optionally offers Back Up + Delete, which saves a snapshot of the current Book's manuscript before deletion. When Back Up + Delete succeeds, its copy appears in the Versions window as a read-only snapshot, not a one-click undo. See Manuscript Snapshots for how to open it.

Open in Minipen: Opens the reference sidebar directly to this scene. Rename: Changes the scene title. Scene Drafts: Saves this scene or compares a saved draft with current writing. New Scene: Adds a scene directly after this one. Merge with scene above: After confirmation, combines both scenes' writing. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) can undo it until you open another chapter, switch between scene, chapter, and book views, or move a scene. Any of those actions makes it permanent. Undo restores the separated writing, name, color, status, characters, locations, items, tags, field data, and saved drafts. Chapter merges cannot be undone. Change Status: Applies Draft, Revised, Polished, or Final as an organizational label without changing prose. Change Color: Adds a small color square to the row. Delete Scene: Permanently removes its writing, notes, field data, saved drafts, character, location, item, and tag assignments, and story and character arc links. Penpoint confirms first. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) cannot restore them. Tip: A stacked-pages icon marks saved drafts on scenes and chapters, including chapters with several scenes. Hover for "This scene has saved drafts" or "This chapter has saved drafts." Once you open a saved draft in its read-only viewer, see Comparing Your Manuscript Drafts to learn how to read the comparison without restoring anything.

New Chapter in Group: Creates a chapter at the end of this folder. Rename Group: Changes the group name. Delete Group: Immediately removes the folder without confirmation. Its chapters move outside in their current order, and their writing stays safe. Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) cannot restore the group.

Click + for New Chapter, New Group, or New Scene when a chapter is selected. A new chapter starts near the selected chapter, or at the end when none is selected. Confirm its position in the dialog. Click a group's name first and the menu offers New Chapter in Groupinstead, which places the new chapter at the end of that folder.

Click the gear icon at the top of the outliner and check Show word counts for counts on chapter, scene, and group rows. A chapter totals its scenes. A group total sits at the far right, separate from its chapter-count badge. Counts refresh after writing saves, so they may settle after the editor's count. Long titles can wrap to a second line while counts show. Tip: With counts hidden, hover over a chapter, group, or scene with writing to see its count. This setting applies to all books and persists between sessions.
Double-click a chapter, scene, or group name to edit it inline. You can also use Rename or Rename Group from its menu.
Use the top collapse button for more writing room, then the expand button to return. Penpoint remembers the choice between sessions.
As you write, you'll need to split your prose into scenes and chapters. Penpoint makes this easy with toolbar buttons and keyboard shortcuts that split content right at your cursor position.

Press Ctrl+Shift+Enter (Cmd+Shift+Enter on Mac) to insert a scene break at your cursor. The text before the cursor stays in the current scene, and everything after becomes a new scene. A visual divider appears between them. You can also click the scene break button in the toolbar (the button that looks like a rectangle split in two; hover over it and the tooltip will say "Scene break"). Scene breaks are useful for marking shifts in time, location, or point of view within a chapter. Tip: You can customize the look of scene dividers in manuscript settings (click the gear icon in the toolbar). Choose from six styles: Quill, Dinkus (the classic * * * mark seen in published books), Line, Fade, Dot, or Blank.

The easiest way to insert a chapter break is to click the chapter break button in the toolbar (the two-columns icon, right next to the scene break button; hover over it and the tooltip will say "Chapter break"). You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Enter (Cmd+Shift+Alt+Enter on Mac). Either way, this splits the current content into two chapters at your cursor position. A small window pops up asking for the new chapter's details: Chapter Title: The name of the new chapter (max 50 characters). In which...: A brief chapter summary, meant to be completed like a sentence, e.g. "In which our hero discovers the truth." This is optional (max 100 characters). Chapter Type: Choose from Standard, Prologue, Epilogue, and several others. This is a label for your own reference. You can usually just leave this on Standard and press Enter. After confirming, everything after your cursor moves into the new chapter and Penpoint takes you there.

You can undo a split, but only right away: before you type anything else or leave the chapter. Once you start editing or move to a different chapter, the undo option is gone. To undo, press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac). For scene splits, one undo step puts everything back. For chapter breaks (which split both a scene and a chapter), pressing Ctrl+Z twice will fully reverse the operation: first rejoining the chapters, then rejoining the scenes.

To merge two scenes back together, place your cursor on the line directly above or below a scene divider and press Backspace or Delete. You can also right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) a scene in the outline sidebar (the chapter and scene list on the left side of the screen) and select Merge with scene above. Either way, Penpoint asks you to confirm first, then combines the two scenes into one. All the writing from both scenes is kept, in order, and the absorbed scene's characters, locations, items, tags, and plot points move across to the scene above it. Notes and other text fields are joined together; where both scenes had a single number or date, the upper scene's value wins. The absorbed scene itself stops existing, so its name, color, status, and any saved drafts on it are removed. The confirmation window says so before you commit. Note: Merged two scenes by mistake? Press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) to undo. Penpoint restores the absorbed scene exactly as it was: its title, color, status, saved drafts, custom field values, and any character, location, tag, or plot point assignments all come back. The undo lasts until you navigate to a different chapter or close the app, so check the merge looks right while you still have it. The text of the second scene should now start where the divider used to be. Tip: If you merge scenes often and would rather skip the confirmation, tick Don’t ask again in the merge window. Backspace and Delete will then merge straight away (the right-click menu still confirms). This applies to every book. To bring the confirmation back, open manuscript settings with the gear icon in the toolbar and re-tick Confirm scene merges.

Right-click a chapter in the outline sidebar and select Merge with chapter above to combine it with the previous chapter. Penpoint will ask you to confirm before merging. All scenes from both chapters are preserved: the scenes from the second chapter are added after the scenes from the first. Note: Unlike scene merges, chapter merges cannot be undone with Ctrl+Z. If you merge by mistake, you would need to manually re-split the chapter using a chapter break. Take a moment to confirm you're merging the right chapters before proceeding.

The toolbar sits at the top of your writing area. From here you can format text, organize your manuscript, and access features like snapshots (saved copies of your entire manuscript), Scene Drafts, and export.

The zoom button is on the far left. It adjusts how large the text appears on screen (from 75% to 200%). You can click the zoom percentage number and type a custom value, or pick from the list: 75%, 90%, 100%, 125%, 150%, or 200%. You can also hold Ctrl and scroll your mouse wheel to zoom in or out.

The core formatting buttons are always visible: Bold (Ctrl+B) Italic (Ctrl+I) Underline (Ctrl+U) Highlight (Ctrl+Shift+H): applies a yellow highlight marker Note: On Mac, use Cmd instead of Ctrl for all keyboard shortcuts in this article (for example, Cmd+B for bold, Cmd+Z for undo).

More formatting options appear when your window is wide enough. If the window is too narrow to show them all, they'll be tucked into a "More" dropdown menu: Paragraph style: Normal text (Ctrl+Alt+0), Heading 1 (Ctrl+Alt+1), Heading 2 (Ctrl+Alt+2) Lists: Bullet list (Ctrl+Shift+8), Numbered list (Ctrl+Shift+7) Indentation: Indent (Tab), Unindent (Shift+Tab) Alignment: Left, Center, Right, Justify Horizontal line: Adds a divider line across the page Breaks: Scene break splits your text into two scenes (Ctrl+Shift+Enter). Chapter break starts a new chapter at your cursor (Ctrl+Shift+Alt+Enter; this shortcut is a handful, so the toolbar button is usually easier). You can undo either break right away with Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac). Insert Image: Adds an image to your manuscript Add comment (Ctrl+Alt+M): Attaches a margin note to the selected text. See Comments & Pinned Notes Tip: When formatting is applied, the matching button lights up. For example, if your cursor is sitting in bold text, the Bold button will look pressed.

Undo (Ctrl+Z) and Redo (Ctrl+Y) work just like they do in any word processor. If there are no more text changes to undo, Ctrl+Z will reverse your last big change instead (like putting a split scene or chapter back together).

On the right side of the toolbar, you'll find: Scene Drafts: Save and restore snapshots of individual scenes (only visible when viewing a single scene) Import: Import a manuscript from .docx, .epub, .rtf (Rich Text, including Scrivener compiles), .md (Markdown), or .txt Export: Export your manuscript to .docx, .pdf, .epub, .md, .txt, and more Versions: Save and view snapshots of your entire book. (Scene Drafts save copies of individual scenes; Versions save a snapshot of the whole book.) Settings: Adjust canvas width (how wide the writing area is), paragraph view (how your paragraphs are spaced and indented), scene dividers (the visual separators between scenes), chapter numbers, spellcheck, and more Flowstate: Start a focused writing session that keeps you moving forward (you won't be able to go back and edit what you already wrote, so you stay in the flow) If your window is narrow, some of these buttons (except Settings and Flowstate) will be tucked into the three-dot button on the right side of the toolbar to save space.

Press Ctrl+F (or Ctrl+H) to open Find & Replace. A search bar will appear below the toolbar with: A search field with match counter ("3 of 12") A case-match button: when turned on, searching for "The" will only find "The" and skip "the" or "THE". When turned off, it finds all of them regardless of capitalization. Previous/Next buttons to jump between matches (Shift+Enter / Enter) Replace and Replace All buttons: Replace All affects whatever you're currently looking at (a single scene, a chapter, or the whole book). You can undo replacements with Ctrl+Z. Press Escape to close the search bar and clear any highlighted matches. Note: While you're in a Flowstate writing session, Replace and Replace All are turned off. You can still search and jump between matches, but you'll need to pause Flowstate or wait for the editing break that follows each writing sprint before you can replace text.

Manuscript snapshots let you save a copy of your entire manuscript at a point in time. The button in the toolbar at the top of your writing area is called Versions: think of each version as a snapshot of your book at a point in time. Snapshots are for looking back and copying text you need; they don't replace your current manuscript. You can always open a snapshot to see exactly what your book looked like and grab anything you want to reuse.

A snapshot captures everything in your manuscript: All chapters with their titles, subtitles, numbering, and which folders your chapters are in All scenes within every chapter, including the full text How your chapters are organized into folders (the snapshot captures everything even if you don't use folders) Snapshots always capture your entire manuscript, not individual chapters or scenes. In a series, that means the whole of the Book you are currently writing in: each Book keeps its own separate set of snapshots, and its own 10 slots. Note: If your series is older than version 1.3.5, snapshots you took back then captured every Book at once rather than one Book, so they are all kept together under your first Book. Open the first Book’s Versions panel to read any of them.

Click the Manuscript versions button (the clock icon) on the right side of the toolbar at the top of your writing area. A window opens with your version list. Type an optional description and click Create. Note: Creating a snapshot leaves your scene drafts (saved alternate versions of individual scenes; see the Scene Drafts article) exactly where they are. The two features keep separate histories, so you never have to choose between them. Descriptions help you remember why you took the snapshot: for example, "Before rewriting Chapter 3" or "Draft 2 complete." If you leave the description blank, Penpoint names it for you automatically: Version 1, Version 2, and so on. Note: You can store up to 10 snapshots per book. When you reach the limit, delete an older snapshot before creating a new one.

Click the eye icon (an open eye shape) next to any snapshot to open it, or click anywhere on that row. The viewer looks and feels like your regular writing screen (with the sidebar for browsing chapters), but nothing can be changed. A "Read-only Snapshot" label at the top confirms you're viewing a snapshot. Click Back to Editor or press Escape to return to your current manuscript.

Edit description: Click the pencil icon to update a snapshot's description. Press Enter to save the description. Delete: Click the trash icon to permanently remove a snapshot. Deletion is immediate with no confirmation step, so be sure before you click. This makes room for a new one if you've reached the 10-snapshot limit. Snapshots are listed newest first. Version numbers (v1, v2, etc.) are assigned in the order you create them: v1 is your first snapshot, v2 the second, and so on. In a series the numbering starts again at v1 in each Book, so the panel header names the Book you are looking at.

Scene Drafts save a copy of one scene before major changes. Unlike manuscript snapshots, they can be restored as your current scene. Before restoring, Penpoint saves your current scene as a draft labeled "Auto-saved before restore" so you can return to it. Note: Manuscript snapshots and Scene Drafts are separate. Snapshots do not include draft history, and creating one does not delete drafts. See Manuscript Snapshots to learn about read-only copies of a whole Book.

Select a scene, not a chapter, in the Outliner. Click Scene Drafts in the toolbar, add an optional description, then click Save Draft. Good descriptions help you find the right draft later: "Before point-of-view change," "Original ending," or "Pre-feedback revision." Tip: Penpoint does not set a limit on how many scene drafts you can save.

Click a draft or its eye-shaped icon to open the dedicated read-only viewer. Its list starts with Current Manuscript, a read-only view of your current scene, followed by saved drafts. Drafts normally appear newest first. An unseen Cloud-preserved draft is prioritized at the top until you view it. Select an entry to switch versions. Select a draft and click Compare. The read-only comparison shows writing removed since the draft on the left and writing added on the right. Comments stay saved but are not compared. If Penpoint cannot calculate or display the comparison, neither copy changes. Turn off Compare to view one version again. See Comparing Your Manuscript Drafts for how to read the highlights and step through the changes.

Click Use This Draft. Before anything changes, Penpoint asks you to confirm and explains the safety draft: Your current scene content is automatically saved as a new draft labeled "Auto-saved before restore" The draft you chose becomes your current scene If you don't like the result, restore the auto-saved draft to go back A draft with no writing in it shows This version is empty and cannot be restored, from the viewer, the Scene Drafts list, or the Chapter Drafts list.

Click the trash icon beside a draft to delete it. A draft you saved yourself, or one with no writing in it, is deleted immediately with no confirmation and no Scene Drafts Undo. A version kept from another device that has writing in it asks first (for example, "Delete the version from Studio Laptop?"; choose Delete Version), because deleting it is the one way to lose that device's words. Deleting never changes your current scene.

In the viewer, right-click a draft (Ctrl+click on Mac) for Use This Draft or Delete This Draft (Use This Version or Delete This Version for a version kept from another device). You can also right-click a scene in the Outliner and choose Scene Drafts. A small stacked-pages icon marks scenes with drafts.

If the same scene is changed on two devices, your newest writing stays in the scene and Penpoint Cloud keeps the other version as a draft. Current Manuscript is the writing that is live in your scene; the preserved copy sits in the list below it. If a scene is edited on one device and deleted on another, the edited scene stays in your book and its writing is kept as a draft too. Each preserved draft carries a label saying where it came from ("Kept from your other device" or "From a deleted scene"), naming the other device when Penpoint knows its name. Until you look at a preserved draft, Penpoint raises a short notice reading Edited on another device on your library shelf, in Penpoint Cloud settings (the library-wide list of every affected book and scene), and in the Save menu inside your book. Inside the book, a message titled A scene was changed on two devices offers Review It (Review Them when there are several, stepping through every scene) or Keep Everything As Is. A scene that was deleted on one device, but still had writing in it on another, is marked "deleted, but iPhone still had writing in it" (with the name of whichever device it was, or "another device" when Penpoint does not know). A small amber stack icon at the right end of the scene's row in the Outliner (or its chapter's row) marks it too; its tooltip reads "Another version of this scene is in Drafts. Click to compare" (or "This scene was deleted, but iPhone still had writing in it, so Penpoint kept it. Click to review"), and clicking it opens just that scene. Opening a preserved draft marks it viewed without restoring it, which clears the notice and the icon. A preserved draft opens in a side-by-side comparison. Your manuscript is on the right, titled In your manuscript; the other device's version is on the left; Newer tags whichever was edited later. A bar under the two sides has a legend that marks what is "Only in the other version" and "Only in your manuscript", and the change arrows ("Change 2 of 5") step through the differences with both sides scrolling together. After Review Them, "Scene 2 of 5" arrows at the top move through the scenes. The version you don't keep stays in Drafts. Keep This One (right side): leaves your manuscript as it is, clears that scene's amber icon, and keeps the other version in Drafts Use This Version (left side): asks you to confirm (for example, "Use the version from Studio Laptop?"; choose Use This Version), saves your current version in Drafts first, replaces your scene with the other one, and lands you back in that scene. If you were stepping through several scenes, the tour ends and the scenes you have not reached keep their amber icons. If Penpoint kept a scene because it was deleted on one device but another still had writing in it, you see only the scene, with Keep the Scene or Delete It Again. Delete It Again asks you to confirm first; if it is the only scene in its chapter, the confirmation covers the whole chapter. A version with no writing in it is marked as seen when the book opens, so it does not raise the notice.

Chapter drafts save an entire chapter, including every scene's writing, title, and order. Saving or viewing one does not change your current chapter. Only choosing to use or restore a draft does that. A scene draft saves one scene instead. Save a chapter draft when you want a snapshot of this chapter before rewriting it. Note: Chapter drafts do not copy worldbuilding links. Existing scenes keep their character, location, item, tag, and other links after a restore. A deleted scene can be recreated with its saved writing and title, but you must re-add its old links.

Select a chapter, then click Chapter Drafts in the toolbar. You can also right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) a chapter and choose View Chapter Drafts. Add an optional description such as "Draft 1 before rewrite," then click Save Draft. Tip: Before every restore, Penpoint saves the current writing, scene titles, and order in a safety draft labeled Auto-saved before restore. You can use Save Draft while the chapter has fewer than 10 chapter drafts. Restore still works at the limit because its safety draft may take the count above 10.

Open a draft to read its saved scenes in a full-screen, read-only viewer. You can select and copy text into your current chapter without restoring. Saved comments appear in this regular view. Click Compare to compare the whole saved chapter or one scene with your current writing. It shows writing and scenes added or removed, plus scene title and order changes. Comments stay saved but are not compared. See Comparing Your Manuscript Drafts for how to compare a whole chapter or one scene.

Click the circular-arrow restore icon in the Drafts panel, then Restore Draft. In the viewer, click Use This Draft, then Use Saved Draft. Penpoint creates the safety draft first, then: Existing scenes return to their saved writing, titles, and order while keeping their links Deleted scenes return with saved writing and titles, but without their old links Scenes added or moved in later are removed from the current chapter, but remain in the safety draft A scene moved out to another chapter stays there and is not copied back Restore does not change the chapter title, subtitle, description, author notes, numbering, header settings, or group placement. To reverse the writing change, restore Auto-saved before restore. It brings back the previous writing, titles, and order, but a scene that must be recreated still lacks its old links.
The toolbar label changes with your view. Select a chapter and it reads Chapter Drafts. Select a scene and it reads Scene Drafts. A chapter with one scene uses chapter drafts.

Click the trash icon next to a draft. Penpoint asks Delete? in the same row; click the checkmark to delete it permanently or the X to keep it. If you have a backup, Backup & Restore explains how to look for an older copy of your book.

A Scene Draft saves one scene. A Chapter Draft saves every scene in a chapter together. Compare places either kind of saved draft beside your current manuscript. Both sides are read-only, so comparing them does not change or restore either copy.

In Manuscript Mode, right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) a scene and choose Scene Drafts, or right-click a chapter and choose View Chapter Drafts. Select a saved draft, then click Compare at the top. The saved draft appears on the left, titled Saved draft, and the current manuscript appears on the right, titled In your manuscript. Each side normally shows a word count and has its own scrollbar; scrolling one side scrolls the other along with it. The matching button beside each title lets you use that version.

Only in the draft: writing found in the saved draft but not in the current version is highlighted and crossed out on the left. Only in your manuscript: writing found in the current version but not in the saved draft is highlighted and underlined on the right. Change stepper: the bar under the two sides counts the separate areas where the versions differ (for example, 4 changes). Use the arrows to jump both sides to the next or previous change. Note: Comment text is hidden from Compare, not deleted or included in the change count. Turn off Compare to read the comments saved with the draft.

In a Chapter Draft, click the chapter name in the sidebar on the left to compare the whole chapter. Click a scene name to focus on that scene. The whole-chapter view can reveal scenes that were added, removed, renamed, or reordered, as well as changes to their writing. If a saved scene was deleted or moved elsewhere, the current version side says This scene is not in the current chapter instead of showing a word count. Note: Compare may show changes to the chapter title, subtitle, or whether its heading is displayed. Restoring a Chapter Draft only rewinds scene writing, scene titles, and order. It does not restore those chapter-heading details, and a scene moved to another chapter stays there.Use This Chapter Draft's Scenes saves your current writing in a draft first, then places the saved scenes in your manuscript. The safety copy is named Auto-saved before restore.

Choose Use This Draft beside the left title to put the saved writing in your manuscript. Penpoint saves your current version in Drafts first. Choose Keep Current Version beside the right title to return to the editor without changing anything; the selected draft stays saved. Whichever version you do not use stays in Drafts. You can also click Exit Compare to continue browsing drafts. If Penpoint shows Comparison unavailable, turn off Compare to return to the standard draft viewer. This is only a display limitation; neither version has changed. A saved draft with no writing in it shows This version is empty instead of its text. It has no button to use it, and the Scene Drafts and Chapter Drafts lists do not offer to restore it either, so it cannot replace your scene.

Comments are notes to yourself, pinned in the page margin beside the exact text they're about: revision reminders, pacing questions, anything to flag without touching the prose. They never appear in your exported manuscript.

Select text, then: Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) and choose Add Comment Click the speech-bubble button in the toolbar above your writing area Press Ctrl+Alt+M (Cmd+Option+M on Mac) A card opens in the margin; type your note and save. Clicking the highlighted text or the card brings it to the front. A comment can't stretch across a scene divider or chapter heading, since each side belongs to a different scene.

Each card's three-dot menu offers Edit comment, Resolve, and Delete. Double-click the text to edit, or click Add more… for a follow-up line. Resolving clears a comment from the margin without deleting anything; find and reopen it from the Comments View menu (below). Deleting removes the comment and its highlight for good; by default Penpoint asks you to confirm first.

When a page has comments, a speech-bubble button at the top right shows how many are open. Its menu lets you: Filter to Open (the default), Resolved, or All comments Hide comments, shrinking every card to a small dot; hover to preview, click to open the full card Turn Ask before deleting on or off (with this off, Delete removes a comment immediately, with no confirmation step) A narrow window shrinks comments to the same small dots automatically. Fullscreen writing and Flowstate (the timed, distraction-free writing mode) hide comments entirely.

You can also pin a note from your Notebook to a line of prose: select text, right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac), choose Pin a Note…, then pick the note. The margin card shows a live preview with an Open in Notebook button. The note itself gains a Pinned in manuscript list of every spot it's pinned; clicking an entry jumps you back there. Note: Pasting commented text elsewhere in your manuscript carries the comment along; both spots share the same comment, so editing, resolving, or deleting from either updates both. Tip: Comments are preserved read-only in manuscript snapshots and scene drafts, so old versions keep their margin notes.

Manuscript settings control the look and feel of your writing environment. Access them by clicking the Settings button in the toolbar at the top of your writing area. These settings apply to all your books, but they only affect how things look on your screen; they don't change the content of any book.

Canvas Width (how wide the writing area appears on your screen) lets you choose the option that feels most comfortable: Narrow: A tighter column, similar to a printed page. Great for focused writing. Standard: A balanced width that works well on most screens (default). Wide: Fills most of the screen. Great for large monitors or longer chapters.

Choose where you start reading when you open a chapter or scene: Beginning: Opens at the top of the page (default). End: Opens at the bottom, so you can pick up writing right away. Where I Left Off: Takes you back to the exact spot you were last working. Penpoint remembers your place in each chapter and scene separately.

Paragraph View controls how your paragraphs look: indented like a printed novel, or separated with spaces like online writing. Choose the layout that suits your writing: Standard: No indent on the first line. Paragraphs are separated by a blank line, like most ebooks. Novel: Each paragraph is indented on the first line, like a printed novel (default).

Turn Chapter numbers on or off to show or hide "Chapter 1," "Chapter 2," etc. above your chapter titles. You can also turn numbering on or off for individual chapters by right-clicking (or Ctrl+click on Mac) them in the chapter list on the left.

Turn Show subtitles on or off to show or hide the subtitle line beneath every chapter title, along with the "Add subtitle..." prompt. This only changes what you see on screen; any subtitles you've written are kept and reappear when you turn it back on.
Turn Spellcheck on or off. When it's on, misspelled words will be underlined as you type. Autocorrect settings (like dash behavior and smart quotes) are also available here.

Turn on Highlight current line to draw a soft band behind the line your cursor is on, so it's always easy to see where you are as you write. A "Line X of Y" counter also appears at the bottom of your writing area. When it's on, two extra options appear beneath it: Line Color: Keep the neutral Default band, pick one of twelve colors, or choose a custom color of your own. Intensity: How strong the band looks: Subtle, Medium, or Bold. Note: The twelve preset colors adapt to whatever theme you're using, so your line stays in harmony with the rest of Penpoint. A custom color stays exactly as you set it.

Choose the visual style for scene breaks: Quill: A quill icon flanked by horizontal lines (default) Dinkus: The classic * * * mark you see in published books to signal a scene break Line: A simple horizontal line Fade: A line that gently fades at the edges Dot: A centered dot with lines on each side Blank space: No visible divider, just empty space

Editor Font lets you pick a different font for just your manuscript writing area, without changing the rest of the app. Your prose, chapter titles, and chapter subtitles will use the font you pick here, while sidebars, toolbars, and settings stay on the font you chose in your main app settings. Useful if you like writing prose in a serif like Source Serif 4 but prefer a clean sans-serif like Inter everywhere else. Pick Use Global Font to match the rest of the app again.

The zoom control is in the toolbar at the top of your writing area (the percentage number on the far left), not in settings. You can adjust it from 75% to 200% by typing a number, picking from the list of sizes, or holding Ctrl and scrolling your mouse wheel. Your zoom level is remembered the next time you open Penpoint. Tip: All manuscript settings are saved automatically and remembered the next time you open Penpoint.

The Chapter Scanner reads through your writing and finds mentions of characters, locations, items, and tags that you've already added to your book. It can also spot new names that might be story elements you haven't tracked yet. The scanner never changes your actual writing; it only updates your tracking lists and chapter connections. Note: The scanner currently works best with English text. Support for other languages may improve over time.

To run a scan: Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any chapter in the chapter list on the left (the sidebar that lists your chapters) Select Scan Chapter for Content (content here means character names, locations, items, and tags that appear in your writing) A brief explanation screen appears: click Scan Now to begin The scanner reads all scenes in the chapter and presents results for your review before making any changes A progress bar shows how far along the scan is. When it finishes, you'll see results organized into sections. Any characters, locations, items, or tags already connected to this chapter are marked as Already linked so you can focus on what's new. Connecting just means Penpoint will remember that this character (or location, item, or tag) appears in this chapter; it never changes your actual writing.

The scanner looks for capitalized words and phrases in your prose that appear to be proper nouns: character names, place names, titles, and so on. It uses a few rules to separate real names from ordinary words that happen to be capitalized: Sentence starts are ignored. Words at the beginning of a sentence or a line of dialogue are capitalized by grammar rules, not because they are names. The scanner skips these positions when deciding what counts as a proper noun. Common words are filtered out. Words like "However," "Meanwhile," "English," and similar everyday words that are always capitalized are excluded automatically. Repetition matters. A name needs to appear more than once in your writing to be reported. One-off capitalized words are usually not story elements worth tracking. Multi-word names are combined. If "Jack" is almost always followed by "Allen," the scanner reports "Jack Allen" as a single name rather than two separate entries. Articles are preserved when consistent. If your text consistently says "the Dark Lord" rather than just "Dark Lord," the scanner keeps the article as part of the name. The scanner also tries to guess whether each new discovery is a character, location, or item based on the words around it. For example, names that appear with dialogue tags ("said," "whispered") are likely characters, while names that appear with spatial words ("in," "near," "traveled to") are likely locations. This guess pre-selects the type dropdown for you, but you can always change it. Tip: The scanner is deliberately conservative: it would rather miss a name than flood you with false results. If it missed something, use the Quick Add button to add it manually. You can also teach the scanner aliases so it catches alternate names in future scans.
Names Penpoint is quite sure about are already selected for you, so just uncheck any you don't want to connect to this chapter.
These are names Penpoint is less sure about: usually a single mention or only a partial name match. Look these over carefully before selecting them.

These are names found in your writing that don't match anything in your book yet. For each one, you can: Pick from the menu what it is (Character, Location, Item, or Tag) Edit the name before adding it to your book Match it to something you've already created using the chain-link button (two linked loops) to the right of each name (handy for aliases like "The Dark Lord" matching "Sauron")

Use the Quick Add button to add something the scanner didn't catch. Type a name, pick from the menu what it is, and optionally match it to an existing character, location, item, or tag, all without leaving the scanner.

Check the boxes next to anything you want to connect or create, then click Apply Selected. The scanner will: Connect existing characters, locations, items, and tags to the chapter Add new names you selected to the appropriate tracking list (for example, add a new character to your character list, or a new location to your locations list) These new additions are only added to your tracking lists, not inserted into your writing. And if the scanner got something wrong, you can always delete anything it creates. No harm done. If nothing is selected, a Continue button appears instead, letting you proceed to the completion screen without making changes.

You can teach the scanner to recognize aliases (what you might think of as nicknames) for your characters. For example, if your character Sauron is sometimes called "The Dark Lord," the scanner will learn to connect both names. These aliases are saved right away and remembered for every scan going forward. You can review and remove saved aliases in the Aliases section at the bottom of the results screen. Ignoring a result tells the scanner to stop suggesting that name in future scans. Ignoring a result doesn't delete anything; it just hides the suggestion. Click the eye icon with a line through it (meaning "hide") on any result to ignore it, or click the Ignored heading to expand it and bring back anything you previously ignored. Tip: After scanning one chapter, click Scan Next Chapter to continue through your manuscript in order. This makes it easy to scan your entire book chapter by chapter. When every chapter has been scanned, the scanner lets you know.

Minipen (a mini version of Penpoint's reference tools) is a slim sidebar that sits along the right side of Manuscript Mode (where you write your prose). It lets you look up your characters, locations, items, and more without leaving your writing.

When closed, Minipen collapses to a small sidebar icon on the right edge of the screen. Click that icon to slide Minipen open. To close it again, click the close button at the top of Minipen. Penpoint remembers whether you left it open or closed. Minipen is resizable: drag the left edge of Minipen to make it wider or narrower.

The row of eight small icons (representing characters, items, locations, and more) below the search box lets you jump between different sections. Hover over any icon to see its name. Characters: See all your characters in a list. Pick one to read their details, or add a new character with the + button. Items: Look up and create items. Locations: Look up and create locations. Chapters: Review your chapter details. Arcs: Check your story arcs (the big plot threads) and character arcs (how characters change over the story). Click the button at the top of the Arcs section to flip between the two. Notes: Browse, create, and edit your notes. Tags: See your tags and which characters, locations, items, chapters, arcs, or notes they are attached to. Settings: Reach your interface, spellcheck, import/export, community & updates, storage & backups, and about screens. The Notes section also holds your Templates folder, so you can start a note from one of your Note Templates without leaving your manuscript. Tip: Press Ctrl+E (or Cmd+E on Mac) while viewing a character, item, location, chapter, or arc to switch between reading and editing without leaving Minipen. You can also click the pencil icon at the top of the detail view inside Minipen. Any changes you make here are saved automatically, just like everywhere else in Penpoint. If you change something by accident, press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) to undo; your previous version is safe. Click the back arrow at the top of the detail view or the section icon to return to the list.
Read a Chapter's Details While You Write

Halfway through Chapter 9 and can't remember whose funeral it was? You can bring a chapter's details up beside you without losing your place. Your cursor stays exactly where it was in your prose, so you check the detail and carry straight on typing. There are three ways to do it, and they all end up in the same place: Right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) any chapter or scene in the list of chapters and scenes down the left side of Manuscript Mode, and choose Open in Minipen. Minipen switches to that chapter no matter what it was showing before, and opens itself first if you had it closed. Right-click a scene (one of the sections within a chapter) and it lands on that scene rather than the top of its chapter. Press Ctrl+Shift+N (Cmd+Shift+N on Mac) for the chapter you're writing in right now. (If that three-key combo is an awkward reach, the button below does the same thing.) Click the small target-style button (a dot inside a circle with short lines poking out, like a little crosshair). Hovering it shows Open the active chapter (or Open the active scene when your cursor is inside a scene). "Active" just means the chapter your cursor is sitting in right now. The button sits both at the top of Minipen's Chapters section and inside a chapter's details, so you can reach your writing chapter without backing out to the list. It appears whenever you have a chapter open in your writing area.
Keep Minipen on the Chapter You're Writing

If you'd rather Minipen keep up on its own, open a chapter in Minipen's Chapters section, then click the little gear (settings) icon at the top of that chapter's details and turn on Link to the active chapter. After that, while you're looking at the Chapters section, moving to a different chapter in your manuscript opens its details here automatically, so your chapter notes are always the ones for the chapter you're writing. You can turn it back off from the same gear any time. It only follows while you're on the Chapters section, so switching chapters never pulls you away from Characters, Arcs, or anywhere else in Minipen. Leave it off and Minipen stays put until you ask it to move.

The search box at the top of Minipen searches across everything in your book: characters, locations, items, chapters, and more. Start typing to search, and results appear after two or more letters. Click a result to jump straight to it inside Minipen. Search results for scenes (the sections within a chapter) work a little differently: clicking a scene result takes you straight to that scene in your manuscript. Scene results also need at least four letters before they appear, since prose turns up far more matches than a name does. Tip: Most search results (everything except scenes) show a small outward-pointing arrow icon when you hover over them. Your manuscript stays exactly where you left it. Clicking this icon takes you to the full page for that character, location, item, or other entry in Worldbuilding Mode (where you manage all your characters, locations, and other details), and you can come right back.

Flowstate is a writing mode that keeps you moving forward, designed to break the habit of endlessly re-editing what you just wrote. As you write, Flowstate protects each finished sentence (temporarily; everything unlocks during editing time, and you can always pause to make changes). Flowstate never deletes or changes your writing — when it ends, all your text is right where you left it, fully editable. It works on a simple timer that alternates between Writing Time and Editing Time. During writing time, your sentences lock once you finish them. When the timer switches to editing time, everything unlocks so you can revise. Then you go back to writing time.

Click the Flowstate button on the right side of the toolbar (the row of buttons at the top of your writing area), or press Ctrl+Shift+F (Cmd+Shift+F on Mac). The button changes to show your current mode and a small timer bar appears above your writing area. The default is 15 minutes of writing followed by 5 minutes of editing, but you can change these anytime in the settings. If the keyboard shortcut feels like too many keys, just use the Flowstate button instead. To stop Flowstate, click the Stop button (square icon) in the timer bar, or press Ctrl+Shift+F again (Cmd+Shift+F on Mac). The timer bar stays on screen after you stop, so you can adjust your settings or start another session straight from the play button. To tuck the bar away, click the Flowstate button.

During writing time (shown in orange), each sentence locks after you finish it. Penpoint recognizes sentence endings (periods, question marks, and exclamation points) and is smart enough to ignore abbreviations (Dr., Mr., etc.), decimals, web addresses, and ellipses. It also handles dialogue punctuation, so a period inside quotation marks won't accidentally lock mid-sentence. A brief countdown appears at the end of each sentence: you have about 1.5 seconds before it locks. Made a mistake? Press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on Mac) within 5 seconds to unlock and fix it. Locked text fades slightly so you can tell it apart from editable text (you can turn this off in settings), and your cursor stays at the end, ready for your next sentence. Everything unlocks when editing time starts, and you can pause Flowstate anytime to make changes. When the writing timer runs out, Flowstate automatically switches to editing time. You'll see a visual countdown on the timer so the transition never catches you off guard.

During editing time (shown in blue), all your text is fully unlocked. Use this time to fix typos, rearrange sentences, or revise your work. When editing time runs out, a visual countdown on the timer lets you know writing time is about to resume. Everything locks back in place and then you go back to writing time.

Click the Pause button to freeze the timer and unlock all text temporarily. This is useful for stepping away from your writing. Click the Resume button (a right-pointing triangle) to continue where you left off. Flowstate also pauses automatically if you switch away from Penpoint, and picks back up when you return.
