Click the Settings icon (gear) in the timer bar to customize: Write: How long you write before switching to editing time (5 to 120 minutes, default 15) Edit: How long you can edit before going back to writing (5 to 120 minutes, default 5) Fade Locked Text: When turned on, locked sentences dim so you can easily tell them apart from text you can still edit. When turned off, locked text looks the same as everything else but is still locked.

When Flowstate starts, Penpoint clears away distractions so you can focus: The chapter list on the left side of the screen and Minipen (the reference panel on the right) tuck themselves away (they come back when Flowstate stops) Formatting buttons in the toolbar fade out (they still work if you click them) The navigation bar at the very top of the window fades during writing time, and the chapter list fades if you reopen it Find & Replace (Ctrl+F, or Cmd+F on Mac) still lets you search, but Replace is only available during editing time. If you need to do a replace right away, just pause Flowstate first.
When Flowstate Stops on Its Own

Flowstate automatically turns off if you switch to a different chapter or scene, add a new scene or chapter break, or merge scenes or chapters (combining two scenes or chapters into one). These kinds of changes reorganize your manuscript, so Flowstate steps aside and lets you start fresh when you're ready. Note: Having your sentences lock behind you might feel strange at first. Give it a try. Many writers are surprised by how much they get done.

These are the tools that turn a big, busy book into something you can move through without thinking. Once they're second nature, you stop hunting through menus and start writing at speed: find anyone in a keystroke, link a character into your prose as you type, spin up a new location without losing your place, and see your whole cast at a glance. They work from anywhere in Penpoint, in either mode.

Search: Press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on Mac) from anywhere and start typing. It searches everything at once: characters, locations, items, chapters, notes, arcs, tags, and the full text of your manuscript prose, with highlighted snippets and instant results. In a series it covers every book. Recent searches and a fullscreen mode are built in. Compendium: An A-to-Z index of everything in your book (characters, items, locations, chapters, and arcs) on one page. Perfect for a birds-eye view, jumping to anything by name, or catching two characters you accidentally named the same thing.

@Mentions: Type @ anywhere on the worldbuilding side and pick a name to drop a live, clickable link to any character, place, item, chapter, note, or arc point. Mentions follow whatever they point to: rename a character and every mention updates itself. Click one to jump straight there. Quick Add Menu: Press Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on Mac) to create a character, location, item, chapter, note, or tag without leaving what you're doing. If your cursor is in a writing area, Create + Mention makes the new thing and drops a link to it right where you're typing, so creating and connecting happen in one move. Tip: The theme here is speed with no dead ends: Search takes you anywhere, @Mentions wires your world together as you write, Quick Add grows it on the fly, and the Compendium keeps the whole thing in view. Learn the two shortcuts (Ctrl+K and Ctrl+N) and the rest follows.

The searchbar is one of Penpoint's most powerful tools. It searches across everything in your book (characters, locations, items, chapters, notes, story arcs, character arcs, tags, and even the prose content in your manuscripts) with instant results and rich context snippets. Whether you're hunting for a minor character mentioned once, tracking down where you described a specific location, or finding a passage you wrote three chapters ago, the searchbar finds it. In a series, search covers the whole series: every Book at once.

Access the searchbar in two ways: Press Ctrl+K (Windows/Linux) or ⌘K (Mac) from anywhere in Penpoint Click on the search field in the navigation bar at the top of your screen The keyboard shortcut opens the search in fullscreen mode, perfect for focused searching. Clicking the search bar opens an inline dropdown below the navigation bar.

Simply start typing. The search activates after you type at least 2 characters, and results appear instantly as you type. No need to press Enter: results update in real-time. Manuscript scene results require at least 4 characters to appear, since shorter queries would match too many passages in your prose. Up to 5 scene results are shown at a time, grouped under a separate Manuscripts heading below your worldbuilding results. Tip: The search is always up-to-date. Create a new character or add a note, and it's immediately searchable.

Search results show rich context to help you find exactly what you're looking for: Icon and color - Quickly identify the type of result (character, location, item, note, chapter, arc, scene, or tag) Title - The name of the result Subtitle - Additional context like character importance or block labels that match your search Snippet - A preview of the content with your search terms highlighted Importance badges - For characters, the importance level (Primary, Secondary, etc.) appears on the right Book badges - In a series, Book-specific results carry a small badge showing which Book (or Books) they belong to; series-wide things like notes and tags don't need one

Each type of content has its own icon and color: Characters - Person icon, custom character color Locations - Map pin icon, custom location color Items - Package icon, custom item color Notes - Document icon Chapters - Book icon Story Arcs & Character Arcs - Arc icon Tags - Tag icon Manuscript Scenes - Pen icon, searches your prose content (shown in a separate group below worldbuilding results) Custom colors (for characters, locations, and items) match the colors you've assigned to them, making them instantly recognizable.

Use your keyboard to quickly navigate and select results: Up/Down arrows - Move between results Enter - Select the highlighted result and navigate to it Escape - Close the search dropdown (inline mode only) When you select a result, Penpoint takes you directly to it and closes the search automatically.

When the search field is empty, you'll see your recent searches. This makes it easy to re-run searches you've done before. Click a search - Re-runs that search immediately X button - Removes that search from your history Penpoint remembers your last 10 searches across sessions. Clear individual searches you no longer need, or let them naturally cycle out as you perform new searches.

For a more focused search experience, switch to fullscreen mode: Press Ctrl+K (or ⌘K on Mac) to open fullscreen search from anywhere Click the maximize icon on the right side of the inline search bar Fullscreen mode shows up to 100 results (compared to 50 in inline mode) and provides more vertical space for browsing results. Your search text carries over automatically when switching between modes. Tip: The searchbar searches across all your content: character names, descriptions, and traits, locations, items, chapter titles and details, author notes, story arcs, character arcs, tags, and the full text of your manuscript scenes. Everything is searchable.

Anywhere you write on the worldbuilding side (a character's description, a note, chapter details, an arc), type @ and start typing a name. Pick a result and it becomes a live link: bold, underlined, and clickable. You can also right-click and choose Insert @Mention.

Characters (aliases count, so typing a nickname finds them too), locations, items, chapters, scenes, notes, and even Story Arc and Character Arc points. Results appear as you type; press Enter or Tab to insert the highlighted one, or Esc to close the list.

Clicking a mention jumps straight to that page. In a series, mentions know their Book: clicking a chapter or arc from another Book switches you to it, and clicking a character who's hidden by the This Book view widens the view so they can be shown (This Book vs All Books).
They Keep Themselves Up to Date

A mention remembers who it points to, not the spelling of their name. Rename a character and every mention of them updates itself, everywhere. If you delete something a mention points to, the link stays in your text and reads "(Deleted)". Note: In Manuscript Mode, typing @ opens the same search but inserts just the name as plain text. Your prose stays pure words, with no links hiding in it. Tip: Typing an email address? Press Esc when the list pops up and it stays closed for that word, so you can finish typing in peace.

The Quick Add Menu lets you create any type of thing (character, item, location, chapter, note, or tag) without leaving whatever you're currently working on. Press Ctrl+N (or Cmd+N on Mac) from anywhere in Penpoint and the menu pops up, ready to go.

The menu opens to a list of everything you can create. Six options are shown, each with a short description. Click an item, or use the arrow keys and press Enter Type a few letters to filter the list: searching for "loc" jumps straight to Location Press Escape to close without creating anything Tip: The Ctrl+N shortcut works everywhere: in the character list, while editing a note, even inside Manuscript Mode (where you write your prose). You never have to go somewhere else first.

After choosing what to create, a short form appears. The fields shown depend on what you're creating: characters ask for a name and importance level (Primary, Secondary, or Background; you can always change this later), chapters ask for a title and optional subtitle and notes, and so on. You have two ways to finish, plus a back button to cancel: Create: saves the item and shows a confirmation. The menu stays open so you can create more. Create & Open: saves and immediately takes you to the full profile page for that new character, location, or item. The left-pointing arrow button in the top-left corner: returns to the list without creating anything.

After a successful creation, a confirmation screen shows you what was just made. From here you can: Create Another: go back to the list to create something else Open [Type]: go directly to the new item's profile page (e.g. "Open Character") Done: close the menu and return to where you were Tip: If your cursor was active inside a writing area when you pressed Ctrl+N, whether in Manuscript Mode (where you write your prose) or a notes box or formatted text area in Worldbuilding Mode (where you track characters, locations, and more), a Create + Mention button will also appear on the creation form (except for tags). This creates the item and inserts its name as a clickable reference link right where your cursor is, so you can keep writing without losing your place.

The Compendium is an alphabetical index of everything in your book: all characters, items, locations, chapters, and arcs in one unified list. It's perfect for quickly checking if you've already named something, finding a character you created months ago, or getting an overview of your entire story world.

The Compendium automatically includes all entities from your book, organized alphabetically by name. Each entry displays relevant details in a compact format: Characters: Shows importance, traits, and custom fields Items: Displays type, importance, description, and first appearance Locations: Includes type, importance, and description Chapters: Lists chapter number, type, summary, and associated characters Story Arcs: Shows arc type, description, and key plot points Character Arcs: Shows arc description and keyframe progression Tip: Articles like "The" and "A" are ignored when sorting alphabetically. "The Hall of Doors" appears under "H", not "T". Note: Notes are not included in the Compendium as they are not considered part of your story's canon.

The left sidebar shows all 26 letters plus a "#" symbol for entries starting with numbers. Letters that contain entries are highlighted and clickable: click any active letter to jump directly to that section. Grayed-out letters indicate no entries exist for that letter in your current book.
Click any entity name to navigate directly to that character, item, location, chapter, or arc. This makes the Compendium a quick reference tool for finding and accessing any element of your story.

Use the Export to Markdown button in the top-right corner to save your entire Compendium as a formatted Markdown file. This creates a portable reference document you can view outside Penpoint or share with others. Note: Compendium exports are one-way only: you cannot modify an exported Compendium file and reimport it back into Penpoint. If you need to export your book for editing and reimporting, see Importing & Exporting for full import/export options.

In Penpoint, your whole series lives together as one book file in your Library: a trilogy, a saga, however many volumes your story needs. It appears as a single stacked card, and clicking the card opens the series' own shelf of Books. The payoff: your cast travels with you. Sherlock Holmes exists once, present in Book 1, Book 2, and Book 3, so when you refine his profile while drafting the finale, he's up to date everywhere. No more duplicating a book for each new volume and re-typing everyone.
What's Yours per Book, What's Shared

Each Book keeps its own: chapters, scenes, manuscript, and Book Arcs. That's the story of that volume. (Arcs are Penpoint's plot-planning page, a bird's-eye view of your story's threads.) Shared between Books: characters, items, and locations. Each one carries a Presence: the list of Books it appears in. (Changing Presence only controls which Books' lists it shows up in; it never deletes anything.) Their Importance is the exception to the sharing: it's kept per Book, so a character can be Primary in one and Background in another. Series-wide: Notes, Tags, Series Arcs, and Character Arcs cover the whole series, no matter which Book you're in. (Notes can also be kept with a single Book, using a Book Notes folder, if you like.) Note Templates reach further still: a template saved in any Book is available in every book and series on your computer.

These guides walk through the whole lifecycle, from the first conversion to the (rarely needed) exit door: Converting a Book to a Series: turn an existing book into Book 1 of a new series Your Series in the Library: the series' own shelf, where you add Books (new or existing), reorder them, and manage each volume Switching Between Books: jump between Books from the bar at the top of the app, without leaving the page Presence: Which Books a Character Is In: control which Books each character, item, and location appears in Importance Across Books: let a character matter more in one Book than another This Book vs All Books: narrow your view to just the Book you're drafting Book Arcs and Series Arcs: plot each volume, and the saga that spans them all Using Dedicated Book Folders: keep book-specific notes in a folder for each Book, while the rest of your Notebook stays series-wide Splitting a Series into Separate Books: break the series back into standalone books, if you ever need to. Your writing survives; each Book becomes its own book file in your Library Note: Search always covers the whole series. Book-specific results carry a small badge showing which Book they belong to. See The Glorious Searchbar.
Converting a Book to a Series
Converting a Book to a Series

Finished (or well into) a book and realized the story needs more volumes? Converting turns your existing book into Book 1 of a brand-new series, with everything you've built coming along for the ride.

Head to the Book Library and find your book's card. Click the three-dot menu (⋮) on the card (or right-click the card; Control-click on Mac) and choose Convert to Series…. Give the series a name ("The Sherlock Holmes Saga", say), add an optional description, and click Convert to Series. Like any book in your Library, a series needs a name no other book or series is using (capital letters don't count); if it's taken, Penpoint tells you and you can pick another. You can change your mind later. A series can be split back into separate books, each becoming its own independent book file. See Splitting a Series into Separate Books.
Your Book Is Safe: Here's What Changes

Nothing is deleted. Your book simply becomes the first volume of something bigger: Your book becomes Book 1 of the new series, keeping all its chapters, scenes, and manuscript exactly as they were. Every character, item, and location gets Presence in Book 1 (Presence = which Books a character, item, or location appears in), ready to be shared with the Books you add next. Your Story Arcs become Book 1's Story Arcs, and the Arcs page gains room for Series Arcs that span the whole saga. Presence and Series Arcs each have their own guides: see Presence: Which Books a Character Is In and Book Arcs and Series Arcs. Tip: Right after converting, the library takes you to the series' own shelf. The natural next step is the "Add Book to Series" card, where Book 2 begins. Already have the next volume as its own book? Bring it in with "Add to Series…" from the Library. Ever want to go the other way? Splitting a Series into Separate Books covers turning a series back into standalone books.

In your Library, a series appears as a single stacked card. Clicking it doesn't open a Book directly; it opens the series' own shelf, where each Book has its own card. This shelf is your series' home base: add Books, reorder them, give each one its own cover. Back to Library returns you to the main Library.

Each Book gets its own card, and you can customize every one with its own cover, color, and description to give each volume a distinct look. Click a card to open that Book. The faded outline card at the end, Add Book to Series, creates a brand-new Book in the series.

Right-click any Book card (or Control-click on Mac), or click the small ⋮ button in the card's top-right corner, for its menu: Edit Book Details… (name, cover, color), Duplicate Book, Move Forward and Move Backward to reorder the series, and Delete Book…. Deleting a Book permanently removes the Book and its chapters, scenes, folders, and Story Arcs: the writing inside it is gone, and this can't be undone. Penpoint always shows a confirmation dialog first, so a stray click can never delete a Book on its own. The dialog also asks what to do with characters, items, and locations that only exist in that Book: Reassign to another Book keeps them in the series, or Delete them with the Book removes them permanently (again, only after you confirm). Anything shared with other Books simply stays where it is. Delete is only offered while the series has more than one Book; to unwind the last Book, split the series instead, which turns it into a standalone book.

The ⋮ Series options button at the right end of the shelf header holds options for the whole series: "Edit Series Details…" lets you change the series' name and description, and "Split into separate books…" breaks the series apart into separate standalone books in your Library. Splitting is permanent, so read Splitting a Series into Separate Books before using it.

You can also fold a standalone book you already have into the series, so a book you wrote before you knew it was a series can join the others. This one starts from the main Library, not the series shelf: right-click (or Control-click on Mac) the standalone book's card, or use its ⋮ menu, and choose Add to Series…. Pick which series to add it to, name the Book inside the series, and choose what to bring over. You'll first choose whether to copy or move the book: Copy keeps the original standalone book in your Library and adds it into the series too, so you have it in both places. Move adds it to the series, then removes the original standalone book (and its saved backups) from your Library, so it lives only in the series. Moving can't be undone, so Penpoint confirms first; any external or cloud backups you set up separately are kept.

If the incoming book shares characters, locations, or items with the series (the same protagonist in every volume, say), Penpoint spots them by name before anything is added and shows them on a Review Duplicates step. Checked matches merge: instead of a second copy, the incoming book's chapter assignments, scene links, tags, and trait choices all land on the entity the series already has, and that one entry simply appears in both Books. Uncheck a match to bring it in as a separate copy instead. Tags with matching names merge automatically. Renamed someone between books? Use the link button on a "new" row to point it at the right series entry by hand: Luke in the old book can merge into Lucian in the series. For merged entries, most things combine on their own: chapters, tags, and any field one book left blank. Where the same entry has different text in each book, the default keeps both: the incoming book's wording is stacked under a divider on the series entry, and you can blend the two by hand later. Prefer a tidier result? Switch to Keep your series' text only and the series wording stays as it is, leaving out the incoming book's conflicting text. Each Book still keeps its own arcs, events, and notes. A few details can't be blended into one value no matter which option you pick: a name, a type, or a number or calculation field always keeps the series' version on a conflict. Importance is the one exception that resolves itself: merging always keeps whichever level is higher, so a character promoted to Primary in the new book stays Primary. Once the merge finishes, anything that couldn't be combined shows up right there on the results screen: which entry it was, which detail, and what it kept. If you'd rather have the other version, open that character, item, or location afterward and change it yourself. Tip: Merging with Copy is the gentler path: your original book stays in the Library, so if a merged entry didn't keep something you wanted, it's still right there to reference. Note: This is different from the shelf's Add Book to Series card, which starts a fresh, blank Book. Reach for Add to Series… in the Library when the book already exists.

In a series, you're always working in one Book at a time: its chapters, its scenes, its manuscript. Switching Books is designed to be effortless, so hopping from Book 1 to Book 3 to check a detail never breaks your flow. And it's safe: switching automatically saves what you've been working on, so hopping between Books doesn't lose your work. It only changes which Book you're looking at.

The navigation bar (the bar at the top of the screen) always shows Current Book: followed by the name of the Book you're in. Click it to open the switcher. Under Switch Book, every Book in your series is listed in order. Click one and you're there. The switcher works the same way in Worldbuilding Mode (your characters, chapters, and notes) and Manuscript Mode (where you write your prose), so you never have to leave the page you're on.

Press Ctrl+Shift+1 through Ctrl+Shift+9 (or Cmd+Shift+1 through 9 on Mac) to jump straight to a Book by its position in the series. The shortcuts appear beside the first nine Books in the switcher, so you never have to memorize them. And if you'd rather use the mouse, clicking a Book in the switcher does exactly the same thing.

Each Book keeps its own place on the Chapters page and in the Manuscript, so you pick up right where you left off. Leave Book 1 mid-chapter to check something in Book 2, and when you switch back, Book 1 is exactly where you left it.

In Worldbuilding Mode, the This Book / All Books toggle sits right beside the switcher, and at the bottom of the switcher menu the "Show only this Book" checkbox does the same thing. Both hide characters, items, and locations that aren't in the active Book. Nothing is removed, and switching back to All Books (or unticking the box) brings them all right back. It's a quicker way to flip the same setting described in This Book vs All Books, which explains how it works everywhere at once.
Presence: Which Books a Character Is In
Presence: Which Books a Character Is In

In a series, your cast is shared. There's one Sherlock Holmes for the whole series: edit his page once, and he's up to date in every Book. Presence is simply the list of Books a character, item, or location appears in.

You'll find the Presence field on each character's page, and in the panel that opens when you click an item or location. It's a list of your Books with a checkbox next to each; tick the ones this character belongs to. Sherlock might be present in all three Books, while a one-off witness only appears in Book 1. Unchecking a Book doesn't delete anything; it only takes the character off that Book's lists. Check it again and they're right back, exactly as they were. New characters, items, and locations start out present in the Book you're currently in. If Sherlock turns out to matter in Book 2 as well, just add Book 2 to his Presence. Note: Every character, item, and location must appear in at least one Book. When only one Book is left checked, that last checkbox locks. To remove a character from the series entirely, delete them from the Characters page; Penpoint asks you to confirm first.

Presence says "this character belongs to this Book". It controls where they show up: the Characters, Items, and Locations pages, plus the matching lists in the writing-mode sidebar. Assigning a character to a chapter is a more detailed note about exactly which chapters they appear in. Mentioning a character in a chapter doesn't change their Presence. Presence is what the This Book view filters on; see This Book vs All Books to control which part of your cast you're looking at. Presence decides whether a character shows up in a Book at all. How much they matter in the Books they're in is a separate setting, kept per Book: see Importance Across Books. Tip: Notes, Tags, and Series Arcs don't have Presence; they belong to the whole series, no matter which Book you're in. Character Arcs don't have a Presence field either: they follow their keyframes (the chapter moments that plot the arc), appearing in whichever Books those chapters belong to.

A character who carries your first book can fade into the background by the third. In a series, Importance is kept separately for each Book, so it can say exactly that. Sherlock stays Primary throughout while Inspector Lestrade drops from Primary in Book 1 to Background in Book 3. Importance is your note about how much a character, item, or location matters, and what your character and item lists sort by. Primary counts as the highest, then Secondary, then Background. One note on capital letters: a Book means one book inside your series, and a lowercase book means an ordinary standalone one.

Which of the two you see depends on the This Book / All Books switch (see This Book vs All Books). In This Book, you see one level, the one that Book uses: Importance: Secondary. Everything reads as it would in a standalone book. In All Books, you get one entry per Book the character appears in, each with a small book icon and the Book's number: 1: Primary, 2: Secondary. Roomier places list every Book; where there isn't room, such as a small card or the narrow sidebar, you get the first few and a count of the rest, like 1: Primary, +2. Note: When every Book agrees, you just see the single level. The list only appears once a character actually differs from one Book to the next, so a series where you've never touched Importance reads exactly like a standalone book.
Setting a Level for One Book

A level belongs to one Book, so you set it while you're looking at one Book. To give Lestrade a different level in Book 3 than he has in Book 1: Go to Book 1 and switch to This Book. In Edit mode, use the Importance box under his name on his character page, or the Importance box on an item or location's details. To skip Edit mode, right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) his page and choose Change Importance. Switch to Book 3 and set his level again there. Step 3 is the one that's easy to miss. The bar at the top of the window shows Current Book: followed by the Book you're in; click it and pick another Book. See Switching Between Books. Setting a level changes that Book alone, and you can change it back whenever you like. The level does belong to the Book, so taking a character out of a Book in Presence takes that Book's level with them. Put them back and they start from their usual level again.
Why the Levels Gray Out in All Books

In the All Books view the Importance box still opens, but the three levels inside it are grayed out, with a line above them saying that Importance can differ per Book and to switch to This Book to set it. With several Books on screen at once, there's no single Book for your choice to land in. Switch to This Book and the levels come back. The right-click menus say the same thing, in the same place.

Turning a finished book into a series changes nothing: everyone keeps the level they already had, in every Book, until you vary one. Adding a character to another Book doesn't leave them blank there either; they start at the level they had before you set any per-Book levels. Duplicating a Book gives the copy the same levels the original had. Splitting a series apart gives each standalone book the level that Book was using, so the Book 3 version of Lestrade opens as Background; see Splitting a Series into Separate Books. Tip: Importance is separate from Presence, which is the list of Books a character appears in. Presence decides whether they show up in a Book at all; Importance describes how much they matter in the Books they're in. See Presence: Which Books a Character Is In. Tip: Sorting by importance in All Books uses each character's highest level across the Books they're in, so someone who leads Book 1 and cameos in Book 3 still sorts with your leads.

A series can hold a lot of cast. The This Book / All Books view decides how much of it you see. You'll find it in three places: as the Show only this Book checkbox in the Book menu in the bar at the top of the window, as a This Book / All Books toggle sitting right beside that same Book menu in Worldbuilding Mode, and as the This Book / All Books switch at the top of the Minipen sidebar (your worldbuilding notes beside your manuscript while you write). It's one global setting: flip it in any of the three and it changes what you see on Characters, Items, Locations, and the Minipen all at once. One note on capital letters: in this article, a Book means one book inside your series.
All Books shows your entire series cast: every character, item, and location, no matter which Books they belong to. This is the default, so when you start Book 2, nobody vanishes.

Switch to This Book and anything you haven't marked as appearing in this Book disappears from your lists (Penpoint calls this Presence; see Presence: Which Books a Character Is In). Nothing is deleted — they're only hidden, and switching back to All Books brings everyone back exactly as they were. Drafting Book 2 without Book 1's one-scene witnesses cluttering the page is exactly what it's for. Tip: The checkbox, the Worldbuilding navbar toggle, and the Minipen switch are all the same setting: flip any one of them and the other two follow. You'll only see them in a series; a standalone book has nothing to narrow. Note: The Notebook follows this view too: the automatic per-Book folders tuck away for the Books you aren't focused on. See Using Dedicated Book Folders. This view also decides how Importance reads: one level in This Book, and in All Books each Book's level side by side once the Books differ. See Importance Across Books.

In the This Book view, you can still follow a link (such as an @Mentions link, or a link in your character's Relationships Block list) to a character who isn't in your actively selected Book. Penpoint flips the view to All Books so the page can show them, and you stay in the Book you were working in. The setting visibly flips and stays on All Books; switch it back to This Book when you're done. Clicking a chapter or arc that belongs to another Book is different: those live inside their Book, so Penpoint switches you to it. You can switch back anytime from the Book menu in the bar at the top; see Switching Between Books.

In a series, the Timeline (the page that lays out your chapters in story order) always shows every Book's chapters; it's the one page built for seeing the whole series at once, so the This Book view doesn't narrow it. Clicking a chapter that belongs to another Book switches you to that Book.

When you're writing a series (Writing a Series), the Arcs page grows to match: alongside each Book's own plot structure, you can chart the threads that run through the entire saga. The war, the romance, the long con. Everything below lives on the Arcs page; open it by clicking Arcs in the sidebar while in Worldbuilding Mode.
The Arcs Page Gains a Third View
In a series, the switcher at the top of the Arcs page offers three views, left to right: Series Arcs, Book Arc (the Story Arcs you already know), and Character Arcs.

A Book Arc is exactly the Story Arc you already know: main plot, subplots, keyframes (the story beats you place along an arc), the visual chart of your plot. It's just renamed to make clear it belongs to one Book. Each Book in your series has its own, and the Book Arc tab always shows the arc for whichever Book you're currently in. Switch Books and the tab switches with you. Everything in Story Arcs applies here unchanged.

Series Arcs are for the storylines too big for any single volume. They span the whole series and stay visible no matter which Book you're working in, so you can draft Book 3 with the saga's shape still in view. On the Series Arcs view, click + New Series Arc to create one. Templates are built for series-scale plotting; each one starts your arc with a few ready-made story beats you can rename or rearrange: Simple Arc: A minimal two-point structure spanning the whole series, for laying out the story beats yourself. Trilogy: One major beat per installment: Setup, Confrontation, Resolution. Epic Saga: A grand conflict building across many books, from Inciting Event to Final Reckoning. Overarching Mystery: A conspiracy threaded through the series, revealed book by book. Rise & Fall: A dynasty, empire, or character tracked from ascent to downfall. Note: Templates are starting points, not constraints: rename, add, or remove points afterward. If you delete one, you'll be asked to confirm first, and only that point is removed; any chapters or scenes assigned to it are untouched. Series Arcs can have subplots of their own, just like Book Arcs.

A character's fortune curve (the line tracking a character's ups and downs across the series) isn't confined to one volume. Character Arcs run across the whole series, so you can chart Sherlock's rise and fall from Book 1 through Book 3 on a single curve. In the This Book view (This Book vs All Books), the chart zooms in on this Book's stretch of the curve, and in the keyframe list, keyframes from other Books gray out and step aside. Nothing is changed or deleted — switch back to All Books and the full curve returns exactly as it was. Note: In the This Book view, characters whose arcs never touch the current Book are hidden from the sidebar. If that empties the list, you'll see "Switch to 'All Books' to see arcs from the rest of the series". Open the Book menu in the bar at the top of the window and uncheck "Show only this Book" to bring everyone back into sight.

Story Arcs (Book Arcs): the plot of one volume: this Book's mystery, this Book's climax. Series Arcs: threads that outlive any single volume: the war, the prophecy, the slow-burn romance. Character Arcs: one character's emotional journey, wherever it takes them across the series. Tip: Not sure where a thread belongs? Ask whether it resolves by the end of this Book. If it does, it's a Book Arc subplot. If it keeps burning into the next volume, give it a Series Arc.

Your Notes are shared across the whole series, which is usually what you want: a character sketch or a scrap of research is handy no matter which Book you're drafting (in this article, a Book means one book inside your series). But some notes really do belong to one volume. For those, every Book in your series gets its own folder in the Notebook, named Book 1 Notes, Book 2 Notes, and so on. Drop a note inside one to keep it with that Book.

The folders sit at the very top of your Notebook's folder list (the strip on the left, sometimes called the Binder, where all your folders live), one for each Book, and Penpoint keeps them for you. When you convert a book into a series, add a new Book, or bring one in from another file, its folder shows up automatically. You never have to create or name them. The name follows the Book's position, so if you reorder your Books the labels renumber to match: the folder for whatever is now your second Book always reads "Book 2 Notes." Because Penpoint manages them, these folders can't be renamed, moved, or deleted (right-click (or Ctrl+click on Mac) on one to see a shorter menu, headed "Automatic series folder"). You can still give one a color and build ordinary subfolders inside it.
Keeping a Note with a Book

Drag a note into a Book's folder and it belongs to that Book. Images, shortcuts (quick links to a character, location, or other part of your book), and subfolders work the same way. Anything you leave outside these folders stays shared across your whole series, right where it's always been.
Following This Book vs All Books

These folders follow the same This Book vs All Books setting as the rest of your series (it narrows your series to just the Book you're working on). In All Books you see every Book's folder; turn on This Book and the folders for the other Books tuck out of sight, so you can focus on the volume in front of you. Nothing is deleted, they are only hidden, and switching back to All Books brings them all straight back.

If you'd rather keep your Notebook plain, turn on Hide Series Folders from the display-settings menu (the small gear icon above your list of notes). The same option lives on the right-click menu too, both on empty space and on a Book folder itself. Turn it off the same way to bring the folders back.
Deleting a Book, or Splitting the Series

If you delete a Book that has notes in its folder, Penpoint asks what should happen to them: move them into another Book, or delete them along with the Book. It's the same choice it offers for that Book's characters, items, and locations, so nothing disappears without your say-so. And if you ever go through Splitting a Series into Separate Books (which turns each Book back into its own separate book file), each book keeps its own Book Notes folder (now just an ordinary folder), and your series-wide notes come along into every book as well. Tip: You'll only ever see these folders in a series. A standalone book's Notebook has no automatic folders.
Splitting a Series into Separate Books
Splitting a Series into Separate Books

Splitting is the exit door: it takes a series apart, turning each Book into its own separate standalone book in your Library. It's there if you need it, but because it can't be undone, Penpoint makes you very sure before it happens.

Step 1: save a backup copy first. Right-click (or Control-click on Mac) the series card in your Library and choose Export Book, then pick a safe place to save the file (your Documents folder, for example). That exported file is your only recovery option once the split completes: if anything goes wrong, or you change your mind later, you can bring the whole series back by importing that file. See Importing a Book for how importing works. Note: Use Export Book for this — not Backup Now. Backups made with Backup Now are stored in the series' backup history, and that entire history is deleted when the split completes. An exported file lives wherever you saved it, so it survives. Step 2: run the split. Open your series from your Library, then click the Series options menu (the three stacked dots ⋮ at the top, next to the series name) and choose Split into separate books…. The confirmation window lists exactly which standalone books you'll end up with. Type the series name to confirm, then click Split into separate books. Note: Any unsaved edits are saved automatically before the split begins, so nothing you just typed is at risk.

Every Book survives intact: its chapters, scenes, manuscript, and Book Arcs all carry over into its new standalone book. Shared characters, items, and locations get a separate copy in every book they appear in (in Penpoint terms, every Book they had Presence in). From then on, editing Sherlock in one book no longer changes him in the others. Each copy keeps the Importance that Book gave it, so a character who was Background in Book 3 opens as Background in Book 3's standalone book. Your Notes and Tags are copied into every standalone book, so nothing you wrote there is lost. A note you kept in a specific Book's folder travels only into that book, where the folder becomes an ordinary one. Each Book's name becomes its standalone book's name. If your Library already has a book with that name (capital letters don't count), the new book gets a number after it, like "Dune #2". The list in the confirmation window already shows the name each book will get. You can rename it any time. Presence (which Books each character appears in) has its own guide: Presence: Which Books a Character Is In, and per-Book Importance is covered in Importance Across Books. Those per-Book notes folders are covered in Using Dedicated Book Folders.

The series itself: the series file, the book switcher (the menu at the top you use to hop between Books), and the stacked card in your Library. Your Series Arcs are not carried over into the standalone books; only Book Arcs survive. Copy anything you want to keep out of your Series Arcs before splitting. The series' backup history is permanently deleted, including any backups you made with Backup Now. Each new standalone book starts a fresh backup history from its first open; the file you exported in step 1 covers that gap. A true undo: there's no one-click way to reverse a split. You can rebuild a series by hand later (convert one book back into a series, then use Add to Series to bring the others in), but that won't restore your Series Arcs or re-link characters that were shared across Books. Importing the file you exported in step 1 is the only way to get the exact original series back. Want to bring standalone books back together instead? Your Series in the Library covers adding an existing book into a series.

Penpoint keeps your work on your own computer and hands it back whenever you want. Bring in a manuscript or worldbuilding (your characters, locations, and other story details) from somewhere else, or send out a polished copy of your book to submit, publish, or share. Exporting only ever makes copies: it never changes or removes anything from your book. Importing adds to your books, and Penpoint makes automatic backups so you can restore an earlier copy if you ever need to (see Backup & Restore).

The tools depend on what you're moving, and they're the same on Mac and Windows: Your manuscript: the prose you write in Manuscript Mode, organized into chapters and scenes. Its tools are in the row of buttons at the top of Manuscript Mode and in the Manuscript section of Settings > Import/Export. Your worldbuilding: your characters, locations, items, notes, chapter outlines, and arcs. Its tools are in Settings > Import/Export.

Exporting Manuscripts: The whole book, a chapter, or a scene as one document: Word, EPUB (e-book file), PDF, Markdown (a plain-text file with light formatting marks), Rich Text, or Plain Text. Standard Submission Format: Formatting set up the way literary agents expect. Exporting to Scrivener: A Scrivener 3 project with chapters and scenes intact: just your manuscript, or the whole book with characters, places, and notes. Pasting Your Manuscript Into a Form: For agencies and contests that want your pages pasted, not attached. Exporting Worldbuilding Data: Any of the six worldbuilding types above as Word, PDF, Markdown, Rich Text, or Plain Text, as one file or a folder. To send your worldbuilding to Scrivener with your manuscript, choose Export Whole Book to Scrivener on the wizard's first page. Generating Templates: Blank fill-in files shaped like your book, to share with someone without Penpoint or give to an AI tool like ChatGPT or Claude. Whatever you fill in imports straight back. Exporting a Book: A whole book as a .penpoint file, to move between your own computers or share with another Penpoint writer. Only Penpoint can open it. Tip: To edit your copy and bring it back in, use Markdown: a Markdown worldbuilding export keeps every detail, image, and @mention (a clickable link to a character, location, or other entry). Word, PDF, Rich Text, and Plain Text are for sharing and reading, not re-importing.

Coming from Scrivener? Importing from Scrivener: Brings a whole Scrivener 3 project in as a new book: chapters, scenes, notes, keywords, comments, snapshots (saved earlier versions of a scene), and the characters and places from its binder. No compiling needed: on the Your Books screen, choose Create New Book, then Import a Scrivener Project. The project itself is never changed. Importing Your Data: Overview of the two content imports: a manuscript from another app (Word, EPUB, Rich Text, Markdown, or plain text), including how to make it a brand-new book, or worldbuilding from Markdown files. Importing Worldbuilding Data: The worldbuilding Import Wizard: any of the six types back from Markdown, with a preview of each file, a choice of what to do when a file matches something you already have (overwrite, skip, or keep both), and auto-created placeholders for anything your files mention. Importing a Book: Open a whole .penpoint file (one you exported or someone shared) as its own book. Worldbuilding and chapter imports add pieces to a book you already have open. Note: Importing only replaces something you already have when you explicitly choose Overwrite or Replace, and each importer shows you what it found before anything is written.

Penpoint gives you several ways to get your work out of the app and into other formats: to submit your manuscript, share your notes with a writing partner, or keep a copy somewhere else. Nothing here ever changes or removes anything from your book; exporting only makes copies.

There are three answers, depending on what you want to end up with: Your written story: the chapters and scenes you've typed in Manuscript Mode (where you write your prose). Use the manuscript export to turn it into a single document (Word, PDF, EPUB, and more) ready to submit or share. Open it from the Export button (an upward-arrow icon) in the row of buttons at the top of Manuscript Mode. Same steps on Mac. Your worldbuilding: your characters, places, items, notes, chapter outlines, and arcs. Even a realistic novel has this. Use the worldbuilding export to save it as documents (Word, PDF, and more). Open it from Settings (the gear icon in the sidebar), choose "Import/Export," then click "Open Export Wizard" (a step-by-step screen). Same steps on Mac. The whole book: everything at once, as a single .penpoint file only Penpoint can open. This is the one for moving a book to another computer or handing it to someone who also writes in Penpoint. Open it from your library (the screen you see when you first open Penpoint): right-click a book (or Ctrl+click on Mac), or click its three-dot menu, and choose "Export Book."
Where Would You Like to Start?

Exporting Worldbuilding Data: Save your characters, places, items, notes, chapter outlines, and arcs to Word, PDF, Markdown (plain text with simple formatting marks), Rich Text (.rtf, opens in most word processors), or Plain Text. Exporting Manuscripts: Turn your written chapters into a single document: Word, EPUB (for e-readers), PDF, Markdown (plain text with simple formatting marks), Plain Text, or Rich Text, with control over what's included and how it looks. Standard Submission Format — a Word document already set to the margins, font, and spacing literary agents expect. Exporting to Scrivener — export your manuscript as a Scrivener 3 project, chapters and scenes already split into the binder (the folder list down its left side). Pasting Your Manuscript Into a Form — for agencies that want your pages pasted into a form or email instead of attached. Generating Templates: Make blank fill-in-the-blank files shaped like your book's worldbuilding. Handy for jotting notes elsewhere, handing to a collaborator, or working with an AI tool. Anything you fill in can be imported back. Exporting a Book: Save a whole book as one .penpoint file: manuscript, worldbuilding, pictures and settings together, ready to move to another computer or share with another Penpoint writer.

The Export Wizard guides you through saving your book's worldbuilding (characters, locations, items, notes, chapter outlines, and arcs) to a file on your computer. Exporting only makes copies; it never changes or removes anything from your book. You can export all of your worldbuilding or just certain types, choose the file format, and decide whether to save it all as one file or organize it into folders. Chapters export as outlines, not manuscript prose.

Go to Settings, select "Import/Export" from the sidebar, and click "Open Export Wizard" in the Export Data section. The wizard will walk you through four steps: Select Data Types - Choose which types of content to export (characters, locations, items, notes, chapters, arcs) Select Characters, Locations, etc. - Pick specific items from each selected type, or use "Select All" to include every one of that type Export Options - Choose export settings like file structure and formatting Review & Export - Confirm your selections and choose where to save the files Want your manuscript too? Below the type cards on the first screen is an Export Whole Book to Scrivener option. It skips these steps and sends your manuscript and your worldbuilding into one Scrivener project. See Exporting to Scrivener for what comes along.

Choose the file format that best fits your needs: Markdown (.md) - A plain text file (its name ends in .md) that opens in any text editor. This is the one to pick if you want to edit your export and bring it back into Penpoint Plain Text (.txt) - Simple text with no styling, opens in any text editor Word Document (.docx) - Opens in Microsoft Word, Google Docs, and similar apps. Great for sharing with editors or publishers Rich Text (.rtf) - A formatted document most word processors can open PDF (.pdf) - A read-only document, perfect for sharing character sheets or reference material someone just needs to read Tip: Not sure which to pick? Use Markdown if you plan to edit your export and bring it back into Penpoint. Use Word or PDF when you're sharing with someone who just needs to read it. Plain Text works almost anywhere, but drops styling like bold and italic.

Choose how your export is organized: Single File - Everything you selected goes into one file, organized by type with clear headings Multi-File - Creates a folder for each type (characters, locations, and so on) with a separate file for every entry. Handy for editing one entry at a time, but it can make a lot of files: one per character, location, and item

Additional formatting choices: Add Timestamp - Includes a header noting when the file was exported and that it came from Penpoint Include Templates - Also exports blank markdown templates in a templates/ folder for creating new content (only available with Multi-File export) Include Pictures - Save profile pictures and any pictures inside your text alongside your character, location, and item files (only available with Multi-File export, when exporting Characters, Locations, or Items)

Each exported file is laid out with clear headings. A character export, for example, starts with the character's name, then their details: Importance, Tags, Bio, and any custom traits you've added. Formatting like bold, italic, and lists is kept in the Markdown, Word, Rich Text, and PDF formats. Plain Text has no styling by design, so it drops bold and italic. A Markdown export is a complete, editable copy of your worldbuilding. Edit the files, then bring them back in and every detail, picture, and @mention lands exactly where it was: custom traits, relationships, and organizational details included. See Importing Worldbuilding Data for how the import process works. Note: When you type a character's or place's name into your text, Penpoint links it to that character or place; those links are called @Mentions. In a Markdown export they're preserved, so if you edit the file and bring it back, each one still points to the right character. In the other formats (PDF, Word, Rich Text, and Plain Text), they become plain text names. Only Markdown exports can be brought back into Penpoint.

A template is a blank fill-in-the-blank file shaped like your book. It has the same sections your character, location, and item pages have (including any custom fields you've added), but with the values left empty for you to fill in. Use one to draft new entries in a text editor, hand to a writing partner who doesn't have Penpoint, or feed to an AI tool. Whatever you fill in can be imported straight back into your book. Note: Generating templates only creates new blank files on your computer. It never changes, moves, or removes anything in your book, and the whole feature is optional; you never have to use it. These files are different from Note Templates, which are notes you save inside Penpoint and reuse in any book.

Go to Settings, select "Import/Export", and click "Generate Templates" in the Templates section. The wizard will guide you through: Select Template Types - Choose which types of templates to generate (characters, locations, items, notes, chapters), then click "Choose Folder" to pick where the templates will be saved Templates Generated - Templates are created in a folder called "templates" inside the folder you picked

Each template is laid out with clear labels, matching your book's setup: The standard sections for each type (for a character, that's Name, Importance, Tags, and so on) Any custom fields you've added: your own character traits, location types, and item categories Placeholder text and short instructions explaining what each part is for

Share templates with co-authors, editors, or beta readers who don't have Penpoint. They can fill out character profiles, location details, or chapter outlines in any text editor, then send the completed files back to you for import. This lets your collaborators contribute content without needing to learn or purchase Penpoint.

Use templates with your preferred writing software, note-taking apps, or plain text editors. Fill them out at your own pace, experimenting with different tools and workflows. Since the format matches your book's structure, everything imports seamlessly when you're ready.

New to AI tools? You can skip this section entirely. Templates work just as well on their own. If you do use one, templates pair nicely with tools like ChatGPT or Claude. Here's the typical workflow: Generate a template for the type you want to create Open the template file so you can see its layout Paste the template into your AI tool as an example to follow Ask the AI to write new entries in that same layout Paste the AI's writing into a text editor (Notepad on Windows, or TextEdit on a Mac), and save the file with a name ending in .md (for example, tavern-patrons.md). Then import it into Penpoint Example prompt: "Here's a character template from my book. Please create 5 unique tavern patrons following this exact format, each with different personalities and backgrounds." Tip: Whether you're working with collaborators, using external tools, or leveraging AI, templates ensure everyone creates content in the exact format your book needs. No manual data entry required. Once your templates are filled out, see Importing Worldbuilding Data to bring them into your book.

Start small - Test with 2-3 entries first to verify the format works correctly Keep the labels - Fill in the values however you like, but keeping the labels (like Importance: or Tags:) helps everything land in the right place. If a label doesn't match, Penpoint still imports it, just as an extra field on that entry that you can sort out later Review before importing - Check that completed templates follow the structure exactly as generated Share clear instructions - When working with collaborators or AI, explain what information each field expects Note: Templates are snapshots of your current book structure. If you add new traits or custom fields later, regenerate templates to include those changes.

Export your manuscript in your chosen format. The wizard covers what to include, how it looks, and where to save it, with a live preview: a small sample that updates as you choose. Note: Exporting never changes or deletes your manuscript. It just makes a copy in the format you choose; your writing in Penpoint stays exactly as it is.
In Manuscript Mode, click the Export button (an upward arrow) at the top of the page. If your window is narrow, click the three-dots icon (⋮) at the top-right and choose Export.
If you're viewing the full manuscript: choose which chapters to include. If you're inside a chapter or scene: choose what to export, from scene to whole manuscript.

Pick which chapters to include; all are selected by default, showing title, word count, and a running total. In a Series, this lists only the current Book, exported separately as "Book N of <Series Name>".

Word Document (.docx): opens in Word, Google Docs, and book formatting apps; the most versatile format for submissions. EPUB: the e-book format for Apple Books and most e-readers. PDF: draft-quality, read-only document for review. Justified paragraphs print left-aligned in a PDF; Word, EPUB, and Rich Text keep them justified. Markdown: plain text with formatting kept as simple symbols, like *italic* and **bold**. Plain Text: no formatting; works with any text editor. Rich Text (.rtf): for older word processors, or when a publisher or contest asks for .rtf files. Exporting to Scrivener: a Scrivener 3 project folder; chapters become folders, scenes become documents. Standard Submission Format: a Word document already set up the way literary agents expect: Times New Roman, double spacing, and a running header. Tip: Not sure which to choose? Word is the safe pick; it opens almost everywhere and is what most agents and editors expect.

A Scrivener Project export replaces most of this section with a short note: fonts, spacing, and the title page are set in Scrivener's Compile, leaving only Paragraph style (under Typography), since that decides each scene's first-line indent.

Check Include title page, then set up: Title: defaults to your book's name. Subtitle: add one, then use Print subtitle on title page to include it. Author: your byline name (Penpoint remembers it). Show word count: prints your approximate word count, rounded to the nearest thousand. Contact Info: optional, for agent or contest submissions: a Contact name (your legal name, if different from your pen name; defaults to your Author name if blank, and vice versa) and a Contact block for address, phone, or email. Title, subtitle, author, and contact details are shared by every format.

For Word and Standard Submission Format exports, Add a running header prints your surname, a short title, and page number on every page but the title page. Header title and Your surname default to your title page's title and author name if blank.

Turn on Include chapter headers for a heading at each chapter's start, with three parts: Include "Chapter N" numbers, Include chapter titles (off leaves a bare "Chapter 1" with no title), and Include chapter subtitles.

Turn on "Include scene breaks" for a separator between scenes, with five styles: Spaced asterisks: * * * Standard manuscript: # Compact asterisks: *** Horizontal line: --- Blank line only: just extra space between scenes Note: Standard manuscript names two things here: this scene-break symbol, and (under Page Setup) a first-line indent size, unrelated to the Standard Submission Format described earlier.

Font: "Match my writing font" follows your writing font. Word, Rich Text, and Standard Submission Format can pick Times New Roman, Georgia, or Courier New; PDF and EPUB always use your writing font. Markdown and Plain Text carry none: the opening app decides. Line spacing: Single, 1.5 lines, or Double (Word, PDF, Rich Text, and Standard Submission Format). Paragraph style: Indented (book style) or Spaced (digital).

For Word, PDF, Rich Text, and Standard Submission Format exports, choose a Paper size: Letter (8.5" x 11"), A4, or Trade (6" x 9"). Expand Margins & Indent to set margins. If Paragraph style is Indented, you can set First-line indent to Compact (0.25") or Standard manuscript (0.5"). Note: The live preview is a close approximation; the exported file may differ slightly depending on format and the app that opens it. Before sending a file, especially for a submission, open it in your actual program (Word, Google Docs, and so on) and confirm it looks right. Reset formatting to defaults, near the bottom, puts every setting and show/hide switch back to that format's defaults, without clearing anything you've typed or changing your paper size.

Click "Export" (labeled with your format, like "Export DOCX") to save the file. Penpoint suggests a filename from your book, chapter, or scene title; if it exists, your save dialog asks before overwriting. Then click "Show in Folder" ("Open Folder" for Scrivener), or "Done" to close the wizard. Tip: Penpoint remembers each format's formatting choices; only chapter selection resets each time. Signed into Penpoint Cloud (Penpoint's optional encrypted backup and multi-device sync)? Those choices reach your other computers too; Paper size stays per computer. Note: Submitting by email or an online form instead of attaching a file? See Pasting Your Manuscript Into a Form.

Literary agents and editors expect a manuscript to look a certain way: Times New Roman, double-spaced, with a running header on every page. Most agency websites don't spell this out because it's assumed. Standard Submission Format is a Word document (.docx) built around that convention, so you don't have to track down the details yourself.

Open the Exporting Manuscripts wizard and pick Standard Submission Format from the list of formats. The first time you pick it, Penpoint sets it up with its own defaults automatically. Pick it again later and it opens with whatever you last left it at.

Standard Submission Format sets (this only affects the exported copy; your book inside Penpoint is untouched): Font: Times New Roman Line spacing: double Scene breaks: a centered "#" Paragraph alignment: left-aligned (manuscripts are ragged-right), so any justified paragraphs in your book export left-aligned; centered and right-aligned paragraphs stay as you set them First-line paragraph indent: half an inch, on every paragraph, including a chapter's first line Margins: one inch on all four sides Paper size: US Letter A title page with your contact details and an approximate word count, rounded to the nearest thousand ("about 92,000 words") A running header reading "Surname / Header Title / page number" on every page except the title page (for example, "Smith / My Book / 12") Chapter subtitles (any extra text typed under a chapter title) turned off No subtitle printed on the title page The file is deliberately plain: every line is black, 12-point, and never bold, in the title page and chapter headings alike; italics in your own prose stay. That plainness, together with the indent on every paragraph, is what separates a submission manuscript from a typeset book: other formats leave a chapter's first paragraph flush left, the way a printed book does; Standard Submission Format indents it like every other paragraph.

A few fields feed directly into the result: Contact name: your legal name, for the title page Contact block: address, phone number, and email, for the title page Header title: a short keyword version of your title, for the running header Your surname: for the running header Note: Penpoint remembers these between exports, so you only need to type them once.

Standard Submission Format keeps its formatting separate from Word, PDF, and every other format: change a setting here, like the font or a margin, and only this format's export changes. Nothing is locked: every field stays editable, and you can mix these defaults with your own adjustments freely. Reset formatting to defaults puts every setting back to Standard Submission Format's own defaults, including hiding the subtitle again, without touching anything you've typed, like your title, author, or contact details.

If an agency's own submission page states a different requirement (a different font, single spacing, no header), follow their page; a specific instruction always wins over the general standard. Some agencies want your manuscript pasted directly into a submission form instead of an attached file; see Pasting Your Manuscript Into a Form. Tip: A Word document works for nearly every agency. If one wants Scrivener project files instead, see Exporting to Scrivener.

If you draft in Penpoint and finish in Scrivener 3, export your book as a Scrivener project instead of a single file. Chapters and scenes arrive already split into Scrivener’s binder (the folder list down the left side of its window). Exporting makes a copy: your writing in Penpoint isn’t changed, and edits you make in Scrivener don’t flow back. Tip: Bringing a Scrivener project into Penpoint instead? See Importing from Scrivener.
Manuscript export: chapters and scenes only. Whole-book export: chapters and scenes plus characters, places, items, notes, arcs, and your timeline.

In Manuscript Mode, click Export (an arrow pointing up out of a tray) in the row of buttons at the top. In a narrow window it moves into the menu with three vertical dots, near the right end of that row. Then pick Scrivener Project. You can also start it from the Manuscript section of Settings > Import/Export. For the wizard and the other formats, see Exporting Manuscripts. Same on Mac and Windows. Because a Scrivener project is a folder, this format skips the Word and PDF page controls (title page, margins, fonts, spacing, page layout). Scrivener owns all of that: it builds a title page when you Compile (its export and formatting screen).
Picking a folder and opening the project

You pick a folder, and Penpoint creates a project named after your book inside it: My Novel.scriv. A project with the same name is never overwritten: exporting into the same folder again creates My Novel 2.scriv beside it, and the confirmation screen names the exact project it built. To open it, launch Scrivener 3, choose File > Open, and then: On a Mac: select My Novel.scriv. On Windows: open the My Novel.scriv folder and select the file inside it with the Scrivener icon, My Novel.scrivx. For one Book inside a Series, the project is named after that Book, not the Series.

Chapter groups (like Act I) and chapters become folders in the Draft (Scrivener’s main manuscript folder) Scenes become documents holding their text A chapter’s subtitle becomes its index card summary (Scrivener’s corkboard card). Its short summary (from its Corkboard card in Penpoint) and Chapter Notes land in its notes, under the headings Synopsis and Author Notes A chapter with its own settings (a type such as Prologue or Epilogue, or Numbered Chapter or Show Chapter Header turned off) gets a short Chapter Details list at the end of its notes, so they come back on a later import into Penpoint A scene’s Description becomes its index card summary, and its Notes become that document’s notes. A scene’s date (from its Calendar block) is added as a readable Scene Date line at the top of those notes, and Penpoint reads it back into the scene’s date on a later import. That works for standard calendar dates; any other date stays as a line in the scene’s Notes Chapter and scene tags become keywords (Scrivener’s version of tags), with each tag group as a parent keyword Colors carry over as labels (Scrivener’s color-coding, not a mailing label), and statuses as statuses Headings keep their levels, links keep their web addresses, and paragraph indents stay as you set them Saved versions of a scene become that document’s snapshots (Scrivener’s saved versions), each with its name and date, and they come back as scene versions on a later import into Penpoint

The whole-book export starts in Settings > Import/Export (see Exporting Worldbuilding Data). On its first page, choose Export Whole Book to Scrivener at the bottom. The next screen lists what goes into the project and what stays in Penpoint. Click Export and choose a folder, and your manuscript and worldbuilding land in one project. Characters become Scrivener character sheets (its template for describing a character) Each part of a character’s page (such as Traits, Relationships, or Chapter Appearances) becomes its own document inside that character, named for the section. Scrivener shows those names in the binder; to see them above each part when you view the character as one page, turn on View > Text Editing > Show Titles in Scrivenings Locations arrive in a folder called Places (Scrivener’s own name for it) Items and notes become Scrivener documents Arcs and your timeline arrive inside the Notes folder, the timeline as one Timeline document Portraits (characters, locations, items) and Notebook pictures come along as image documents (JPG and PNG only; other picture types stay in Penpoint) Extra details (a character’s importance, a place’s type) become short lines in that document’s notes, so the document holds only your own writing Tags on characters, places, items, and notes become keywords too A note’s color and a Notebook folder’s color become labels, and a pinned note is marked as pinned in its notes For one Book inside a Series, the manuscript and story arcs (plus any Series Arcs) are that Book’s; characters, locations, items, and notes come from the whole Series. A chapter from one of your other Books is named with its Book, such as Book Two, Chapter 3: Natalie, in a character’s Chapter Appearances and on the timeline.
Pictures placed inside your prose Inline comments Any other scene fields you have added beyond Description, Notes, and the scene date
Pasting Your Manuscript Into a Form
Pasting Your Manuscript Into a Form

Some agencies and contests do not accept file attachments at all. Instead, their submission form (or their instructions) ask you to paste your query, synopsis, or first pages directly into a text box or the body of an email. If you paste from a Word document, the formatting rarely survives the trip: fonts, indents, and page breaks turn into stray characters or vanish unpredictably, and the pasted text can look worse than typing it by hand.

Export your pages as Plain Text (.txt) or Markdown (.md) instead of Word, PDF, or Rich Text (all are format choices in the same export step, the same place you'd pick to save a Word document as a .docx). Both are built to be copied and pasted: open the exported file, select the text, and paste it into the form or email. There is nothing left to strip out because neither format keeps fonts, indents, or page breaks. Plain Text drops all formatting completely. Bold and italic words are not converted to anything; the emphasis (the bold or italic styling itself) is simply gone, so a line that mattered because it was italicized will read as an ordinary line. Markdown (a way of writing bold and italic using plain symbols like asterisks, used by some websites and forms) keeps a record of emphasis using those characters: an italic word becomes *word* and a bold word becomes **word**. That is useful if the form reads Markdown and displays it as styled text, but if it does not, the reader will see the asterisks themselves sitting in the text. If you cannot tell which kind of box you are pasting into, choose Plain Text: it never leaves stray symbols behind. Chapter headings and scene breaks still appear in both formats as plain lines of text (a chapter title on its own line, a scene break marker like a row of asterisks), just without any special styling. That is exactly what a paste-in-a-textbox destination needs. Tip: Most agencies asking for pasted pages want only the first few, not the whole manuscript. In the chapter selection step of the export wizard, select just the chapters you need before exporting, rather than exporting everything and trimming afterward. Note: Formatting requirements vary a lot between agencies, and many state none at all. Always check the specific submission instructions on the agency's own page for how many pages they want and where to paste them. See Exporting Manuscripts for the full export wizard walkthrough, including title pages, chapter selection, and other formats.
Penpoint lets you bring content into your books from outside files. Which tool you want depends on what you’re bringing in.

A Scrivener project: you don’t need to export or compile anything in Scrivener. On the Your Books screen, choose Create New Book, then Import a Scrivener Project. A Word, EPUB, RTF, Markdown, or text file, as a brand-new book: on the Your Books screen, choose Create New Book, then Import a Manuscript. Chapters from a file, into the book you have open: use the Import button in the row of buttons at the top of Manuscript Mode. Worldbuilding files you exported from Penpoint: use Settings > Import/Export. A .penpoint book file: double-click it, or use Import Book… on the Your Books screen. Importing adds to your books. Something you already have is replaced only when you choose Overwrite (worldbuilding) or Replace My Copy (a .penpoint file) yourself. Penpoint also makes automatic backups of your books, so you can restore an earlier copy if you ever need to (see Backup & Restore).

This brings your worldbuilding (characters, locations, items, notes, chapters, and arcs) back into your book from markdown files (plain-text files with simple formatting marks, the kind Penpoint makes when you export). Edit those files, then import your changes back. The Import Wizard in Settings walks you through it: it checks each file, shows you what it found, and, if a file has the same name as something already in your book, asks how you’d like to handle it before writing anything. New entries appear alongside your existing ones; nothing you already have is touched unless you choose to overwrite it. See Importing Worldbuilding Data for the full walkthrough.

If you have a manuscript written in another app, you can import it directly into Manuscript Mode (where you write your prose). It accepts a Word document (.docx), an ebook file (.epub), a rich text file (.rtf, which is what Scrivener compiles to), a plain text file (.txt), or a markdown file (.md). If your book is in Scrivener, use Import a Scrivener Project instead; it keeps your chapters, scenes, and notes (see Importing from Scrivener). You can also open the manuscript importer from Settings, or from the welcome screen you see the first time you open Manuscript Mode in a book with no chapters yet. Chapter breaks are found automatically, and you get to look everything over and fix it before it’s final Scene breaks become separate scenes: a line holding only a mark like #, * * * or a divider starts a new scene. The preview shows how many scenes each chapter will get; untick Split scenes at scene breaks to keep each chapter as one scene Bold, italic, and other formatting are kept Imported chapters are added to your book; your existing writing is never replaced If you pick a file from inside a Scrivener project folder (.scriv), Penpoint points you to Import a Scrivener Project instead Going the other way? See Exporting Your Data for sending content out of Penpoint, or Exporting to Scrivener for making a Scrivener project.

Your whole Scrivener 3 novel (Mac or Windows) arrives as a new Penpoint book: chapters, scenes, notes, keywords, comments, snapshots, and the character and place pages in your binder (the folder list down the left side of Scrivener’s window). Penpoint reads the project itself, so there is nothing to export or compile first. In short: Find your project in Scrivener. On Your Books, choose Create New Book, then Import a Scrivener Project. Pick the project. Answer a few screens and click Import. Note: Your Scrivener project is only read, never changed, and nothing is added to your library until you click Import on the last screen.

Use a Scrivener 3 project. If Scrivener 2 (Mac) or Scrivener 1 (Windows) last saved it, open it once in Scrivener 3, which offers to update it and saves a copy of the old version beside it. Import the updated project, not that copy. If your project is in iCloud Drive, OneDrive, or Dropbox, keep it on this computer first. It only keeps a copy here; it deletes nothing. On a Mac with iCloud Drive, Control-click the project and choose Keep Downloaded. In OneDrive, choose Always keep on this device. In Dropbox, choose Make available offline. A project from Scrivener for iPad or iPhone lives in Dropbox’s Apps/Scrivener folder; import it from there once it has synced. Pick your project itself, not one of Scrivener’s backups. Scrivener saves its backups as .zip files, which Penpoint can’t open. If a backup is all you have, unzip it first and import the project inside. Have a compiled file instead? A Word or RTF file you compiled from Scrivener goes through Import a Manuscript, which brings in chapters only.

Open the project in Scrivener. Choose File > Show Project in Finder (Mac) or File > Show Project in File Explorer (Windows). A folder window opens with your project selected. Note which folder it is in (usually Documents, if you never picked a spot). Close the project in Scrivener. If it’s still open, Penpoint might miss your latest typing. Nothing in Scrivener is harmed either way.

Go to the Your Books screen. If a book is open, Penpoint saves it first and returns you to your library. Click the Create New Book card at the end of your books (dashed outline, plus sign). You can also right-click (or Control-click on a Mac) an empty spot on the screen and choose Create New Book. In the window titled New Book, click Import a Scrivener Project.
A file window titled Import a Scrivener Project opens. Go to the folder you noted in Step 1. Picked the wrong thing? You just see a message and can choose again; nothing changes.
Select the .scriv project itself, for example A Study in Scarlet.scriv, and click Open.

A Scrivener project is an ordinary folder with a .scrivx main file inside. Double-click the .scriv folder to open it. Select the one file inside (A Study in Scarlet.scrivx) and click Open. Tip: Pick the file with the Scrivener icon (the file window lists only .scrivx files, so a folder without one looks empty).
