Windows often hides file extensions (the letters after the dot), so the file may show as just the project name. To see them, open File Explorer, choose View > Show, and turn on File name extensions. Penpoint shows Reading your project... for a few seconds, longer for a big project. If you close the file window without choosing anything, you return to the New Book window and nothing is created.

On every remaining screen, Cancel is at the bottom left; Back and Next are at the bottom right. On the first screen, Back reads Choose another project. Until you click Import on the Review screen, you can go back and change any choice.

Penpoint reads your Draft folder (called Manuscript in many projects) and sorts its items into parts, chapters, and scenes. Each row shows a Part, Chapter, or Scene tag and its word count. Several drafts: Penpoint asks which one is your current draft (the likeliest is preselected). The others come into your Notebook (Penpoint’s place for notes and research); untick Also bring my other drafts into the Notebook to leave them behind. If those folders are really parts of one book (Act I, Act II, Act III), pick All of them and the whole book comes in. Numbered acts and parts are usually recognized on their own, so you won’t see the question at all. Chapters are: if Penpoint guessed wrong, open this menu and pick the choice that matches your chapter folders, such as Folders like "Chapter Two". The checkboxes: a tick means it becomes a chapter or scene. Penpoint pre-ticks what you had set to Include in Compile in Scrivener. Unticked items go to your Notebook (in a folder called Left out of your Scrivener manuscript), and unticking a folder unticks everything inside it. Check the line under the list, which totals what you ticked, such as 3 chapters, 4 scenes, 8,390 words (w means words). Tip: If scenes you know have text show 0w, their files probably did not finish downloading. Nothing has been created yet, so canceling is safe: click Cancel, make the project available offline (see Before You Start), and begin again. Click Next.

Tell Penpoint which folders hold characters, places, items, or general notes. Scrivener has no “character” or “place” type, so Penpoint guesses and you confirm. Tip: Not sure about a folder? Choose Notes. Whatever you leave as Notes comes into your Notebook with its folders intact. Each unlocked folder or document has a dropdown with six choices: Characters: each document in the folder becomes one character. Locations: each document becomes one location. A place holding other places keeps them inside it, like a city holding its streets. Items (objects that matter to your story, like a locket): each document becomes one item. Notes: the folder comes into your Notebook. Previous version: this folder or document is one earlier draft of your book. It goes into your Notebook under Previous Versions: a folder of chapters becomes one note per chapter, and a single document becomes one note named after it. Skip: the folder is left out of Penpoint and stays in Scrivener. A small gray line under a folder says why Penpoint guessed it, and its documents show what they’ll become, such as Becomes a Character. A small padlock means Penpoint has decided this one: your Research folder always comes in as notes (you can still change the folders inside it), and Scrivener’s blank template sheets are skipped. If a folder holds whole earlier versions of your book (Previous Versions, V2 to V11), its row reads Holds old drafts, and each version arrives in your Notebook as its own folder of notes. Penpoint only guesses this when the folder is named like one (Previous Versions, Old Drafts) or each version inside is a real share of your book, so a folder of short scenes or sketches stays Notes. Penpoint’s guess missed one of your old drafts, or picked the wrong folder? Choose Previous version on any folder or document yourself, even one inside Research. Everything inside it locks and reads Previous version while that choice stands, and none of it becomes a character, place, or item. Choose something else on the row to unlock it again. Click Next.

Penpoint fills in your Scrivener project’s name. Change it if you like, and choose how the book looks in your library. You can change all of this later. Book Name: up to 50 characters. It can’t match a book you already have, and can’t use these symbols: < > / \ | *. Next stays dimmed until the name works. Description: optional, up to 100 characters. Book Color, Texture, and Cover Image (upload a picture and crop it). A live Preview shows the card as you go. Click Next.

This is the last stop before anything is written. The defaults suit most writers. What will be created: counts of everything coming over, including tags (Penpoint’s version of Scrivener keywords). Manuscript options: Bring in scene titles is ticked by default; untick it if your scene titles are only drafting labels (chapter titles are never affected). Also bring in labels and statuses as tags is off by default, since they are often out of date. Use as chapter subtitle appears only when your chapters carry a custom field you added in Scrivener; pick it to make its value each chapter’s subtitle. What won’t be imported, if there is anything to list, and Warnings. Warnings are worth a look but don’t stop the import. See What Stays in Scrivener below. Click Import. A progress bar names what is being copied; larger projects take longer. Leave Penpoint open until it finishes. If something goes wrong, a red message appears on the Review screen and Penpoint removes the unfinished book. Your Scrivener project is untouched. Click Import to try again, or Back to change a choice.

The finished screen tallies what came over. If anything went to the Notebook, a line says where: under Imported from Scrivener: (your book’s name). Not imported and Warnings list what did not come across. Open my book opens the new book. Not sure? Choose this one; you can run the scanner later. Find them in your chapters opens the book in Manuscript Mode (where you write your chapters) with the Manuscript Scanner running over all your imported chapters at once. It finds your characters, places, and items by name (even ones not in any folder) and links them to their chapters. You review what it found before anything is applied, and it doesn’t change your writing. To run the scanner later, open Manuscript Mode, right-click your book's name at the top of the chapter outline on the left, and choose Scan Manuscript for Content. See Chapter Scanner for how reviewing matches works (one chapter at a time). Check a chapter or two against Scrivener. Your project stays where it was; changes in one app don’t flow to the other. To look around first, click Close to stay on the Your Books screen, where your new book is waiting.

Fonts, text sizes, and text colors don’t come over; Penpoint uses its own. Chapters, parts, and scenes: Draft folders become parts, chapters, and scenes using your binder titles; an untitled chapter takes the first words of its text as its title. An Act or Part folder holding chapters comes in as a part, whether those chapters are folders or documents with scenes inside them. Chapter headings: if a chapter’s binder title is only a number (1, Chapter 1) and its text opens with lines you styled as headings in Scrivener, Penpoint uses them for the chapter’s name. A heading that repeats the number is left out (Penpoint already shows CHAPTER 1), the next heading becomes the chapter title, and the one after it the subtitle, unless the chapter already has one. Plain text is never moved, and a chapter with a real title in the binder keeps it. Scene text and formatting: bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, highlighting, lists, block quotes, and headings. Headings come from styles with Heading or Title in the name, or text Scrivener marked with a heading level (scenes keep two heading levels), and block quotes from styles named Block Quote. Synopsis (index card text) and document notes: a chapter’s synopsis becomes its subtitle (unless you picked a custom field for that on the Review screen) and a scene’s its Description; a scene’s notes become its Notes and a chapter’s its author notes. Labels and statuses: a label becomes a color (the nearest of Penpoint’s twelve). Statuses map to Penpoint’s four (Draft, Revised, Polished, Final): names like First Draft become Draft, Second Draft becomes Revised, Final Draft, Done, and Complete become Final, and anything else becomes Draft (No Status stays unset). The optional Review checkbox also makes tags from label and status names (a label that is only a color word, such as Red, is skipped). Keywords: become tags (nested keywords stay grouped) and stay attached to their chapters, scenes, characters, locations, items, and notes. Comments & Pinned Notes: Scrivener comments, footnotes, and inline annotations become comments attached to the same words (footnotes start with "Footnote:"). In notes and character pages, comments go at the end under a Comments heading. Scene Drafts (saved earlier versions of a scene, like Scrivener's snapshots): each snapshot becomes one, named for the snapshot and dated to match. Penpoint keeps the newest 100 per document and tells you if older ones were left behind. Images, links, and tables: pictures in your text (PNG or JPEG) become inline images. Web links stay links, and links to another Scrivener document that came over link to that page in notes, a scene’s Notes, and character, location, and item pages; in scene text only the link words stay. A table in a note stays a table; in a scene, each row becomes a line of text. Custom fields: become “Field: value” lines in a chapter’s author notes, a note, or a character’s bio, unless you chose one as the chapter subtitle.

Characters: a document in a Characters folder becomes a character, its text going into the Bio. Lines using Scrivener’s template labels (Age, Occupation) fill the matching character sheet fields when your book has a field with that name; the rest stays in the Bio. A folder with its own text plus sub-documents becomes one character, each sub-document under its own heading. The first picture in the character’s binder folder becomes the profile picture (PNG or JPEG). Locations and items: the document text becomes the description, and a picture in its binder folder the profile picture. Notebook notes: everything left as Notes, plus Research, front and back matter, other drafts (in Other drafts), earlier versions of your book (in Previous Versions), and unticked manuscript documents (in Left out of your Scrivener manuscript). Each document becomes a note, with its synopsis and notes under Synopsis and Notes headings; picture items become Notebook images captioned with the synopsis.

The Trash: not copied, and still safe in Scrivener. Drag items out first if you want them. Blank character or location sheets: an untouched Scrivener template is skipped and listed under What won’t be imported. PDFs, audio and video, and web pages: listed by name and location, since Penpoint has no home for them. Collections, project bookmarks, and writing targets: listed under What won’t be imported. Compile formats and layout settings: left in Scrivener. Penpoint only reads which documents you had ticked to compile. Screenplay layout: a Screenplay project comes in as ordinary paragraphs; the words stay, the script layout does not. Compile placeholders: special codes like <$PROJECTTITLE> come in as plain text, and the Review screen counts how many it found.

Skip this if you are importing a single book. A series is a set of books that share one cast and world. Note: This is the one import that can change what you already have: Scrivener text can be added to characters, locations, and items already in your series. Penpoint keeps automatic backups, so you can restore an earlier copy if needed (see Backup & Restore). Start from the shelf: on the Your Books screen, click the series' stacked card to open its shelf, then click the Add Book to Series card. The window is titled Add a Book to followed by your series name and offers the same Import a Scrivener Project choice; the other steps are the same except as below. See Your Series in the Library for the shelf. Step 5: a name that matches a character, location, or item already in your series shows Linked to (name) from your series, and your Scrivener text is added to that entry instead of making a duplicate. The match ignores capital letters and extra spaces, and applies only when exactly one entry has that name. Click Unlink for a separate entry instead. Names with no match show New. Step 8: the Notebook folder sits inside the new Book’s own notes folder, and Open my book opens the series with the new Book selected. Scene synopses and notes: if the series’ scene layout has no Description or Notes field, they go to your Notebook instead, in a Scene notes folder, and the Import Complete screen says so.
“This project was made with an older version of Scrivener”
Update it in Scrivener 3 (see Before You Start). Then click Choose another project and pick the updated project, not the old-version copy beside it.
“That doesn’t look like a Scrivener project folder”

Penpoint could not find the project’s main file. Redo Step 3: the .scrivx file on Windows and Linux, the .scriv project itself on a Mac. For a backup (a .zip file), extract it first and import the project inside.

Close it in Scrivener, make sure it is fully downloaded if it lives in a cloud folder, and try again. If it still fails, copy the project into a plain folder such as Documents (in Finder or File Explorer, choose Copy on the project, then Paste inside Documents) and import the copy.

Usually the project had not fully downloaded from a cloud folder. Make it available offline and import again under a different name (two books cannot share one). Once you are happy with the second book, delete the first Penpoint copy on the Your Books screen (see Deleting Books), never the Scrivener project.

See Step 7. If an unfinished book ever does remain on the Your Books screen, delete it (see Deleting Books) and try again. Still stuck? Open the (?) help menu and choose Contact Support. It is in the top bar inside a book, and on the Your Books screen too. Tip: Going the other way? See Exporting to Scrivener to send a Penpoint book back to Scrivener 3. For other file types, see Importing Your Data.

The Import Wizard brings markdown files (the text files Penpoint creates when you export) back into your book. It works with all six kinds of worldbuilding: characters, locations, items, notes, chapter outlines, and arcs. A file you exported from this version comes back in cleanly, with every detail, picture, and @Mentions link landing exactly where it was. Best of all, before anything is written you'll see a summary of what each file contains and anything new that would be created. You can import a single file or an entire folder at once. Note: Files exported by this version of Penpoint import back perfectly. Older exports, filled-in template sheets (the blank fill-in files Penpoint can generate), and even hand-written files still import too. Penpoint reads them as best it can and shows you what it understood before writing anything. The one exception: a file exported by a newer version of Penpoint than you're running can't be imported until you update.

Go to Settings > Import/Export and click "Open Import Wizard" in the Import Data section. The wizard follows these steps: Choose What to Import - Pick a type (Characters, Locations, Items, Notes, Chapters, or Arcs), or choose Everything to bring in a whole export folder. Penpoint reads each file by its contents, so you don't have to get this exactly right; whatever you pick, each file still imports as what it actually is Before You Import - A quick page of tips on formatting and templates Choose Import Mode - Select whether to import a single file or an entire folder Automatic Check - Penpoint double-checks the files for anything that might trip up the import Review Results - See what Penpoint found in each file (every entry, and anything new it would create) along with any warnings, before you import Resolve Conflicts - Decide how to handle entries with duplicate names Complete Import - View statistics on what was created, updated, or auto-generated

Penpoint checks each file for common issues before importing: Whether the file matches the format Penpoint expects Required fields like names Valid values for importance levels and other settings Duplicate names within the same file Files with errors can't be imported until fixed. Files with warnings can usually be imported anyway - Penpoint will skip or default any problematic values. If you're importing a folder and one file has a problem, Penpoint skips just that file and imports the rest.

When an imported file has the same name as something already in your book, you'll be asked to choose how to handle it: Overwrite existing - Replace the existing entry with what's in the file, including its links, tags, and traits. This permanently replaces the original, so if you're not certain, make a backup of your book first — the note just below shows how, and how to restore it. Skip this file - Keep what you already have and import nothing from this file Keep both - Import as a new entry with a numbered name (e.g., "Sherlock Holmes (1)"), leaving the original untouched Your choice applies to the whole file, so if one file holds several entries that already exist, one decision covers all of them. When you're importing many files at once, use the "Overwrite All", "Skip All", or "Keep Both (All)" buttons to handle them the same way in one click. Note: Before importing with Overwrite, it's a good idea to create a manual backup of your book in Settings > Storage & Backups. If anything doesn't look right after importing, you can restore from that backup. For more details, see Backup & Restore.

When your markdown files mention other characters, locations, items, or chapters (like a character's relationships or chapter appearances), Penpoint checks if those already exist in your book. If they don't, it creates placeholders with just a name so the connections work correctly. These placeholders appear in your normal character, location, item, and chapter lists alongside your other entries. Tip: After importing, you can fill out the auto-created placeholders or import additional files for them. This makes it easy to build out your world piece by piece.

When the import completes, you'll see a summary showing: How many new entries were created How many existing entries were updated Which placeholders were auto-created from mentions in your files Any warnings that occurred during import Note: Importing new entries won't change your existing data. If you chose Overwrite for any conflicts, you can restore from a backup you created beforehand. See Backup & Restore for details on creating and restoring backups.

Settings is your control center for customizing Penpoint to match your workflow and story needs. From character layout customization to theme preferences, Settings gives you the tools to tailor Penpoint to your writing process.

Settings are organized into categories, each focused on a specific aspect of Penpoint: Design your character page layout and choose which information to display Create custom traits to track character attributes unique to your story Manage tags for categorizing and organizing characters Define item types and location categories that fit your world Import and export your work, or bring in existing manuscripts Customize the interface with themes, fonts, and animation preferences Manage backups, storage, troubleshooting tools, and view version information

Character Sheet Setup: Build your ideal character page layout by adding, removing, and arranging blocks. Each block displays different information (traits, relationships, items, etc.) and can be customized to your needs. Traits: Create custom traits like "House Affiliation" for wizarding schools, "Magic System" for fantasy novels, or "Political Alliance" for epic sagas. Define the options for each trait and choose how they display. Tags: Set up character tags for quick categorization and filtering. Assign colors to tags for visual organization across your character lists. Item & Location Types: Define categories for both items and locations in your story. Item types range from "Weapons" and "Artifacts" to "Documents" and "Vehicles", while location types let you create categories like "City", "Landmark", "Region", or custom types specific to your world-building needs. Interface: Choose your preferred theme (light or dark), customize typography, and adjust animation speeds to match your working style. Import/Export: Export your characters, locations, items, notes, and chapters in multiple formats. Import edited data back into Penpoint, or bring in existing manuscripts from .epub, .docx, .rtf, .md, or .txt files. Community & Updates: View announcements, join or leave Penpoint Hub, and review privacy settings. Storage & Backups: Configure automatic backups, manage storage locations, and set up secondary backup protection. Advanced: Troubleshooting tools like hardware acceleration control and support log export for when you need help diagnosing issues. About Penpoint: Check your current version, view changelog information, and check for software updates.

Navigate to Settings from the main navigation bar at any time. Most settings are book-specific, meaning each book has its own character layout, traits, tags, and customizations. Interface settings (theme, font, animations) are global and apply across all books.

Explore the child articles below to learn about specific settings categories: Calendar Settings - Set up dates, eras, and moons for your book Customizing Character Layout - Customizing your character page layout Managing Location Types - Setting up location type categories Managing Traits - Creating and managing custom character traits Managing Tags - Organizing characters with tags and colors Managing Item Types - Defining item categories and archetypes Interface Settings - Customizing themes, fonts, and animations Spellcheck & Autocorrect - Catching typos as you type and building your own dictionary Exporting Your Data - Exporting worldbuilding data, manuscripts, and templates Importing Your Data - Importing worldbuilding data and manuscripts Community & Updates - Announcements and Penpoint Hub Advanced Settings - Hardware acceleration and support logs Backup & Restore - Automatic backups and data protection Penpoint Cloud Settings - Encrypted cloud backup and sync

Character sheets can be as diverse as the characters you are writing in your book! That's why Penpoint doesn't force you to use a predetermined layout. You choose which blocks (the individual sections on your character sheet) to include and how to arrange them. Add, remove, reorder, and configure blocks to track exactly what matters for your story. Access the layout editor at Settings > Character Sheet Setup.

The layout editor is a two-column page. The left side is where you build your layout: adding, removing, and arranging blocks. The right side is a live preview that shows how your layout will look on actual character pages. Your layout applies to all characters in your book. When you add a "Height" number block, every character gets a height field; each character has their own unique value. Add new blocks anytime, and they'll appear on every character sheet. Adding a new block doesn't fill in data for existing characters. All your existing character data stays exactly as it is. You will need to go through your character list to fill in the new field as needed. Note: The Character Name block is locked at the top and cannot be removed or moved since the name and importance of every character is fundamental to how Penpoint organizes your work.

Click Add Block to choose from two categories: Basic blocks (Text, Paragraph, Number, Divider, Calculate (lets you add up number values, for example, totaling a character's skill points), and Image (attach a portrait or other visual reference)) and Character Data blocks (Trait (a dropdown where you pick from a list of options you define, like eye color or personality type), Tags, Events (key story moments involving the character), Relationships, Items, Locations, Chapters, Character Arc, and Notes (show a Notebook note, folder, or set of tags on the character sheet)). Some blocks (like Items) can only be added once. If a block is already in your layout, it appears faded and can't be clicked again in the Add Block menu.

Each block in the layout editor has a row of small buttons in the top-left corner. These let you manage the block without opening its settings: Drag handle: a vertical row of dots. Click and drag to move the block to a new position in the layout. Settings: a gear icon. Click to open the block's settings, where you can change its label, hint text, and other options. You can also click anywhere on the block itself to open settings. Half-width: a two-column icon. Click to switch the block between full-width and half-width (see Half-Width Layouts below). Available on all blocks except Character Name and Divider. Quick Create: a lightning bolt icon. Quick Create is a shortcut menu that lets you fill in key fields right when you create a new character, without having to open the character page first. When this button is highlighted, the block's field will be included in that menu. Available on Text, Paragraph, Trait, Number, and Tags blocks. Text and Paragraph blocks are included by default. Each block also has an ✕ button in the top-right corner to remove it from the layout.

Removing a block does not delete your data. When you click the ✕ button on any block, Penpoint asks you to confirm, then archives it: hiding it from all character pages but preserving all character data. If you removed a block by accident or want to bring it back, scroll to the bottom of the page and click the Deleted Blocks button to see a list of archived blocks and the data they contain. Tip: From the Deleted Blocks list, you can click Restore to bring a block back into your layout. To permanently delete a block and all its data, click the Forever Delete button next to it. Penpoint will ask you to confirm before anything is deleted.

Drag blocks by the drag handle (a vertical row of dots in the top-left corner) to rearrange your layout. As you drag, a highlighted line shows you where the block will land. Character Name always stays at the top.

Click any block in the layout editor (or click its gear icon) to open its settings right below the block. Common options include labels, the hint text shown in empty fields, minimum/maximum values (for numbers), and which trait list to use. Changes save automatically as you type, and you can always change settings back if you change your mind. Tip: Hover over any block in the layout editor to highlight it in the live preview on the right side of the page.

Want to put "Eye Color" and "Hair Color" next to each other, or "Strength" and "Intelligence" side by side? All blocks except Character Name and Divider support half-width layouts. Click the two-column icon on any block to switch it to half-width, or drag a block to the left or right side of the highlighted area between blocks to place it in a side-by-side row. To swap two blocks in the same row, drag one over the other until a swap icon (two arrows pointing left and right) appears, then drop it.

Each block on a character page has a small arrow next to its title. Click the header to collapse that block's content, leaving just the title and icon visible. Click again to expand it. This is handy when your character sheet has many blocks and you want to focus on specific sections. Collapse preferences are remembered separately for the Characters page and the Mini Penpoint sidebar (a compact reference area that can appear alongside your manuscript), so you can have a different view in each. The Character Name block and dividers cannot be collapsed.

The right side of the layout editor shows how your layout looks on actual character pages. The preview updates instantly as you make changes and highlights blocks as you hover over them in the editor. For details about specific block types, see Block Types.

Location types are customizable categories you can assign to your locations. Unlike character importance levels (which are fixed at Primary, Secondary, Background), location types are entirely up to you.

Think of types as a way to categorize your locations by their function or scale. Common types might include: Continent, Country, Region City, Town, Village Building, Room, Landmark Forest, Mountain, River You decide which types exist and what they're called. The types you create are specific to each book - a fantasy novel might use "Realm, Kingdom, City", while a thriller might use "Country, City, Building".

Location types and importance levels are separate things. Type describes what kind of place something is (City, Forest, Building), while Importance describes how significant it is to your story (Primary, Secondary, Background). A location can have both. For example, "The Shire" might be type "Region" and importance "Primary".

Create, edit, delete, and reorder your location types in Settings > Location Types. In the Location Types settings, you can: Create new types with custom names Rename existing types Reorder types using the small up and down arrow buttons next to each type name Delete types you no longer need — this does not delete any locations. Those locations will simply show "No type selected" until you assign them a different type.

When you select "By Type" from the Sort menu at the top of your locations list, locations are grouped by their type and then sorted alphabetically within each group. The type groups appear in the custom order you set in Location Types settings, so the order you arrange your types matters. Tip: Arrange your types from broadest to most specific (Continent, Country, City, Building) to create a natural top-to-bottom organization when sorting by type.

The Traits settings page is where you define trait categories and their dropdown options. Traits are reusable character attributes like alignment, eye color, or personality type that can be assigned to multiple characters.

Traits help you track categorical attributes across your cast. Instead of typing "Lawful Good" repeatedly in different characters, create an Alignment trait once with all possible values (Lawful Good, Chaotic Neutral, True Neutral, etc.). Then assign the appropriate value to each character. Once defined here, traits appear as dropdown menus in character edit mode via the Trait Block.

Click Add New Trait to create a new trait category. Give it a descriptive name like "Eye Color", "Personality Type", or "Faction". Tip: Use trait names that describe the category, not individual values. For example, name the trait "Alignment" (not "Lawful Good") and add alignment options like "Lawful Good", "Chaotic Evil", etc.

Click any trait card in the grid to select it. The selected trait's options appear in the detail panel below, where you can add, edit, archive, or delete individual options. Add options: Click "Add Subtrait" in the detail panel header. Use the +1 button to add multiple options at once before saving Edit options: Hover over an option and click the edit icon to rename it Archive options: Hover over an option and click the archive icon Delete options: Hover over an option and click the trash icon

Use the Sort dropdown in the detail panel to control how options are ordered: A-Z: Alphabetical order Date Added: Most recently added first Most Used: Options assigned to the most characters appear first Custom Order: Drag and drop options to arrange them in any order you like Tip: When you drag an option to rearrange it, the sort mode automatically switches to Custom Order.

Archive hides traits or options from view but preserves character assignments. Use this when you want to stop using a trait without losing existing data. Delete permanently removes the trait or option and clears it from all characters. Use this for traits you created by mistake or truly don't need. Tip: Toggle Show Archived in the header to view or restore archived traits and options.

After creating traits here, add Trait Blocks to your character layout in Settings > Character Sheet Setup. Each Trait Block links to one trait definition and displays its dropdown menu in character edit mode.

Tags are universal markers that work across everything in your book: characters, items, locations, chapters, and notes. Think of them as colored labels that help you group and find related content instantly.
Traits belong to a single character. Tags don't. Tag a character with "Rebels" and a location with "Rebels," then view everything Rebellion-related in one place on the Tags page.

Tags shine when tracking concepts that span multiple areas of your story: Factions & Affiliations: "Royal Family", "Magic Order", "Merchant Guild" Story arcs: "Act 1", "Rebellion Arc", "Resolution" Themes & Motifs: "Nature Symbolism", "Political Intrigue", "Prophecy" Status tracking: "Needs Development", "Ready for Review", "Plot Critical" Character roles: "Protagonist", "Antagonist", "Comic Relief" Tip: Tags are book-wide. Create them once, use them everywhere. A tag created while editing a character is immediately available for locations, items, chapters, and notes. In a series, that means the whole series: one set of tags shared across every Book.

Add New Tag: Click the "Add New Tag" button to create a tag. Give it a name and select a color. Colors help you visually distinguish tags at a glance. Display Order: Choose how tags are sorted throughout the app: Most Used: Tags you use frequently appear first (default) A-Z: Alphabetical order for easy lookup Recently Created: Newest tags appear first This setting affects tag ordering everywhere in Penpoint, not just in the Tags Manager.

Once you have more than a couple of dozen tags, a flat list stops being useful. Tag Groups let you file related tags together under a heading: "Factions", "Themes", "Draft Status". A group is only a filing cabinet. Putting a tag in one changes nothing about where that tag is already assigned, and a tag lives in one group at a time. Groups appear everywhere you pick or browse tags, not only on this page. Create Tag Group: Click this button, name the group, and it appears as a section in your tag list. Tags you haven't filed anywhere sit in a section called Ungrouped at the bottom.

Filing is safe to experiment with: nothing is deleted, and a tag in the wrong place just gets dragged somewhere else. Drag it: Pick up a tag and drop it anywhere inside a group's section. The whole section lights up as you hover over it. Drop a tag on the Ungrouped section to pull it back out of its group, and let go away from any section to call the whole thing off. Use the menu: Hover over a tag and click the small folder button (rest on it and it says "Move to group"), then pick a group. The same menu offers "No group" to take a tag out of one, and "New group…" to make a group and file the tag into it in one step. Do a batch: Tick several tags and a dark bar appears above your tag list. Click Move to Group there to file all of them at once. Dragging any one of the ticked tags brings the rest with it. Set it when you create it: Once you have at least one group, the Create New Tag window (opened by Add New Tag) gains a Group dropdown, so a tag can go straight where it belongs.

Every group's heading carries a small row of buttons, faint until you hover over them, to rename the group, give it an icon, assign it a color, or delete it. A group color takes over the display of every tag inside it, so a whole category reads as one block at a glance. Your own tag colors are kept, not overwritten: choose Remove group color from that same color button and every tag returns to the color you gave it. While the group color is in charge, each member tag's own color button is deliberately unavailable, since the group is deciding.

Anywhere you pick tags, clicking a group's heading folds it away, and it stays folded everywhere else you pick tags until you open it again, including the next time you open Penpoint. A category you're not working on today stops taking up room on every character sheet and note. Headings don't fold here in the Tags Manager: this is where you organize groups, so they stay open. To change the order groups appear in, drag a group up or down by the grip at the far left of its heading (the column of small dots). That order is used everywhere, and Ungrouped always sits last.

One of the two ways to delete a group reaches past the group and deletes the tags themselves, so the window spells out both outcomes and the tag count before you choose. Neither choice can be undone. Delete Group, Keep Tags: Only the heading goes. Every tag survives untouched, still attached to each character, chapter and note it was on. The tags simply become ungrouped. Delete Group and N Tags: The tags are deleted outright and removed from every character, item, location, chapter, scene, note and arc they were on. An empty group is removed with a single Delete Group button, since there is nothing to decide.

Hover over any tag card to reveal management options: Change Color: Click the color swatch to pick a new color Edit Name: Click the pencil icon to rename the tag Merge Tags: Combine two tags into one, preserving all assignments Move to group: File the tag into a Tag Group, or take it out of one Delete: Remove a tag from your book (removes from all assignments)

If you've created duplicate tags or want to consolidate similar tags, merging moves all assignments from one tag to another, then deletes the source tag. For example, merging "Magic Users" into "Mages" will update all characters, locations, and other content to use "Mages" instead. Note: When deleting a tag, you'll be prompted to either delete it permanently or merge it with another tag. Choose merge if you want to preserve the categorization under a different name.

Select multiple tags using the checkboxes (visible on hover) to perform actions on many tags at once: Set Color: Apply the same color to multiple tags for visual grouping Move to Group: File every selected tag into the same group at once Merge: Consolidate multiple tags into a single target tag Delete: Remove several tags at once, taking them off everything they were assigned to. You're asked to confirm first, and it can't be undone

Assign tags to any content by entering Edit mode and using the Tags Block. View all content with a specific tag in the Tags page, where you can filter by type (characters, items, locations, chapters, notes).

Start with broad categories and add specific tags as your book develops Use consistent naming conventions (e.g., "Royal Family" not "Family Royal") Assign colors strategically. Similar tags can share colors, contrasting concepts use different colors Don't over-tag early; let your tagging system evolve with your story Wait until a pattern appears before making groups. Groups are worth it once a flat list gets hard to scan, not on day one Visit the Tags page regularly to discover unexpected connections
Tags Block - Learn about the Tags Block for assigning tags to characters Tags Viewer Page - Discover how to view all content associated with a specific tag
Penpoint's interface settings let you customize the look and feel of the app to match your writing preferences. Find these settings in Settings > Themes.

Choose from eight color themes to find the one that's easiest on your eyes. Penpoint offers both light and dark themes: Parchment - A warm, cream-colored theme perfect for long writing sessions Linen - Clean and professional with crisp white backgrounds Catppuccin - A soothing pastel dark theme by the Catppuccin community Slate - A professional dark theme with cool tones Cloud - Soft grays for a neutral, modern look Ocean - Deep blue tones inspired by ocean depths Midnight - Pure black for terminal-style minimal distraction Matrix - Black and green for that iconic hacker aesthetic Your theme choice applies across the entire app and persists between sessions.

Select the typeface that makes your character notes most readable. Four carefully chosen fonts cover different writing styles: Source Serif 4 - A classic serif font ideal for long-form writing and traditional manuscripts Inter - Modern sans-serif that's clean and easy to scan JetBrains Mono - Monospaced font designed for technical content Source Code Pro - Classic typewriter-style monospace for a retro writing vibe Tip: The font you choose affects all text in Penpoint—character names, notes, descriptions, and more.

Make text larger or smaller to suit your screen and eyesight. Use the minus and plus buttons to adjust in 10% increments, from 80% (smallest) to 150% (largest). The visual progress bar shows your current size. Click the Reset button to return to 100% (default size) at any time. Tip: Use Ctrl+Shift+"+" (Cmd+Shift+"+" on Mac) to increase font size, or Ctrl+Shift+"-" (Cmd+Shift+"-" on Mac) to decrease it with your keyboard.

Decide what you see when you launch Penpoint: Reopen my last book - Opens the book you were working on, right where you left off (default) Open my Book Library - Starts you on your shelf so you can pick a book. Penpoint won't reopen your last book. Most writers prefer "Reopen my last book" for quick access to their current project. Choose "Open my Book Library" if you frequently switch between multiple books. This applies every time Penpoint opens, including after an update restarts it. If you ever launch Penpoint and land on your Library when you expected your book, this setting is why.

Adjust the vertical spacing between lines of text. Five presets cover different reading preferences: Single (1.0) - Tightest spacing, like a traditional manuscript Compact (1.08) - Slightly more breathing room for dense information Normal (1.15) - Comfortable spacing for everyday use (default) Relaxed (1.5) - Generous spacing for easier scanning Double (2.0) - Maximum spacing, like double-spaced drafts Tip: Tighter spacing fits more on screen; looser spacing is easier to read. Find the balance that works for your eyes.

Spellcheck & Autocorrect has its own settings page with multi-language support, Your Dictionary, autocorrect controls, and automatic entity name whitelisting. See Spellcheck & Autocorrect for full details.

Penpoint can display a clock in the header bar so you can keep track of time while writing. Click the clock to open a dropdown with quick options. Three settings let you customize the clock: Show clock in header - Enable or disable the clock display. When disabled, a small clock icon remains for quick access. Time format - Choose between 12-hour (2:30 PM) or 24-hour (14:30) display. Defaults to your system preference. Show seconds - Add seconds to the clock display for a more precise readout.

Turn on OpenDyslexic to switch your interface and manuscript editor to a typeface designed to reduce common reading errors for people with dyslexia. One toggle replaces both your Typography choice and any font pinned specifically for the manuscript editor. Turn it off and Penpoint remembers what you had before.

The Community & Updates page keeps you connected with Penpoint news and is where you join or leave Penpoint Hub, the place where writers add up what they have written. You can control when you see announcements, check for new ones, and manage your Hub membership.
Penpoint automatically checks for new announcements when you open the app. You’ll see a notification overlay with any new updates, features, or tips.
The Check for Announcements Now button lets you manually check for new announcements at any time. When clicked, Penpoint will check for the latest announcements and display them if any are available.

The Announcement History section displays all announcements you've received, organized from newest to oldest. Each announcement shows: An icon indicating the announcement type (update, tip, promotion, or general announcement) The announcement title A status badge (New, Dismissed, or Expired) Published date and expiration date (if applicable) Each announcement has action buttons: View: Opens the full announcement content in an overlay Unread: Restores a dismissed announcement to your new announcements list Tip: Expired announcements remain in your history for reference, but won't appear as new announcements even if you mark them unread.

Penpoint Hub is where writers add up what they have written. Joining is optional, and Penpoint works the same whether you join or not. Members share a few anonymous numbers once a day, and see how many writers are writing today and how many words the community has written. Join Penpoint Hub: Opens a window that lists exactly what is shared, then joins You’re in: Shows once you have joined, with a Leave button beside it Show Raw Contribution Data: Inspect exactly what data is being shared at any time Leave asks first. Leaving deletes the anonymous numbers you have shared with the Hub, and that cannot be undone. Your own stats and writing on this computer are not affected, and you can join again at any time. Note: Hub numbers are completely anonymous and contain no personal information or writing content. Only counts like words written, session time and activity are shared.
Penpoint can optionally display your writing activity in your Discord profile status using Discord's Rich Presence feature. This is disabled by default and must be turned on manually.

When enabled, Penpoint communicates with the Discord desktop app running on your computer to show what you're working on. Your Discord status will display two lines of information: A description of the section you're in, such as "Working on Characters" or "Working on the Manuscript" Your current mode: "Worldbuilding Mode" or "Manuscript Mode" The status updates automatically as you navigate between pages. The possible statuses are: Worldbuilding Mode: Working on Characters, Working on Chapters, Working on Notes, Working on Story Arcs, Working on the Timeline, Working on Relationships, Working on Items, Working on Locations, Working on Tags, Browsing the Index, Checking Progress, In Settings, Reading the User Guide Manuscript Mode: Working on the Manuscript

Use the Turn on button in the Discord Rich Presence card to connect. The Discord desktop app must be running on your computer for the connection to succeed. If Discord isn't running, you'll see an error message. Once enabled, Penpoint will automatically reconnect to Discord each time you launch the app. Use the Turn off button to disconnect and stop sharing your status. This takes effect immediately. Note: Your writing content is never shared. Discord only sees which section of Penpoint you're using (e.g., "Working on Characters"): no character names, project titles, or prose are ever transmitted. All communication happens locally on your device between Penpoint and the Discord desktop app.

Announcement checking is completely private. Penpoint doesn’t collect any tracking data when checking for announcements. Dismissed announcement records are stored locally on your device only. Penpoint Hub is separate from announcements and is entirely opt-in. You can inspect the exact data being shared at any time, and leaving the Hub stops all outbound data immediately. Note: Announcements are stored separately from your books and won't affect your book data or exports.
The Advanced page in Settings > Advanced contains troubleshooting tools and system-level settings that most writers won't need day-to-day, but they're here when you need them.

Penpoint uses your computer's graphics hardware to render the interface smoothly. On most machines this works perfectly, but on some systems it can cause visual problems: flickering, black screens, graphical glitches, or other display issues. If you're experiencing any of these issues, try switching hardware acceleration to Disabled using the dropdown. This tells Penpoint to use software rendering instead, which is slower but avoids graphics driver conflicts. After changing this setting, you'll need to restart Penpoint for it to take effect. A restart banner will appear with a Restart Now button: click it when you're ready. Tip: If everything looks fine on your screen, leave this set to Enabled. You only need to change it if you're seeing visual problems. Note: This setting is only available on Windows. macOS and Linux handle graphics rendering differently and don't need this toggle.

If something goes wrong and you need help troubleshooting, Penpoint can export its internal logs as a zip file. These logs record what the app was doing behind the scenes: things like which pages you visited, what actions you took, and any errors that occurred. Click Save Logs to Disk to choose where to save the file. You can then share the zip with support or attach it to a bug report. What's NOT in the logs: Your manuscript and the text of your book are never included. Logs can mention the names of things like characters or chapters. The saved copy also has your computer's user name, folder paths, email addresses, and sign-in tokens removed. The log files on your computer are not changed. Tip: Penpoint keeps its logs across restarts, so you can still save them after restarting. Older entries are dropped after a while, so save the logs soon after something goes wrong.

Penpoint protects your work with automatic backups and gives you full control over when and where your books are saved. Backups are saved as .penpoint files containing your entire book: all characters, locations, items, chapters, notes, and settings. All backup and storage settings are located in Settings > Storage & Backups. For encrypted cloud backup and multi-device sync, see Penpoint Cloud. Your Note Templates aren't part of any one book, so book backups don't include them. They stay on this computer, and with Penpoint Cloud they're also kept on your other computers.
Penpoint automatically backs up your books to protect against accidental data loss. All automatic backups are saved in a dedicated backup folder alongside your book files.

Opening a book: Penpoint always creates a backup when you open a book, creating a restore point before any changes Closing a book: If enabled, Penpoint saves a backup when you close or switch away from a book While working: Penpoint periodically saves backups at your chosen interval (every 5–60 minutes)

In Settings > Storage & Backups, the Automatic Backups section lets you configure: Create backup when closing a book: Turn this on to save a backup each time you close or switch away from a book. Opening a book always creates a backup regardless of this setting. Perform backups every X minutes: How often Penpoint saves backups while you're working (5–60 minutes) Keep backups from the last X days: How many days of backups to retain (1–365) Tip: The periodic backup interval and retention settings are only available when "Create backup when closing a book" is enabled. Recent backups are kept in full. Older backups are automatically thinned to one per day to save space.

For additional protection, you can save a second copy of all your backups to a different location. The ideal setup is to point your secondary backup at a cloud-synced folder like Dropbox, OneDrive, or iCloud: this gives you automatic offsite protection without any extra effort. In Settings > Storage & Backups, find the Secondary Backup section to enable this feature and choose your backup folder. Why use a secondary backup? Protect against hardware failure: If your hard drive dies, your backups are safely stored somewhere else Automatic cloud sync: Point it at a Dropbox, OneDrive, or iCloud folder and your backups upload automatically Access from multiple computers: Your backup files are available wherever your cloud folder syncs Zero risk to your active work: Secondary Backup only copies finished backup files, so it never interferes with your book while you're writing
Why Not Just Store My Books in a Cloud Folder?

It's tempting to move your entire book storage into Dropbox or OneDrive so everything syncs automatically. We strongly recommend against this. Cloud sync services work by watching for file changes and uploading them in the background. Penpoint's database writes to its files frequently while you work. This can cause the sync service to upload a half-written file, leading to data corruption or loss. The risk is even higher if you open Penpoint on two computers at the same time. Secondary Backup is the safe alternative. Your books stay on your local hard drive where Penpoint can write to them without interference, and finished backup snapshots are copied to your cloud folder. You get cloud protection without the risk. Tip: Secondary Backup is a simple way to get offsite protection for your work. For a dedicated solution with encryption, version history, and multi-device sync, see Penpoint Cloud.

In addition to automatic backups, you can create backups yourself at any time. There are two ways to do this: Backup Now: Creates an instant backup that goes into your backup history (the same list you see when restoring). You can find this in the Saved indicator in the toolbar while the book is open. With Penpoint Cloud active this row reads Sync now, and one press saves the backup here and sends the book to your cloud. Export Backup: Saves a .penpoint file to a location you choose, like your desktop or a USB drive. Useful for sharing your book with others or keeping a named copy at an important milestone. You can find this in the Saved indicator or in Settings > Storage & Backups. When exporting, Penpoint suggests your book's title as the filename, but you can call it anything you like as long as it still ends with .penpoint.

There are three ways to restore a backup. If you're not sure which to use: Something went wrong and you want to go back?: Use Restore from Backup History to roll back to a previous version Have a .penpoint file from someone else, another computer, or an exported copy?: Use Import a Book File to bring it in as a new book Want to completely replace your current book with a backup file?: Use Restore from File Tip: When you restore from backup history or from a file, Penpoint automatically creates a safety backup of your current book first. If you change your mind, you can restore from that safety backup to get back to where you were.

Brings a .penpoint file into your library as a book, without touching your other books. It's the easiest way to open a book someone shared, or to move one between computers: double-click the file, or use Import Book… from the Your Books screen. If it's a book you already have, Penpoint tells you which version is newer and asks whether to Replace My Copy or Keep Both. See Importing a Book for the full walkthrough.

Restore a specific book to a previous automatic backup directly from its backup history. You can access this from three places: Your Books: Click the menu on a book and select Restore from Backup... Settings: Go to Settings > Storage & Backups and click Browse Previous Backups Saved indicator: Click the Saved indicator in the toolbar and choose Restore from Backup All three open the same backup browser where you can see your full backup history with timestamps and backup types. Select the backup you want and click Continue. You'll then choose how to restore: Restore as New Book: Creates a separate copy from the backup. Your current book stays untouched. Overwrite Current Book: Replaces your current book with the backup. A safety backup is created first, so you can undo it if needed.

Replaces your current book with a .penpoint backup file from your computer. This is useful if you have a backup from another device or shared by someone else. Open the book you want to replace Go to Settings > Storage & Backups Click Or restore from an external file in the Restore from Backup section Choose your .penpoint file and confirm Penpoint creates a safety backup of your current book before replacing it, so you can undo this if needed. The app will reload automatically after restoration completes.

In Settings > Storage & Backups, the Storage Location section shows where your books are stored on this computer. Click Browse for Location to select a new folder Click Move to New Location to move all your books Penpoint will restart automatically after migration If you're using a custom location, you can click Reset to System Default to move your books back to the default folder.

Penpoint will warn you if your storage location is inside a cloud-synced folder (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive, or iCloud). Storing your active book database in a cloud folder can cause data corruption or loss, especially if Penpoint is open on more than one computer at the same time. Tip: For cloud protection, use Secondary Backup or Penpoint Cloud instead of moving your storage location. Both keep your active book files on your local hard drive where they are safe from sync conflicts.

Use descriptive names for manual backups: Include dates or milestones (e.g., "MyNovel-Draft1-Complete.penpoint") Enable Secondary Backup: Point it at a cloud-synced folder for automatic offsite protection Consider Penpoint Cloud: Encrypted cloud backup with unlimited version history and optional multi-device sync Check your backup settings: Ensure automatic backups are configured to match your workflow Share with others: Send .penpoint files to beta readers or collaborators Test restoration: Occasionally restore a backup as a new book to verify your backups work
Ensure the file has the .penpoint extension and hasn't been renamed incorrectly.
The restored book is missing recent changes
Backups are snapshots from when they were created. Check if you have a more recent backup by using the Restore from Backup... option on the book's context menu in Your Books.

Penpoint creates a safety backup before every restore, so you can get your book back. Open the backup browser (from the Saved indicator, Settings, or the book's context menu in Your Books) and look for the Safety backup entry at the top of the list: that's your book from right before the restore happened. Select it and restore to undo the change.
Where are my automatic backups stored?

Automatic backups are saved in a folder next to your book files. If you moved your storage location, the backups folder moved with it. Tip: For additional help, export your application logs from Settings > Advanced to troubleshoot backup issues.

Penpoint checks your spelling as you write and can automatically convert common patterns: straight quotes into curly quotes, or double dashes into em dashes. Manage everything in Settings > Spellcheck & Autocorrect.
Use the Spellcheck section in Settings to enable or disable spell-checking. When disabled, all red underlines disappear immediately. When re-enabled, your manuscript is re-checked.
Your Characters, Locations, and Items Are Recognized Automatically

Penpoint automatically recognizes the names of your characters, locations, and items, including character aliases. You won't see red underlines on "Aragorn" or "Rivendell" as long as they exist in your book. When you add a new character, location, or item, the spellchecker picks it up automatically.

For words that aren't character, location, or item names (slang, made-up terminology, or anything else specific to your writing), add them to Your Dictionary. It's one list for all your writing: a word you add counts as correct in every book, and you can manage the list in Settings even with no book open. There are two ways to add a word: From the editor: Right-click a red-underlined word and choose "Add to Dictionary" From Settings: Type the word into the search box in the Your Dictionary section and press Enter or click Add To remove a word, hover over it in the dictionary list and a small delete button (X) appears on the left. Click it to remove the word; it will be spell-checked again going forward. Each word row also has a small paper-airplane (send) icon. Click it to suggest that word to Penpoint for the Authors Dictionary, a shared list of fiction-writing words covered just below. Using Penpoint Cloud? Your Dictionary follows you to your other computers together with your settings, as long as Sync my settings across all my computers is on in Settings > Penpoint Cloud.

Fiction is full of words a standard dictionary marks as misspelled: "sigil," "wyvern," "grimoire," and countless others. The Penpoint Authors Dictionary is a curated set of words common to fiction writing, added alongside the English dictionary so fewer genre terms end up underlined in red. It is on by default, and it covers all your books at once, so you never set it up book by book. This is just an extra word list downloaded to your app. It never reads or sends anything from your books. Penpoint keeps it current for you, so it grows over time on its own, and you can turn it off any time in the Spellcheck settings. It works for English; in another language it simply stays inactive until a list exists for that one. Missing a word you use often? You can suggest it, and we add the ones that fit. Contributing to the Authors Dictionary walks through how.

Penpoint ships with English built in. To write in another language, use the Language section in Settings to search for and download additional dictionaries. Over 50 languages are available. Once downloaded, click a language name to switch to it. Penpoint remembers your language choice, so you only need to set it once. To remove a downloaded language, it must not be the one you're currently using. Switch to a different language first; the old language will then appear in the list below with a trash can icon you can click to delete it. Writing different books in different languages? Turn on the switch at the top of this page and the Language and Autocorrect cards change only the book you have open, so you don't have to switch back and forth. See Book Language. Spellcheck skips Japanese, Chinese, and Thai text automatically, because those languages are written without spaces between words and Penpoint has no dictionary for them. Note: Downloading a language requires an internet connection. The dictionaries are small (usually a few hundred kilobytes) and only need to be downloaded once.
The Autocorrect card lets you control three automatic text replacements that happen as you type.

Choose how Penpoint handles dashes when you type hyphens in a row: Standard (default): Typing -- inserts an em dash (—), the long dash most writers use for interruptions and asides. This matches the behavior in Microsoft Word and Google Docs. Typographer: Typing -- inserts an en dash (–), the shorter dash used for ranges like "pages 10–20." Type --- to get an em dash instead.

When enabled, Penpoint automatically converts straight quote marks into curly (typographic) quotes as you type, so "hello" becomes "hello" and 'world' becomes 'world'. If you need straight quotes (for example, when writing code or working in a language that doesn't use curly quotes), you can disable this.

Turn this on and Penpoint capitalizes the first letter of every sentence for you, so a long writing session never breaks stride on the Shift key. It applies everywhere you write: your manuscript, your notes, and the writing fields on your character, location, item, chapter, and arc pages. It is off by default. Changed your mind about a capital? Press Backspace right after it and the lowercase letter comes back. That window is one keystroke wide: type another letter, or move your cursor, and Backspace goes back to deleting. A period doesn't always end a sentence, so Penpoint leaves the next word alone when it recognizes one that doesn't. Abbreviations such as "Mr.", "Dr.", "e.g." and "etc." are covered, along with decimals, web addresses, and ellipses, so "He paused... then walked on" stays exactly as you wrote it. Note: After a line of dialogue closes, the next word is left in lowercase. A dialogue tag ("Get out!" she said.) and an action beat ("Get out!" She turned away.) are equally common in fiction and look identical to the app, so it never guesses: past a closing quotation mark, the capital is yours to type.

The Penpoint Authors Dictionary is built from words that fiction writers actually use. When you hit a word that spellcheck flags but shouldn't, you can suggest it for the shared list so every writer benefits.

First, add the word to Your Dictionary: right-click it in your manuscript (or Ctrl+click on Mac) and choose "Add to Dictionary," or type it into the Your Dictionary box in Settings > Spellcheck & Autocorrect. Then find the word in the Your Dictionary list and click the small paper-airplane (send) icon beside it. A short form opens with the word already filled in. Add a sentence about why it belongs in the dictionary if you like, then send it. That's all there is to it. We review every suggestion and add the ones that fit. Tip: We don't ask for your name, and we never read or send anything from your books. Just the word and your optional note.

The Authors Dictionary is for words many writers would use, not names specific to one story. Penpoint already recognizes your own characters, locations, and items automatically, so those never need suggesting. Great suggestions: genre vocabulary like "spellcaster," "hyperdrive," "revenant," or "portcullis": real words that standard dictionaries often miss. Skip these: a character's invented name ("Zyliaxa"), a place unique to your world ("Kaeldrin"), or a plain typo. Invented names belong in Your Dictionary instead. Note: Not sure whether a word fits? Send it anyway. Reviewing suggestions is how the dictionary learns what writers need, and there is no harm in one that doesn't make the cut.

Writing one book in French and another in English? Give each book its own spellcheck language and autocorrect style, so you never have to change settings when you switch books. The switch is at the top of Settings > Spellcheck & Autocorrect.

Open the book, go to Settings, and choose Spellcheck & Autocorrect. Turn on "Use separate settings for" your book's name. The Language and Autocorrect cards get a tag with the book's name, and anything you change in them applies to that book only. Penpoint starts from the settings you already use, so nothing changes until you pick something different. Turn it off again and the book goes back to your usual settings. The Language and Autocorrect cards then change your settings for all your books. Penpoint remembers the book's choices, so turning it back on later picks up where you left off.

Language: the dictionary spellcheck uses for this book Smart quotes: on or off, and which quote marks you write with Dash behavior: what typing two or three hyphens turns into Auto-capitalize sentences: on or off These apply everywhere you type while the book is open: your manuscript, your notes, and the fields on your character, location, and item pages. Turning spellcheck on or off for every book still happens in Settings > Spellcheck & Autocorrect. Tip: Want to change the settings your other books use while this book has its own? Turn the switch off, make your change, then turn it back on. The book's own choices are kept the whole time.
In a series, the setting covers the whole series: every book inside it uses the same language. If you move or copy a book into a series, it follows the series' setting.

Choose Japanese, Chinese (Simplified), Chinese (Traditional), or Korean and Penpoint also picks matching fonts for those characters. Serif fonts like Source Serif 4 and EB Garamond pair with a Mincho (Song or Myeongjo) style, and the other fonts pair with a Gothic style. Penpoint uses the fonts already installed on your computer. If a Mincho font isn't installed, the text uses a Gothic font instead. Penpoint doesn't have spellcheck for Japanese or Chinese, so spellcheck is off for a book set to either one. Spellcheck also skips Japanese, Chinese, and Thai text in every book, so a few words of Japanese in an English story won't get red underlines.

The setting is saved inside the book, so it travels with it through Penpoint Cloud. If the book's language needs a dictionary your other computer doesn't have yet, Penpoint downloads it the first time you open the book there. Spellcheck for that book stays off until the download finishes. Note: Downloading a dictionary needs an internet connection. If it can't finish, the Language card shows a Retry button.

Your book's calendar shapes how every date appears in your story: from a character's birthday to the day a kingdom falls. Calendar Settings is where you choose the system that fits your world, and dial in the details. You'll find this page at Settings > Calendar. Changes save automatically as you type, and sample dates on the right side of the Calendar Settings page update as you change settings, so you can see what your dates will look like before committing.

Penpoint offers three calendar modes. Pick the one that matches your story. You can switch any time, but switching clears the dates inside your Calendar blocks (the small date markers you place inside scenes), and nothing else. Your characters, chapters, notes, and everything else stay safe, and Penpoint will pop up a confirmation dialog with a Cancel button before anything happens.

The standard real-world calendar: twelve months, seven-day weeks, leap years, the works. This is the default and works for any contemporary, historical, or near-future story. If your book is set on Earth, this is almost certainly what you want.

Just a number. "Day 1", "Day 47", "Day -12". No months, no weekdays. Useful for stories where the actual date doesn't matter, only the passage of time: Survival or post-apocalyptic stories that count days from a triggering event Mission logs and ship's-day journals in science fiction Any narrative structured around "Day 1, Day 2..." rather than calendar dates

Build your own calendar from scratch: design your months, weekdays, hours per day, leap days, and epochs. Best for fantasy and science fiction worlds where Earth's calendar doesn't apply. Custom Calendar walks through every option in depth.

Note: Switching calendar modes clears every calendar date in your book, but ONLY the dates inside Calendar blocks (small date fields you can drop into any scene). Everything else in your book stays safe: chapters, characters, items, locations, notes, tags, moons, arcs, and your manuscript prose. A confirmation dialog shows up before anything is cleared, and there is a Cancel button if you change your mind. Penpoint preserves your Custom calendar configuration when you switch away from it. So if you spent an hour designing a 13-month fantasy calendar, then decide to try Day Counter mode for a chapter, you can switch back to Custom later and find your months, weekdays, and rules exactly as you left them.

For historical fiction set before the modern era, turn on Epochs to display "44 BCE" or "44 BC" instead of just "-44". Penpoint offers two notation styles: BCE / CE: Before Common Era / Common Era. The modern academic standard. BC / AD: Before Christ / Anno Domini. The traditional Christian notation. Click the style you prefer. The change applies to every Calendar block in your book: negative years get the "before" label, positive years get the "after" label. Custom calendars get a richer version of this: pick from BCE/CE-style with your own labels ("Pre-Dragon" / "Post-Dragon") OR full named eras (named periods like "Reign of King Valdris" with their own start years). See Custom Calendar for the full walkthrough.

Moons are available in every calendar mode. Add up to eight orbiting moons for your world, and their phases will appear below every Calendar block date, so you (and your readers, if you reference moons in prose) always know what the night sky looks like.

Click Add moon to create a new moon row, or Add Earth's Moon for an instant ready-made Luna with a real surface image and a 29.53-day cycle. Each moon has these settings: Name: How the moon is labeled in scenes (e.g., "Luna", "Selene", "The Red Sister") Orbit: How many days the moon takes to complete one full cycle. Decimals are allowed: Earth's moon is 29.53 days. On Day 1, Year 1: What phase the moon is in on the very first day of your calendar. Pick from the eight classical phases (New Moon, Waxing Crescent, First Quarter, Waxing Gibbous, Full Moon, Waning Gibbous, Last Quarter, Waning Crescent). Every other date calculates from there. Moon Color: Pick a face color from the palette, or click Use image to upload a custom moon surface (which gets cropped to a circle). On each moon row you'll see a small arrow on the right (click to fold the moon's settings out of the way) and a trash icon (click to delete the moon). Removal is instant: there's no confirmation dialog, so click carefully. The trash icon only deletes the moon definition (your scenes, prose, and dates aren't touched), so the worst case is you re-add the moon and re-pick its color or image.

The Display moons switch at the top of the Moons section controls whether phases appear below every Calendar block date. It turns on automatically when you add your first moon. Turn it off if your moons exist for worldbuilding reference only and you don't want them showing up in scenes. Tip: Each Calendar block also has its own moon settings: you can hide moons on a specific block, choose whether to show each moon's name and current phase next to its picture (or just show the picture, with the name and phase appearing on hover), and pick a moon size. The page-level Display moons switch is the main on/off switch: it controls whether moons show at all; the per-block settings only matter when moons ARE showing.
How Calendar Settings Affect Your Book

Every Calendar block in every scene reads from these settings. A Calendar block is a small date field you can drop into a scene to mark when it happens (a single moment, or a date range). Change Epoch settings here, and they update on every Calendar block at once. Add a moon, and it appears on every date. Note: The Timeline page doesn't show calendar dates. Calendar dates live inside Calendar blocks on individual scenes.

As you change settings, the preview pane on the right side of the page updates instantly. Every Calendar block has two states: Edit Mode (what you see when picking a date in a scene) and View Mode (what shows up afterward in your prose). The preview shows two stacked examples (Edit Mode above View Mode) so you can confirm your changes look right before saving them across your whole book.

When Earth's calendar doesn't fit your world (a fantasy realm with three moons, a generation ship's onboard timekeeping, an alien planet with a 28-hour day), Custom mode lets you redesign every part of the calendar from the ground up. You can rename time units, set how many months are in a year, build your own week, define leap days, and label whole eras with whatever names suit your story. To enable Custom mode, head to Settings > Calendar and pick "Custom Calendar" from the menu at the top of the Calendar Settings page. Penpoint will pop up a confirmation box before switching. Only the dates inside Calendar blocks (small date markers you place in scenes) get cleared; your characters, chapters, notes, moons, and everything else stay safe. Tip: Don't feel like you need to fill in every option. The defaults already match a real-world calendar: start by changing only the parts that matter to your story. You can always come back later.

Time Units lets you give every unit of time its own vocabulary. The defaults (Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute) work for most worlds, but you can rename any of them. Keep names short so they fit cleanly on date displays. A fantasy world might call them Cycles, Moons, Suns, Bells, and Ticks A space station might use Standard Years, Mission Months, Watches An ancient setting might use the original real-world Latin names Below the names, two more fields control the length of a day: Hours per day: Default 24. Set to 28 for a longer day, 16 for a shorter one, or whatever your world demands. Minutes per hour: Default 60. Set to 100 for a decimal-hour world, 50 for shorter hours, etc. Tip: Renaming units only changes labels on date fields and Calendar blocks. The underlying date data stays the same, so you can rename freely without breaking any existing dates you've already entered.
Week Structure controls how many days are in your week, what each weekday is called, and which weekday Day 1, Year 1 falls on. Everything else flows from there.

Set anywhere from 1 day per week up. Most fantasy calendars use somewhere between 5 and 10. As you change the number, weekday name fields appear and disappear to match. Note: Past 14 days per week, the calendar grid in the Calendar block gets cramped on narrow screens. A heads-up warning shows up at this threshold. Your dates still work normally; only the visual layout is affected.

Each weekday gets a name field. Keep names short: each one fits on the same line as the day count. The first weekday in the list is "weekday 1": the default weekday Day 1 of Year 1 lands on (you can change which weekday it lands on with the Anchor Day setting below), and the day every month begins on if you turn off continuous weeks (more on that below).

Day 1, Year 1 has to fall on SOME weekday: pick which one. Penpoint calculates every other weekday in your calendar from this starting point. So if your weekdays are named, say, "Firstday" through "Seventhday", and you anchor Day 1, Year 1 to "Firstday", then Day 2 is "Secondday", and so on.

The Weeks flow continuously across month boundaries switch (continuous weeks) is on by default, just like Earth's calendar, where the last day of January and the first day of February are consecutive weekdays. Turn continuous weeks off for stylized fantasy calendars where every month starts on the same weekday (a per-month reset). This is useful for ritual calendars, where (for example) every month begins on "Firstday" and ends on "Lastday" regardless of where in the year you are. Note: When you turn continuous weeks off, the Anchor Day setting doesn't apply: every month starts on the first weekday in your list automatically. Penpoint dims the Anchor Day picker as a reminder.

Months is where you shape your year. Add as many months as you need, name each one, and set how many days each runs. The total adds up to your year length, displayed in a summary row at the bottom of the section. For each month you can set: Name: Keep names short so they fit cleanly on the calendar grid. Numbered defaults like "Month 1" appear if you don't pick a name. Day count: How many days in the month. Use the up/down arrows or type a number directly. Intercalary (festival-style days that sit outside the normal week): A button that marks the month as a festival period outside the normal weekday cycle (more below).

An intercalary month is a stretch of days that sits outside the normal weekday count. Their days don't shift the weekday cycle: a 5-day intercalary festival doesn't push the next month's weekdays five steps ahead. They're a real-world feature too: the Mayan Wayeb (5 unlucky days at the end of the year), the French Revolutionary calendar's "Sansculottides" (festival days outside the normal months).
