They make a great place for fantasy festivals, mourning periods, or "days out of time." Click the Intercalary button on a month to mark it. Intercalary months are highlighted with a tinted left border and a subtle background so you can spot them at a glance.

When at least one intercalary month exists, an extra switch appears at the bottom of the section: Show intercalary months as separate calendar pages. On: Each intercalary (festival) period gets its own page in the Calendar block's grid view. Useful when the festival is a distinct thing readers should think about as separate from the surrounding months. Off: Intercalary days are appended to the previous month's grid. Useful for short festivals that feel attached to the month before them.

Calendars drift if your year length doesn't match your world's actual orbit. Leap days fix that. Penpoint supports anything from a single extra day every few years to the full real-world Gregorian rule set. Skip this section entirely if your calendar doesn't need leap days (many fantasy calendars don't). But if you have a specific orbital cycle in mind, this is where you encode it.

Click Add leap day to create a new leap day row. Each leap day has these settings: Name: How the leap day appears in scenes (e.g., "Festival Day", "Mid-Summer", "Leap Day"). Attached to: Which month the leap day belongs to. Pick from a dropdown of your existing months. After day: Which day of the month the leap day sits after. Set to 0 to put it BEFORE day 1 of the month. Type: The Intercalary button works the same way as for months: turn it on if the leap day shouldn't shift the weekday cycle. Year offset: Tells Penpoint where your world is in the leap-day cycle. If your last leap day fell three years before your story starts, type -3 here so future leap days fall on the right years.

Under Fires when, every leap day has at least one rule. The default is "Every 4 years": a simple cycle that fires the leap day every fourth year. You can change the number to anything (every 5, every 10, every 1000).

Click + Add exception to layer additional rules. The conditions are evaluated together to decide whether the leap day fires in any given year: Every: A regular firing rule. The leap day fires on these years. Except every: An exception rule. These years cancel out a regular rule. Combine them to get Earth's "every 4, except 100, every 400" pattern. The classic real-world example is three rules together: every 4 years fires the leap day; every 100 years cancels it; every 400 years reinstates it. That gives you Earth's actual leap-year rules. Tip: Don't want to set those three rules by hand? The Use Gregorian preset button at the bottom of the section seeds the full real-world leap-year rule set in one click (every 4 years fires the leap day, every 100 years cancels it, every 400 years reinstates it), attached to your second month after day 28.

Like intercalary months, intercalary leap days don't shift the weekday cycle. Useful for festivals that only happen on leap years (a once-every-four-years celebration, a centennial rite) where you don't want the rest of your weekday math to budge.

The Eras section is where you decide how dates read in your story. Just numbers? A founding-event split like BCE/CE? Full named periods like "Reign of King Valdris"? Pick whichever fits your world. The setting in this section applies to every Calendar Block in the book at once. At the top of the section is a Display style picker with three choices: Plain years: Just numbers, no labels. "Year 5025" or "5025" depending on context. BCE/CE-style: A single before/after split anchored at year 0. You type your own labels: "Pre-Dragon" / "Post-Dragon", "Before the Calling" / "After the Calling", or any other pair you like. Named eras: Full reigns, ages, or epochs. Each era has its own name and start year, and dates inside that era read as "Year 3, Reign of King Valdris" (or one of three other phrasings). Tip: Switching between styles never deletes your work. If you build a list of named eras, then switch to Plain years to see how it reads, your eras stay safely saved; switch back to Named eras to see them again. Same for BCE/CE labels.

BCE/CE means Before Common Era / Common Era, and it works for any one-event split. Use this when your world has one big anchor event that everything else dates from (a founding, a calamity, a deity's arrival). Pick the BCE/CE-style option, then fill in the "before" and "after" names. Keep them short so they fit on date displays. Negative years get the before-label, positive years get the after-label, so "-50" might read as "50 BD" and "100" might read as "100 AD", whatever your world calls them.
Named Eras: Reigns, Ages, and Epochs

Use Named eras when your world tracks time inside named periods: the reigns of monarchs, mythic ages, scholarly epochs. Each era has a name (like "Age of Wonder" or "Reign of King Valdris"), a start year, and an optional duration in years. Every Named eras setup includes a Base era at the top: Penpoint creates it for you and it can't be deleted. The base era is the safety net: any date that doesn't fall inside one of your other eras is labeled with the base era's name. So if your first defined era starts in year 1500, a date in year 200 will read with the base era's name. Rename it to whatever fits your world ("Age of Wonder", "Pre-History", etc.). To add a new era, click + Add era at the bottom of the section. Each new era gets: Name: How the era appears on dates. Up to 28 characters: Penpoint stops you from typing more so date displays don't get cramped. Starts: The year (and optionally month and day) the era begins. Duration: How many years the era lasts. Optional. If you skip this, the era runs until your next era starts (or forever, if it's the last one). Set a duration when you want a defined end, for example a 42-year reign that ends in a known year. Tip: Changing an era's start year shifts its end year along with it, so the duration stays the same. So if you set up "Reign of Valdris" starting in year 1500 with a duration of 42, then later realize it should start in 1490 instead, just change the start year; the duration stays at 42 and the end year shifts to match. Tip: Building a run of consecutive reigns? Once you've set a duration on an era, an Add next era button appears beneath it. Click it and Penpoint creates a new era that starts exactly one year after this one ends, with no arithmetic needed. If you haven't set a duration yet, the button still appears and inserts a new era right after this one in the list; just fill in the start year yourself.

When Named eras is active, a Display style picker appears below the Style picker, with four phrasings to choose from. The picker shows each phrasing using your actual era names, so you can pick the one that reads best for your story: Year 3, Reign of King Valdris: Year first, then era name (the default). Reign of King Valdris, Year 3: Era name first, then year. Year 3 of the Reign of King Valdris: Connected with "of the". 3rd Year of the Reign of King Valdris: Ordinal year ("1st", "2nd", "3rd"). Below the Display style picker is a live Preview row that shows what one of your real eras looks like in the chosen format, so you can confirm it reads right before saving.

New eras get added in the order you create them. If you add them out of chronological order, click Sort by start date at the bottom of the section to put them in proper sequence. The Base era stays at the top; only the others reorder. If two eras don't quite line up (say one era ends in year 550 and the next doesn't start until year 600), the 50-year gap shows up between the eras as a labeled divider ("50 Year Gap"). Dates in that gap fall back to the Base era automatically, so you don't need to define every period of unrecorded time as its own era. Useful for "the lost centuries" or any unrecorded stretch between known reigns. Note: + Add era, Sort by start date, and Reset all eras all sit in a row at the bottom of the section. Add next era appears beneath each individual era. Reset all eras clears every era except the Base era. The change can't be undone, so Penpoint will ask you to confirm with a dialog before anything happens, and you can hit Cancel.
Picking an Era When Editing a Date

When Named eras is active, every Calendar Block date picker shows an Era: selector above the month and year. Click it to jump to a different era; Penpoint takes you to the start of that era so you can pick a date inside it. The year input shows era-relative numbers (Year 3 instead of Year 1503), so you can think in reign-relative years without doing math. Calendar Blocks are the small date fields you drop into scenes. See Calendar Block for everything they can do.

Note: At the bottom of the Calendar Settings page is a Reset to Gregorian defaults button. Your existing Calendar block dates stay put, but they'll read against the Gregorian structure afterward, so a date like "Stormwane 30" won't make sense once the months are renamed. Re-check existing dates after a reset. The button rebuilds every Custom-mode setting from a fresh real-world template: twelve months with their standard names and day counts, seven-day weeks named Monday through Sunday, 24-hour days with 60-minute hours, no leap rules, no era labels. A confirmation dialog asks before any of this happens, with a Cancel button if you change your mind.

Let's walk through building a calendar for a fantasy world: 13 months of 28 days each, plus one "Day Out of Time" intercalary day at year's end, 7-day weeks named after the seven gods of the realm, and a leap day every 4 years on the final festival. Switch to Custom mode. From the menu at the top of the Calendar Settings page, pick "Custom Calendar." Penpoint shows a confirmation dialog with a Cancel button before committing. Only dates inside Calendar blocks get cleared; your chapters, characters, notes, moons, and Custom calendar settings are all untouched. Set Time Units (optional). Leave Year/Month/Day as-is, or rename them. Hours per day: 24. Minutes per hour: 60. Build the week. In Week Structure, set Days per week to 7. Rename each weekday after a god (say, Solday, Lunaday, Marsday, Mercuriday, Jupiterday, Veneriday, Saturday). Pick the anchor weekday for Day 1, Year 1: Solday is a fitting choice. Build the months. In Months, set Months per year to 14. Name the first 13 with your world's month names, each with 28 days. Name month 14 "Day Out of Time" with 1 day, and click its Intercalary button. Total days in a year: 365 (13 × 28 = 364, plus 1). Add a leap day (optional). In Leap Days, click Add leap day. Name it "Long Festival." Attach it to month 14 (Day Out of Time), after day 1. Leave the default rule "Every 4 years." Pick a date-label style (optional). In the Eras section's Display style picker, choose BCE/CE-style if your world has one big founding event (then fill in your before/after labels, like "Pre-Sundering" / "Post-Sundering"). Choose Named eras if you'd rather track time inside named periods like "Reign of King Valdris" or "Age of Wonder." Or leave it on Plain years if you don't need labels at all. Check the preview pane. The right side of the page shows live Edit Mode (what you see when picking a date in a scene) and View Mode (what shows up afterward in your prose) examples using your new calendar. Pick a date in the preview to see how it formats.

Every Calendar block in every scene reads from your custom settings. Add a Calendar block to any scene, switch into Edit Mode, and writers will pick dates using YOUR weekdays, YOUR months, YOUR era labels. The grid picker (the calendar grid that pops up when picking a date) shows your week structure; the date displays use your unit names. Ready to start designing? Head to Settings > Calendar and pick Custom Calendar from the menu at the top of the Calendar Settings page. For a refresher on calendar modes, eras, and moons (which work the same way across all modes), see Calendar Settings.

Penpoint Cloud keeps an encrypted copy of every book in the cloud. If something happens to your computer, sign in on another one and bring your books back. It's built right into Penpoint, so backing up is automatic.

Keeps your books safe: every book and every version, backed up automatically. Lost laptop, dead hard drive: your work is still there. Write on more than one computer: Penpoint Sync copies your latest writing between them (that's what "syncing" means), so a book stays the same everywhere you sign in. Private encryption: your books stay yours alone. You protect them with a password, and everything is encrypted on your computer before it leaves. Penpoint stores your books but cannot read them, and neither can anyone else. If you forget your password, your Recovery Kit is your backup (a 12-word phrase you save when you set up Cloud; see Your Password and Recovery Kit below).

Penpoint Cloud comes in two sizes: Penpoint Backup ($5/month or $45/year): encrypted cloud backup from one computer at a time, with unlimited version history (go back to any earlier draft of your book). Penpoint Sync ($10/month or $96/year): everything in Backup, plus up to 5 computers kept in step automatically, plus the Penpoint phone app. Penpoint itself is yours forever, one payment, and works completely offline. Penpoint Cloud is optional.

Setting Up Penpoint Cloud: Creating your account, choosing a plan, and saving your Recovery Kit Your Password and Recovery Kit: How your books are encrypted, and what to do if you forget your password Managing Your Subscription: Choosing a plan, switching plans, and canceling or resuming Managing Your Devices: Adding computers, switching your active device, and removing devices Syncing and Restoring: How sync works, version history, and restoring from the cloud Penpoint Cloud Settings: The Penpoint Cloud settings panel

Your books live on your computer first. Penpoint Cloud copies them to a secure online backup. Setup ends with a Recovery Kit: think of it as a spare key, 12 words you save somewhere safe rather than memorize.

Open Settings > Penpoint Cloud and click Set up Penpoint Cloud. Enter your email address and Penpoint sends you a 6-digit code. Check your inbox (and your spam folder, just in case) and enter the code.

There are two plans. Penpoint Backup keeps a secure online copy of your books. Penpoint Sync does that and also keeps your books in step across more than one computer. Both are available monthly or yearly (yearly saves around 20-25%). Penpoint then opens checkout in your browser; complete the purchase and it detects it automatically. If it does not show up right away, give it a moment and try again. See Managing Your Subscription for a full comparison of the two plans. Tip: You can change or cancel your plan at any time in Penpoint Cloud settings.

This password encrypts your books (it scrambles them into a secret code so no one else can read them) before they leave your computer. It is not a login password. Penpoint never receives this password, so no one, including Penpoint, can reset it for you. There are two separate secrets: the emailed code signs you in, and this password unlocks your books on this computer. Choose something you will remember, and save it in a password manager Minimum 8 characters, no special character requirements You enter it once per computer, then Penpoint remembers it securely. Note: Important: if you ever forget this password with no saved Recovery Kit and no computer still signed in, no one can recover your backups, including Penpoint. So save your password now, and your Recovery Kit in the next step. Your books on this computer are never affected either way.

Penpoint generates a 12-word Recovery Kit. If you ever forget your password, this is your way back into your backups. You can download, copy, or print it Store it somewhere other than this computer, like a password manager or a printout You must confirm you have saved it before finishing setup You will only see it once during setup, but you can download a fresh one at any time from Penpoint Cloud settings (a new one replaces the old, so discard old copies)

Penpoint uploads encrypted copies of your books. You can keep writing. If you close the app or put your computer to sleep, the backup picks up where it left off. See Your Password and Recovery Kit for more on how encryption works and what to do if you forget your password.

Your books on this computer are always safe, no matter what happens with the cloud. They are the originals; cloud sync is just a copy. Penpoint Cloud keeps your writing private: before a book leaves your computer it is encrypted with a password only you know (scrambled so it is unreadable without it). Neither Penpoint nor anyone else can read it. Three things sound similar: your password unlocks your books, the sign-in code emailed to you proves it is you, and your Recovery Kit is a spare key for forgotten passwords.
How Your Password Protects Your Books

You create your password once at setup and enter it once per device; it never leaves your computer, and Penpoint remembers it securely. For shared computers, you can require it every time you open Penpoint.

The Recovery Kit is a 12-word phrase generated at setup, a spare key you do not memorize. If you forget your password and get signed out of the cloud, it gets you back into your backups. Store it somewhere safe: a password manager (an app that remembers passwords for you), a printout, or another device. Not just on this computer. Changing your password does not change your Recovery Kit; it keeps working. While a computer stays signed in, re-download a fresh Kit from Penpoint Cloud settings; the old one stops working, so discard old copies.

Open Settings > Penpoint Cloud, click Change password, enter your current one, and choose a replacement. Your Recovery Kit keeps working. Other signed-in devices keep working; they pick up the new password when next they need it.

Open Settings > Penpoint Cloud and click Change Email. Penpoint sends a 6-digit code to your current address and another to the new one; enter both to confirm. Nobody is signed out: your devices stay signed in under the new address. Your books, subscription, and Recovery Kit are all unchanged.
What If I Forget My Password?

Note: Important: your books on this computer are never affected. The risk is your cloud backups: with no saved Kit and no signed-in computer, no one can recover them, not even Penpoint. So save your password and Recovery Kit somewhere safe.
On the password screen, click "Use your Recovery Kit." Enter the 12 words and choose a new password. Done.
I Forgot My Password but a Device Is Still Signed In
If a computer still has Penpoint Cloud unlocked, your books are safe there; change your password from its settings.
I Lost Both My Password and My Recovery Kit

Your books on this computer are always safe. But with no computer still signed in, the cloud copy cannot be unlocked: only you ever had the key. The way forward: sign in with your email, use the "Forgot your password and lost your Recovery Kit?" link, and set a new password. Penpoint clears the old cloud copy (unreadable anyway) and re-uploads from your computer. You lose your cloud version history (older cloud snapshots kept as extra backups) but not your book or chapters. Tip: If you no longer have access to your computer either, check whether you had a Secondary Backup enabled (Penpoint saving copies of your books to a cloud drive such as Dropbox, OneDrive, or iCloud). Those backup files are independent of Penpoint Cloud and can be used to recover your books. See Backup & Restore for details.
Penpoint Cloud is an optional paid subscription, separate from your one-time purchase. Your books always live on your computer; the cloud is an extra copy.

What Happens If My Payment Fails

Your local books are never affected. Syncing pauses; your cloud data follows the same 30-day grace as a cancellation, then permanently deletes. To update your payment method, open Settings > Penpoint Cloud and click Card and billing details. Your local books are always safe regardless of how you manage your devices. Nothing in this screen deletes any writing from any computer. Every computer you sign in to Penpoint Cloud on becomes a registered device: one the app remembers, whether or not it is currently backing up.

Penpoint Backup: one active device at a time. Your active device is the one computer that sends your books to the cloud. Other registered computers save locally but do not back up. Penpoint Sync: up to 5 devices, all syncing automatically. Both plans allow up to 5 registered devices.

Install Penpoint on the computer and sign in with the same email you used during setup. Enter your password, or your Recovery Kit if you have forgotten it (the 12-word phrase you saved when you set up Penpoint Cloud; see Your Password and Recovery Kit). The device then appears in your device list. If you are on Penpoint Sync, it starts syncing immediately. If you are on Penpoint Backup, it registers but does not back up unless you make it the active device.

Penpoint Backup only. To change which computer backs up to the cloud: Open Settings > Penpoint Cloud, click Manage devices, and click Make this the active device on the computer you want to use. Your first activation is free and does not count toward the limit. After that, each active-device switch counts toward your two. You can switch up to 2 times per rolling 30-day window. If you switch twice, a slot opens again about 30 days after the first of those two moves. Replacing a dead computer uses one switch, but a used switch always comes back, so you are never stranded. If you get stuck sooner, email support@penpoint.app and we can help.

Removing a device signs that computer out of Penpoint Cloud. No books are deleted when you remove a device. Open Settings > Penpoint Cloud, click Manage devices, and click the trash icon next to the device you want to remove. You can remove the device you are currently using; it stops backing up until you sign in again. If you have reached your device limit, remove one before adding another.
Click the pencil icon next to any device to give it a recognizable label for your reference, such as "Desktop" or "Laptop".
What If This Computer Isn't Backing Up?

If you are on Penpoint Backup and this computer is not the active device, Penpoint Cloud settings say so at the top, under Backup health: "This computer is not backing up", with an Activate this computer button that takes you straight to your device list. Your local books are always safe and local backups keep running.
Penpoint Cloud backs up your books automatically. Your work is copied safely to the cloud as you write, and kept in step across all your computers, so you never have to remember to save or upload.

Books save to the cloud automatically when you close a book or quit the app While you write, sync runs shortly after you stop typing, and at least every five minutes during continuous writing You can also sync manually: click the Saved indicator (the word "Saved" next to a small cloud check mark, in the toolbar) and choose "Sync now", or open the cloud status menu at the top of your Book Library and choose "Sync now" Your entire library syncs to every device, so every book is available offline on each machine The word Saved always means your writing is safe on this computer. The small mark beside it shows how your cloud is doing: a plain checkmark means your cloud is catching up, and a checkmark with a little cloud means that book has landed there too. If you are offline, keep writing. Everything saves on this computer as usual, and your cloud catches up on its own when you are back online. The Saved indicator shows two clocks: one for the copy on this computer, one for your cloud. They often differ, and that is normal, not a sign anything is broken. The local clock is the timestamp of a backup file your computer writes at intervals, so it can lag; your cloud copy still updates about half a minute after you stop typing, so nothing is at risk. "Sync now" refreshes both in one press. Penpoint Cloud does not replace your local backups. Your existing backup settings (automatic backups, secondary backup to a cloud folder) keep working as before; Penpoint Cloud is simply an extra online backup, stored separately from your computer.

Every book has unlimited cloud version history for as long as you subscribe. Versions are grouped by time: Today, Yesterday, This month, This year, and Earlier. The cloud keeps approximately hourly snapshots. For finer undo between them, use your local backups on that computer. Before restoring, a read-only preview shows word counts and your latest chapters, characters, locations, and items, so you can confirm it is the right version.

To restore an earlier version, go to your Book Library, right-click the book (or Ctrl+click on Mac, or click its three-dot menu), and choose Restore from Backup. The browser has two tabs: "On this computer" for local backups, and "Cloud" for cloud versions. Pick a version, then restore as an overwrite or as a separate book. Overwriting saves your current version first, so you can always get it back, then replaces your book with the one you selected. To recover a book that is not on this computer (one you deleted, or one that has not finished arriving), use the Restore from Cloud option in the cloud status menu at the top of the Book Library. For more on local backups and restore options, see Backup & Restore.
Bringing Your Books to Another Computer

Enter your email address and Penpoint sends you a 6-digit code to sign in with. Then type your Penpoint Cloud password, the one you created when you set Cloud up, to unlock your books. Your library appears automatically, and Penpoint downloads your books in the background; you can start on any book as soon as its download finishes.

Changes made on different devices merge automatically when they do not overlap. When they do overlap, nothing is thrown away. For a worldbuilding detail like a character's age, the most recent edit becomes the live value, and Penpoint saves a "Before sync" backup on this computer just before merging, so the earlier value is still there in Restore from Backup. For a scene changed on two devices, your newest writing stays in the manuscript and the other version is kept in Scene Drafts. If a scene was edited on one device and deleted on the other, the edited scene comes back: the deletion does not win, and its writing is kept in Scene Drafts as well. Penpoint tells you when this has happened, with Edited on another device. It appears in three places: your Book Library shelf, Settings under Backup health, and the Saved indicator menu while the book is open. On the shelf and in the Saved indicator menu it is a short notice you can click, and clicking it takes you to Settings under Backup health. That is the library-wide list: every affected book, and every scene inside it, each one clickable to open the comparison. Inside the book, you will see a message titled A scene was changed on two devices (or Some scenes were changed on two devices). It names the first few scenes, marks any that were deleted on one device but still had writing on another with "deleted, but iPhone still had writing in it" (naming that device, or "another device" if Penpoint does not know its name), and says nothing was lost: your newest writing is in your manuscript and everything else is saved in Drafts. Choose Review It (Review Them when there are several) to step through the scenes one at a time, or Keep Everything As Is to leave your manuscript alone; the other versions stay in Scene Drafts either way. Until you have looked at a scene's second version, a small amber stack icon sits at the right end of its row in the Manuscript outline (a chapter row shows it when one of its scenes has one). Its tooltip reads "Another version of this scene is in Drafts. Click to compare." (or "This scene was deleted, but iPhone still had writing in it, so Penpoint kept it. Click to review." for a scene that was deleted on one device but still had writing on another). Clicking it opens just that scene's comparison. The icon disappears once you have looked. The comparison shows your manuscript on the right, titled In your manuscript, and the other device's version on the left. Whichever was edited later is tagged Newer. A bar under the two sides has a legend that marks what is "Only in the other version" and "Only in your manuscript", and the change arrows ("Change 2 of 5") step through the differences with both sides scrolling together. The version you don't keep stays in Drafts. Choose Keep This One to leave your manuscript as it is, which also clears that scene's amber icon. Or choose Use This Version to switch: Penpoint asks you to confirm, saves your current version in Drafts first, and lands you back in your scene. If you started with Review Them, "Scene 2 of 5" arrows at the top move through the scenes, and Keep This One moves on to the next; switching ends the tour, and scenes you have not reached keep their amber icons. If the scene was deleted on one device, you see only the scene Penpoint kept, with Keep the Scene or Delete It Again. A version with no writing in it is marked as seen when the book opens, so it does not raise the notice; if you open one anyway, it says This version is empty and cannot be restored.

Deleting a synced book does not erase it right away. It removes the book from your active cloud library, which is exactly what moves it into a 30-day recovery window: for a full 30 days you can bring it back from the Restore from Cloud browser. Before deleting, Penpoint also offers to export a backup file as an extra safety net. Your secondary backup folder (if you set one up) is never touched by a delete

You can temporarily stop Cloud on this computer from Settings > Penpoint Cloud by clicking Pause Penpoint Cloud on this computer. Your local books are unaffected and keep saving normally. Click Resume Penpoint Cloud when you are ready; you do not need to enter your password again.
The Penpoint Cloud settings panel is located in Settings > Penpoint Cloud. It is the central place to manage your cloud backup, subscription, account, and devices.

The Backup health section shows how many books are backed up and how many need attention, such as a sync conflict or a failed upload. Books needing attention show a cloud icon on their cover. Sync means your books stay identical everywhere, so a change on one computer appears in the cloud and on the rest. A status line shows whether your books are up to date, with a Sync now button to sync manually.

Shows your plan, billing period, and renewal date. You can switch to yearly billing, cancel or resume, and open Card and billing details to update your card and billing address in your browser. See Managing Your Subscription for details on the two plans and how to change or cancel.

The Account card shows your Penpoint Cloud email and gives you: Your Password and Recovery Kit: change your password Re-download Recovery Kit: replaces the Recovery Kit you saved during setup with a fresh one. Any signed-in computer can make a new one here Change Email: update your Penpoint Cloud account email

The devices card lets you: Manage devices: see which computers are signed in, rename them, or remove old ones Pause Penpoint Cloud on this computer: pauses cloud backup and sync here until you choose Resume. Your local books keep saving normally, and resuming does not require your password. Ask for my password each time I open Penpoint: off by default. Turn it on to lock your cloud backups behind your password at every launch, useful on a shared computer. Sync my settings across all my computers: your theme, fonts, quote style, Note Templates, Your Dictionary, and other preferences follow you across your devices Sign out of Penpoint Cloud: signs this computer out. There are two options for removing your cloud data. Permanently erase all cloud backups: your local books are never affected. This deletes every cloud backup, with no undo. It is the smaller action: your account and subscription stay active, so you can back up again later. Close my Penpoint Cloud account entirely: your local books are never affected. This is the larger, final step: it deletes your cloud data, cancels your subscription, and removes your account. Locked out? If you forgot your password with no saved Recovery Kit and no signed-in computer, erasing your cloud backups is how to start fresh: it clears the old encrypted data so you can set a new password and back up again.
What Happens to My Data If I Cancel?

If you cancel, syncing stops at the end of the period you paid for, and the cloud copy is kept for 30 days after that: those days keep your data safe, but they don't hold the plan open, because a canceled subscription can't be restarted once the paid time has run out. After the 30 days, your cloud data is deleted by destroying the encryption key that unlocks it, so it can never be read or rebuilt again (Penpoint sends warning emails first); Choose a plan comes back then, and starting again means a new password and a fresh upload from this computer. A subscription that lapsed because a payment failed is the different case: update your card in Card and billing details and the cloud copy picks up where it left off, same password, nothing to re-upload. If you close your account entirely, your account record and email are removed immediately, and your cloud data is gone within 24 hours. Because your books are encrypted with a key only you hold, once it is gone nothing is left to recover. Your local books are never affected by cancellation or account closure. They stay on your computer and keep working offline as always.

Some writing goals come with a date on the calendar. The guides in this section pair a particular event with the Penpoint tools that fit it, so you can get set up quickly and spend the rest of your time writing.

Writing a Novel in a Month with Penpoint: A planning checklist, a daily routine for 1,667 words a day, and how to finish with a draft you can export. Note: Looking for the Events you log on characters, items, and locations? Those are moments in your story. See Events.
Writing a Novel in a Month with Penpoint
Writing a Novel in a Month with Penpoint

Fifty thousand words in thirty days comes to 1,667 words a day. That is a real pace, but it is a steady one, and a little preparation makes it much easier to keep. This guide is a checklist for the whole month: what to set up beforehand, what to do each day, and how to be sure your draft is safe when you finish. It fits Novel November, any 50,000-word challenge, or a month-long deadline you set for yourself.

Preptober: set up your book, your cast, your places, and a loose chapter outline. Pick your daily number (1,667 words) and watch it in your writing stats. Draft in Manuscript Mode. Write first; worldbuild later. Save a snapshot each week, and let backups protect the rest. When you finish, export a Word file.

Preptober is the planning month before the writing starts. You do not need a finished plan. You need just enough that you never sit down to a blank page wondering what happens next. Create your book: Creating Your First Book. Choose a starting template that fits your genre (Understanding Book Template Types); you can change everything later. Meet your cast: Characters. Start with the people in your first few scenes and add the rest as they turn up. Map your places: Locations. A few key places are plenty to begin with. Gather your ideas: the Notebook holds research, the rules of your world, and loose thoughts in one place. Outline your chapters and scenes: Creating Chapters and Scenes builds the structure. The Corkboard lays your chapters out as index cards you can rearrange, and Placeholder Cards hold a spot for chapters you have not figured out yet. The outline carries straight into the writing: the chapters and scenes you plan are the ones you write in Manuscript Mode. Tip: Plan in scenes, not just chapters. If a scene runs around 1,500 to 2,000 words, one scene a day carries you to the finish line.

Pick your number before day one. For 50,000 words in 30 days it is 1,667 a day. These checkpoints keep you honest: Day 7: about 11,700 words Day 14: about 23,300 words Day 21: about 35,000 words Day 28: about 46,700 words Day 30: 50,000 words Penpoint keeps count for you. Click the bar chart icon in the toolbar at the top of the screen to open your writing stats. Under Today, Manuscript shows the words you have added to your manuscript so far today. That is the number to compare with 1,667. Worldbuilding words are counted separately, so planning notes never pad your total. Below it, Manuscript size shows how long your book is. If you use Penpoint Cloud on more than one device, Today also counts the words your other devices have already sent to the cloud, so give it a few minutes after writing on one before checking another. Penpoint's writing day starts at 4 AM, so a late night of writing stays in one day. If you start right after midnight on November 1, the words you write before 4 AM count toward October 31, and your November count starts at 4 AM. Those early words are not lost: they are saved under October 31, so add them to your own total if you are counting toward 50,000. In Manuscript Mode, the bar along the bottom of the writing area shows the word count of whatever you are viewing. Click it to add your Book's total and watch the number climb toward 50,000. See Manuscript Mode. Your Writing Journey, in the same panel, counts your current streak and your longest streak of consecutive writing days. Week two is where many drafts stall, and a short day still keeps a streak going. On a bad day, write something small and stop. To see how long you actually spend writing, start the writing timer from the clock at the top of the screen. See Tracking Your Time.
Your Daily Routine: Write First, Worldbuild Later

The month goes better when drafting and planning stay separate. Draft first. Fix the world afterward. Draft in Manuscript Mode: click Manuscript, the pen icon at the top of the left sidebar, to switch to the writing side, where your planned chapters and scenes are waiting. Keep your world beside you: Minipen is the sidebar that shows your characters, locations, and notes next to the page, so checking a name or a detail never means leaving your draft. Do not stop to build: when someone turns up unexpectedly, press Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on Mac) to open Quick Create and jot them down, then keep writing. Fill in the details after the month ends. Quick Add Menu shows how it works. Write in sprints: Flowstate runs timed cycles of writing and editing, and locks each finished sentence behind you so you keep moving forward instead of revising. The default is 15 minutes of writing and 5 of editing, and you can change both. Go fullscreen: click Fullscreen Mode in the bottom-left corner of the writing area (or press F11 on Windows and Linux) to hide the toolbar and sidebars and leave just your page. Fullscreen Mode and Flowstate work independently, so use either, both, or neither.

Autosave: Penpoint saves as you type. There is no save button to remember. Automatic backups: Penpoint backs up your books on its own and lets you restore an earlier copy. Backup & Restore covers how to keep a second copy in a Dropbox, OneDrive, or iCloud folder. Weekly snapshots: at the end of each week, click the Manuscript versions button in the Manuscript toolbar and save a snapshot with a note like “Week 1, 11,700 words.” A snapshot is a read-only copy of your whole manuscript that you can open and copy text from, and you can keep up to 10 per book. See Manuscript Snapshots. Before a big rewrite: Scene Drafts save alternate takes of a scene without losing the original.

Penpoint Cloud keeps an encrypted copy of your books online and, with the Sync plan, keeps the same book up to date across your devices. It is optional, and your books always live on your own computer first. During Novel November 2026, Penpoint offers a free month of Cloud: What you get: the full Penpoint Sync plan, with no card needed. Who can claim it: accounts that do not already have a subscription. When it ends: December 1, 2026 at 12:00 UTC, whenever you start. After that: Cloud pauses on your devices. Subscribe to keep it going; otherwise your cloud copy is kept for 30 days and then deleted. The books on your computer always stay yours. To claim it, open Settings > Penpoint Cloud and choose Set up Penpoint Cloud. When you are eligible, the plan step shows a card offering Cloud free until December 1, with a Start now button, instead of the usual plans. See Setting Up Penpoint Cloud for the full walkthrough and Managing Your Subscription for plans and canceling. Note: Cloud is separate from the free trial download. The trial is Penpoint itself; Cloud is an optional online service with its own account. If you do not see Penpoint Cloud in your Settings, your copy does not include it, and everything else in this guide works without it. Tip: If you set up Cloud, save your Recovery Kit. It is the spare key to your encrypted books. See Your Password and Recovery Kit.

When you reach your number, or the month runs out, export the draft. In Manuscript Mode, click the Export manuscript button in the toolbar at the top of the writing area and choose a format. Word (.docx) is the safe pick because it opens almost everywhere; EPUB, PDF, Markdown, plain text, and RTF are there too. Exporting never changes your manuscript. See Exporting Manuscripts. A finished draft is a first draft. Step away for a while; your snapshots and drafts will be waiting when you come back to revise.

If you are trying Penpoint for Novel November, it is free to use through December 1, 2026, with the whole app unlocked and no account or card needed. After that, Penpoint is a one-time $40 purchase that keeps everything: your books, your settings, and every feature. Your books stay on your computer either way, and you can export them whenever you like, even after the trial ends. If you already own Penpoint, none of this applies to you, and the rest of the guide does. Note: Penpoint is not affiliated with any writing organization.
